topics.title: Making an electromagnet
topics.summary: A current in a coil of wire makes a magnet you can switch on and off — and make stronger.

images.caption: A simple electromagnet: a coil of wire round an iron nail, joined to a cell and a switch.

table.title: What changes the strength of an electromagnet?
head: Change
Effect on strength

facts: A **current** flowing through a wire makes a **magnetic field** around the wire. Every electromagnet is built on this idea.
Winding the wire into a tight **coil** — a **solenoid** — concentrates the field. The coil behaves like a **bar magnet**, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other.
Put a **core** of **soft iron** inside the coil and the magnet becomes **much stronger**. Iron is magnetised easily and **loses its magnetism** as soon as the current stops.
An **electromagnet** is a magnet you can **switch on and off** by switching the current on and off.
**Make it stronger:** a **bigger current**, **more turns** (coils) of wire, and an **iron core**. A core of copper, aluminium or wood does not help — they are not magnetic.
Turn the cell round and the current flows the other way: the **poles swap over**.
Like every magnet, its field gets **weaker further away** — paper clips are only picked up close to the core.

**Investigating strength:** count how many paper clips it holds. Change **one** thing (say, the number of turns) and keep the rest the same — current, core, the same clips. A big current makes the wire **hot**, so switch off between readings.
This builds on Year 7 circuits: a bigger potential difference (more cells) pushes a bigger current, which makes a stronger electromagnet.

topics.title: Electromagnets at work
topics.summary: Why some devices use electromagnets and others permanent magnets — bells, cranes, circuit breakers and loudspeakers.

images.caption: An electric bell: the electromagnet pulls the armature, and the contact opens and closes many times a second.

table.title: Permanent magnet or electromagnet?
head: Permanent magnet
Electromagnet
rows: yes, all the time it is on

facts: A **permanent magnet** is magnetic **all the time**: it needs no power, but you **cannot switch it off** or change its strength.
An **electromagnet** can be **switched on and off**, and its strength **changed** by changing the current — but it needs a current (and uses energy) the whole time it is on.

**Choose an electromagnet** when you need to **let go** or switch: scrapyard cranes, electric door locks, bells, circuit breakers, relays. **Choose a permanent magnet** when it must work **with no electricity**: fridge door seals, cupboard catches, compasses.
**Scrapyard crane:** current on — it lifts a steel car; current off — the car drops. It cannot lift aluminium, which is not magnetic, so it also sorts metals.

**Electric bell:** press the switch → current flows → the electromagnet pulls the **iron armature** → the **hammer** hits the **gong** → the armature moves off the **contact screw**, breaking the circuit → the magnet switches off → the **spring** pulls the armature back → the circuit is complete again… over and over.

**Circuit breaker:** if the current gets too big, an electromagnet becomes strong enough to pull an iron catch, a spring flicks the switch **open** and the current stops. Unlike a fuse, you just **reset** it.
**Loudspeaker:** a **changing current** in a coil makes a changing magnetic field. A **permanent magnet** pushes and pulls the coil, so the cone **vibrates** and makes sound waves.
**Relay:** a small current in one circuit works an electromagnet that closes a switch in a second circuit carrying a **big** current — like a car's starter motor.

**Improving a design:** more turns, a bigger current or an iron core make it stronger; a smaller gap helps too. But a bigger current wastes more energy heating the wire and runs batteries down faster.

topics.title: Magnets, poles and magnetic materials
topics.summary: The two poles of a magnet, which materials are magnetic, and how the force changes with distance.
facts: Every magnet has two **poles**: a **north-seeking pole (N)** and a **south-seeking pole (S)**. The magnetic force is **strongest at the poles**.
**Like poles repel** (N and N, S and S). **Unlike poles attract** (N and S). It sounds like the rule for charges in Year 7 — but magnetic poles and electric charges are different things.
**Magnetic force** is a **non-contact force**: it acts across a gap, and even through paper, plastic, wood or water.

**Magnetic materials** are attracted by a magnet: **iron, nickel and cobalt**, and **steel** (which is mostly iron). Most metals are **not** magnetic — copper, aluminium, gold, silver, brass — and neither are non-metals.
A magnet **attracts** a magnetic material with **either** pole. Only **another magnet** can be **repelled**: **repulsion is the test** for a magnet.

A **permanent magnet** is magnetic all the time. A piece of iron near a magnet becomes an **induced magnet** — it is only magnetic while the magnet is close. That is how a chain of paper clips hangs from a magnet.
The force is **bigger** when the magnet is **stronger**, and when the object is **closer**. It falls off quickly as the distance grows.
Cut a bar magnet in half and you get **two smaller magnets**, each with its own N and S pole. You can never get a single pole on its own.

topics.title: Magnetic fields and field lines
topics.summary: Drawing field lines to show the direction and strength of a magnetic field, around one magnet and two.

images.caption: The field round a bar magnet: lines go from N to S and are closest at the poles.
Two magnets: unlike poles attract, like poles repel and leave a neutral point between them.

facts: A **magnetic field** is the space around a magnet where a magnetic material, or another magnet, feels a force.
We show it with **field lines**. Arrows on them point **from the north-seeking pole to the south-seeking pole** (outside the magnet).
**Lines close together = strong field.** They crowd together at the poles and spread out further away, where the field is weaker.
Field lines **never cross**, and every line runs from an N pole to an S pole.
**Iron filings** sprinkled on paper over a magnet line up along the field lines: they show the **shape** of the field, but not its direction.

A **plotting compass** shows the **direction**: its needle lines up with the field, its N end pointing the way the arrows go. Mark where it points, move it on, mark again, then join the dots to draw a line.
**Unlike poles facing (N and S):** the lines run **straight across** the gap from N to S — a strong field, and the magnets **attract**.
**Like poles facing (N and N):** the lines **bend away** from each other. Between them is a **neutral point** where the two fields cancel: no force there. The magnets **repel**.
A steel ball rolled past a magnet **curves towards it** — most sharply where it passes closest, where the lines are crowded. An aluminium ball rolls straight on.

topics.title: Earth's magnetic field and compasses
topics.summary: Why a compass points north, and how walkers, sailors and pilots use it to find their way.

images.caption: Earth's field is shaped as if a giant bar magnet were inside it. A compass lines up with the field and points north.

facts: The Earth has a **magnetic field**, made by molten iron moving in its **core**. Its shape is like the field of a **giant bar magnet**.
A **compass** needle is a tiny **magnet** that can turn freely. It lines up with Earth's field lines, and its north-seeking end points towards the **Arctic**.

Unlike poles attract — so the magnetic pole under the Arctic is really a **south-seeking** pole. That is why it pulls the compass's **north-seeking** end. (That is also why the N pole is called *north-seeking*: it seeks the north.)
Outside the Earth the field lines run from the **Antarctic** end up to the **Arctic** end, just as they run from N to S round a bar magnet.
**Magnetic north** is not exactly at the **geographic North Pole** (true north). It is a few hundred kilometres away and slowly **moves**, so maps give a small correction.
**Navigation:** with a map and a compass you can find your direction in fog, at night or at sea, with **no batteries and no signal**.
Keep a compass away from **magnets**, **iron and steel** and **wires carrying a current** — they have fields of their own and pull the needle the wrong way.
Earth's field is **weak** at the surface — much weaker than a fridge magnet — but it surrounds the whole planet. Birds and sea turtles use it to find their way.
The field also **steers charged particles from the Sun** towards the poles, where they make the glowing **Northern Lights**.

topics.title: Energy resources
topics.summary: Where our electricity comes from: renewable and non-renewable resources, and how a power station works.

images.caption: A fuel-burning power station: the fuel heats water, the steam spins a turbine, the turbine turns a generator, and power lines carry the electricity to homes.

table.title: Some energy resources
head: Resource

facts: An **energy resource** is anything with stored energy that we can release in a useful way — a fuel, the wind, moving water or sunlight.
**Fossil fuels** — **coal**, **crude oil** and **natural gas** — formed over millions of years from the remains of plants and animals that lived long ago.
**Non-renewable** resources cannot be replaced, so they will run out one day: the fossil fuels and **nuclear** fuel (uranium).

**Renewable** resources are replaced naturally and will not run out: **solar**, **wind**, **waves**, **tides**, **hydroelectric** (water falling from a dam), **geothermal** (heat from hot rocks underground) and **biomass** (wood, crops, animal waste).

In most power stations a **fuel** is burned to **boil water**. The **steam** spins a **turbine**, the turbine turns a **generator**, and the generator makes the electricity. **Power lines** (the National Grid) carry it to our homes.
Wind, wave, tidal and hydroelectric power stations turn the turbine **directly**, with no fuel and no boiler. **Solar cells** turn light straight into electricity.
Burning fossil fuels gives off **carbon dioxide**, a greenhouse gas that adds to **climate change**. Burning coal also gives off gases that cause **acid rain**.
Every resource has **advantages and disadvantages**, so the UK uses a **mix**: gas power stations can be turned up quickly when everyone puts the kettle on, but wind and solar depend on the weather.

When **demand** for electricity rises, a country can build more power stations (ideally renewable), store energy for calm, dark days, and help people **use less** — better insulation and more efficient devices.

topics.title: Paying for electricity
topics.summary: Power, kilowatt-hours and how to work out what a device costs to run.

table.title: Typical powers of devices at home
head: Device
Power in W
Power in kW

facts: **Power** is how quickly a device transfers energy. It is measured in **watts (W)**. A 2000 W heater transfers 2000 joules every second — twice as fast as a 1000 W heater.
**1 kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W.** To change watts into kilowatts, divide by 1000: 60 W = 0.06 kW.
We pay for electricity by the **amount of energy** we use, measured in **kilowatt-hours (kWh)**. 1 kWh is the energy a 1 kW device transfers in 1 hour. Bills call it a **unit**.
**Energy (kWh) = power (kW) × time (hours).** Change minutes into hours first: 30 minutes = 0.5 h, 6 minutes = 0.1 h.
**Cost = power (kW) × time (hours) × price per kWh.** A 2 kW heater for 3 hours at 25p per kWh: 2 × 3 × 25 = **150p = £1.50**.
Devices that **heat** things — showers, kettles, heaters, ovens, tumble dryers — have the highest powers, so they cost the most to run.
**Filament bulbs** waste most of their energy heating the surroundings. **Fluorescent** (energy-saving) and **LED** bulbs give the same light for a much smaller power, so they are far cheaper to run.
A meter counts the kWh used. **Units used = new reading − old reading.**
To cut a bill: switch devices off rather than leaving them on **standby**, use LED bulbs, take shorter showers, boil only the water you need, dry clothes outside, and turn the heating down a degree.

topics.title: Energy in food and activities

images.caption: A food label gives the energy per 100 g and per portion, in kilojoules (kJ) and kilocalories (kcal).

table.title: Energy an adult transfers in different activities (rough figures)
head: Activity
kJ per minute

facts: Food is a **store of energy** — a **chemical store**. Your body releases the energy in **respiration**.
The unit of energy is the **joule (J)**. **1 kilojoule (kJ) = 1000 J.**
**Food labels** give the energy in food in **kilojoules (kJ)**, usually with **kilocalories (kcal)** beside it.
Labels show energy **per 100 g**, so you can compare foods fairly, and **per portion**, so you know what you actually eat.
Fatty foods store the most energy: a gram of **fat** holds about twice as much as a gram of carbohydrate or protein.
The more active you are, the more energy you transfer each minute: **running** uses several times as much as **sitting**.
Even asleep your body needs energy to keep your **heart beating**, to **breathe** and to **keep warm** (about 37 °C).
If you take in **more** energy than you use, the body stores the extra as **fat**; if you take in **less**, it uses up its stores.
UK labels compare food with an adult's **reference intake** of 8400 kJ a day. Growing teenagers and very active people need more.

topics.title: Energy stores
topics.summary: The energy stores that fill and empty when something happens — thermal, chemical, kinetic, gravitational potential and elastic.

images.caption: Five everyday examples, each with energy in a different store.

table.title: Energy stores
head: Store
Filled when…
Example
rows: (emptied when a chemical reaction transfers energy to the surroundings)
a book on a high shelf
a material is stretched or squashed
a stretched elastic band, a squashed spring

facts: We explain how jobs get done with an **energy model**: energy is in a **store** at the start, and is **transferred** to another store by the end.
**Thermal store** — filled when an object **warms up**. The hotter it is, the more energy in this store.
**Chemical store** — in **food, fuels and batteries**. It empties during **chemical reactions** (burning, respiration) as energy is transferred to the surroundings.
**Kinetic store** — any **moving** object. It fills when the object **speeds up**: the faster it goes, the more energy.
**Gravitational potential store** — filled when an object is **lifted higher**. The higher (and heavier) it is, the more energy.
**Elastic store** — filled when a material is **stretched or squashed (compressed)**. The more it is stretched or squashed, the more energy.
There are a few more stores you will meet later (nuclear, magnetic, electrostatic).
**Light, sound and electricity are NOT stores** — they are ways of **transferring** energy from one store to another.
Energy is measured in **joules (J)**.
keywords: a place where energy is held, e.g. kinetic or chemical
filled when an object is warmed up
emptied in chemical reactions as energy goes to the surroundings
filled when an object speeds up
filled when an object is raised
filled when a material is stretched or compressed

topics.title: Energy transfers
topics.summary: How energy moves from one store to another — mechanically, electrically, by heating and by light or sound — for example in a hand-crank torch.

images.caption: A hand-crank (wind-up) torch, cut open to show the generator, the rechargeable battery and the LED.

table.title: Describing a transfer: store → how → store
head: What happens
Store emptied
How
Store filled

facts: Energy moves between stores in four main ways: **mechanically** (a force moves something), **electrically** (an electric current), **by heating** (from hotter to cooler), and **by radiation** — **light** and **sound**.
Describe any change as **store at the start → how → store at the end**: kicking a ball is chemical store of your muscles → mechanically → kinetic store of the ball.
**Conservation of energy:** energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred. The **total** at the end is the same as at the start.

**Hand-crank torch:** the chemical store of your **muscles** empties as you turn the **handle** (mechanically) → the **generator** spins (kinetic store) → it transfers energy **electrically** to the **chemical store of the rechargeable battery**.

When the torch is switched on, the battery transfers energy **electrically** to the **LED**, which gives out **light** — the useful part. Some energy always **heats** the parts and the surroundings, and turning the gears makes a little **sound**.
A falling object: its **gravitational potential** store empties and its **kinetic** store fills.
Burning a fuel: the **chemical** store of the fuel empties and energy is transferred **by heating** to the **thermal** store of whatever is heated.
A **generator** transfers energy from a spinning (kinetic) store electrically; a **motor** does the opposite.
keywords: energy moving from one store to another
transferred by a force making something move
transferred from a hotter object to a cooler one
transferred by light or sound waves
energy cannot be made or destroyed, only transferred
turns a spinning motion into an electric current

questions.stem: Describe the energy transfers in a hand-crank torch, from turning the handle to the light coming out.

acceptablePoints.point: energy from the chemical store of the person's muscles
is transferred mechanically (by the force on the handle) to the kinetic store of the handle / generator
the generator transfers energy electrically, to the chemical store of the battery (or straight to the bulb)

award.4: four of the points, in the right order

markScheme.modelAnswer: Energy in the chemical store of my muscles is transferred mechanically as I push the handle round, filling the kinetic store of the spinning generator. The generator transfers energy electrically to the chemical store of the rechargeable battery. When I switch on, the battery transfers energy electrically to the LED, which transfers energy by light to the surroundings. Some energy is wasted at every step, heating the parts and the surroundings and making a little sound.

topics.title: Wasted energy
topics.summary: Why some energy is always dissipated, how to work out useful and wasted energy, and why a pendulum or bouncing ball cannot go on for ever.

images.caption: A Sankey diagram: the width of each arrow shows how much energy goes that way.

table.title: Roughly how much of the input each source wastes
head: Energy source
Useful (electricity)
Wasted

facts: In every energy transfer, some energy spreads out into the surroundings in ways that are not useful. We say it is **dissipated** (wasted). It usually ends up in the **thermal store of the surroundings**, warming them very slightly.
Energy is **conserved**: **energy in = useful energy out + wasted energy**.
So **useful energy = energy in − wasted energy**, and **wasted energy = energy in − useful energy**.
Dissipated energy is spread so thinly that it is very hard to use again.
Much of the waste comes from **friction** and **air resistance**, which warm the moving parts and the air, and from **sound**.
A **Sankey diagram** shows energy transfers as arrows. The **width** of an arrow shows the amount; useful energy goes straight on, wasted energy bends away.
**Efficiency** = useful energy out ÷ energy in × 100%. A filament bulb turns only about 10% of its energy into light; an LED wastes much less.

A **swinging pendulum** or a **bouncing ball** cannot go on for ever: at every swing or bounce some energy is dissipated by air resistance, friction and sound, so it rises a little less each time until it stops.

We can waste less by **oiling (lubricating)** moving parts to cut friction, **streamlining** to cut air resistance, and **insulating** to cut heating losses. Renewable sources waste energy too — compare their percentages.
keywords: spread out wastefully into the surroundings
energy transferred to where we want it
energy transferred to where we do not want it, usually heating the surroundings
arrow diagram whose widths show the amounts of energy
a force between surfaces that dissipates energy by heating
oiling moving parts to reduce friction

into the ball's gravitational potential store

questions.stem: How could you reduce the energy wasted by friction in a bicycle chain?

questions.stem: In a Sankey diagram, a wider arrow means more energy.
questions.explain: Arrow widths are drawn to scale: twice as wide means twice as much energy.

questions.stem: The total energy after a transfer is less than before, because some is wasted.
questions.explain: The total stays the same (conservation of energy). Wasted energy still exists — it is just spread out in the surroundings.

questions.stem: A filament bulb and an LED bulb give the same light. Which is the better choice, and why?

the LED, because it creates extra energy
questions.explain: The LED wastes much less energy heating the surroundings, so it needs less energy for the same light.

questions.stem: A ball is dropped onto the floor. Explain, in terms of energy, why it cannot keep bouncing for ever.

acceptablePoints.point: as the ball falls, its gravitational potential store empties and its kinetic store fills (and the reverse on the way up)

the energy is not destroyed — it ends up spread out in the thermal store of the surroundings

award.3: three points, including that energy is dissipated at each bounce

markScheme.modelAnswer: As the ball falls, energy moves from its gravitational potential store to its kinetic store. Each time it hits the floor, some energy is dissipated by sound and by heating the ball and the floor, and air resistance warms the air as it moves. So each bounce leaves the ball with less energy, it cannot rise as high, and finally it stops. The energy has not been destroyed — it has spread out into the thermal store of the surroundings.

questions.tip: Say where the energy goes at each bounce, and why that makes the next bounce lower.

topics.title: Work done
topics.summary: When a force moves something, work is done and energy is transferred: work done = force × distance.

images.caption: An electric motor winds up a string and lifts a weight: the motor does work on the weight.

facts: In Year 7 you met four ways of transferring energy. **Work** is the name for the **mechanical** one: energy is transferred whenever a **force moves an object**.
**Work done (J) = force (N) × distance moved (m).** Work is measured in **joules (J)**, like every other amount of energy.
The **bigger the force**, or the **further** the object moves, the **more work** is done. Pushing a box 4 m takes twice the work of pushing it 2 m with the same force.
The distance must be **in the direction of the force**. Pushing hard on a wall that does not move does **no work** on the wall — nothing moves.
**Lifting** something: the force you need is its **weight** (mass × 10 N/kg). Lifting a 3 kg bag up 2 m: 30 N × 2 m = **60 J**, which fills its **gravitational potential store**.

**An electric motor raising a weight** is doing work: it pulls up on the string with a force, and the weight moves up. Energy goes from the **battery's chemical store**, **electrically** to the motor, then **mechanically** to the weight's **gravitational potential store**. Some is wasted heating the motor.
**Deformation** — stretching, squashing or bending an object — also takes work. Stretching a spring fills its **elastic store**.
**Displacement** is how far an object ends up from where it started. Work uses the distance moved along the force.
Rearranged: **distance = work ÷ force**, and **force = work ÷ distance**.
keywords: energy transferred when a force moves an object, in joules (J)
the unit of work and of energy
how far an object has moved from where it started
stretching, squashing or bending an object — it takes work
the force of gravity on an object: mass (kg) × 10 N/kg

topics.title: Levers, pulleys and wheels
topics.summary: Machines make work easier: a smaller force moved a longer distance, or less friction.

images.caption: A lever lifting a rock. You push far from the pivot; the rock is close to it.

table.title: Three kinds of lever
head: What is in the middle
Examples
What it gives you
rows: a big output force when the pivot is close to the load
a big output force from a small input force
a smaller output force, but the load moves further and faster

facts: A **machine** makes a job easier, usually by letting you use a **smaller force**. Levers, pulleys, ramps, gears and wheels are all machines.
The force you put in is the **input force** (effort). The force the machine puts on the object is the **output force**.
A **lever** is a **rigid bar** that turns about a **pivot**. Push **far from the pivot** with the load **close to it**, and a small input force gives a **big output force**.
The catch: your end moves a **long way** while the load moves only a **short way**. You swap a big force for a big distance.
**A machine never saves work.** Work in = force × distance at your end; work out = force × distance at the load. At best they are equal — with friction, the work out is a little **less**.
Example: push down 100 N through 0.6 m (60 J). The rock rises 0.2 m, so the output force can be up to 60 ÷ 0.2 = **300 N** — three times the push.
**Pulleys:** one fixed pulley just **changes the direction** (pull down to lift up). With **two supporting ropes** you need about **half** the force — but you pull **twice as much** rope.
**Ramps** work the same way: a longer, gentler slope needs a smaller push. **Wheels** make jobs easier by **reducing friction** — rolling instead of dragging.
Different levers suit different jobs (see the table): a wheelbarrow gives a big force; tweezers give a small, careful one and move the tips further than your fingers.

topics.title: Temperature and thermal energy
topics.summary: Temperature and thermal energy are different; energy flows from hot to cold until both are the same temperature.

images.caption: A hot drink cools and a cold drink warms, until both reach room temperature — fast at first, then slower.

facts: **Temperature** tells you how hot something is, in **degrees Celsius (°C)**, measured with a **thermometer**. It is a measure of how fast the **particles** are moving or vibrating — their energy on average.
**Thermal energy** is the **total** energy stored in an object because of its moving, vibrating particles. In Year 7 you called this the **thermal store**.
The thermal energy of an object depends on its **mass**, its **temperature** and **what it is made of**.
So a warm **bath** (40 °C) holds far **more thermal energy** than a cup of hot tea (80 °C) — the tea has the higher temperature, but the bath has much more water.
When there is a **temperature difference**, energy is transferred from the **hotter** object to the **cooler** one. Cold does not flow: your hand feels cold on ice because energy leaves your hand.
The transfer goes on until both are at the **same temperature**. Then there is no overall transfer.
**Cooling over time:** a hot drink cools **quickly at first**, then **more and more slowly**, and levels off at **room temperature**. The bigger the temperature difference, the faster the transfer.

**Heating over time:** a cold drink warms up the same way, rising fast at first and levelling off at room temperature. Water heated on a cooker rises to **100 °C**, then stays at 100 °C while it boils.
The same energy warms different materials by different amounts: 1 kg of cooking oil heats up faster than 1 kg of water. More mass takes more energy for the same temperature rise.
keywords: how hot something is — a measure of the motion and energy of its particles, in °C
the energy stored in a substance because its particles move and vibrate

markScheme.modelAnswer: The cocoa's temperature falls. Energy is transferred from the hot cocoa to the cooler air and table around it. topics.title: Conduction, convection and radiation
topics.summary: Thermal energy moves in three ways: through particles by conduction and convection, and as waves by radiation.

images.caption: A convection current carries warm air from the radiator round the whole room.

table.title: Three ways thermal energy moves
head: Way
How the energy travels
Where it happens
Example
rows: particles vibrate and pass energy on to the particles next to them
best in solids — metals best of all
a metal spoon in hot soup gets hot
a heated fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises; cooler fluid sinks — a current

facts: Heating is one of the ways energy is transferred (Year 7). Thermal energy moves in **three** ways: **conduction**, **convection** and **radiation**. Conduction and convection need **particles**; radiation does not.
**Conduction:** particles in the hot part vibrate more and **bump into their neighbours**, passing the energy along. It works best in **solids**, where particles are close together.

**Metals** are the best **thermal conductors** (they also have free electrons that carry energy quickly). **Thermal insulators** — wood, plastic, wool and especially **air** — let heat through only slowly.
Liquids conduct poorly and **gases** very poorly: their particles are further apart and collide less often. That is why **trapped air** is such a good insulator.

**Convection** happens only in **fluids** (liquids and gases). The heated fluid **expands**, becomes **less dense** and **rises**; cooler, denser fluid **sinks** to take its place. This loop is a **convection current**.
The particles do not get bigger when heated — they move faster and spread **further apart**, so the fluid takes up more space.
**Radiation** is energy carried by **infrared** waves. It needs **no particles**, so it can cross a **vacuum** — that is how energy from the Sun reaches us.
All objects give out infrared; **hotter** objects give out more. **Dull (matt) black** surfaces are the best at giving out and taking in radiation; **shiny** or **white** surfaces reflect it.
A metal bench feels colder than a wooden one at the same temperature: metal **conducts** energy away from your hand faster.
keywords: transfer of thermal energy by vibrating particles passing it on
transfer of thermal energy when a heated fluid rises and cooler fluid sinks
transfer of thermal energy as a wave (infrared) — no particles needed
a material that lets heat move quickly through it
a material that lets heat move only slowly through it

the loop of rising warm fluid and sinking cool fluid

topics.title: Keeping heat in: insulation
topics.summary: How flasks, houses and clothes cut energy loss by conduction, convection and radiation.

images.caption: A vacuum flask cut in half: every feature cuts one or more ways of losing energy.
Ways to insulate a house so less energy escapes to the cold outside.

table.title: Insulating a house
head: Method
How it works
Mainly cuts
rows: thick wool traps air above the ceiling
foam fills the gap between the walls, trapping air in tiny pockets
two panes with a layer of air or gas (or a vacuum) between
stop warm air escaping through gaps
reflects infrared back into the room
an insulating layer that traps air over the floor

facts: **Insulation** slows down the transfer of thermal energy. It can keep something **hot** (a house in winter) or **cold** (a cool box) — it works both ways.
**Trapped air** is the key to most insulation: air is a poor **conductor**, and trapping it in small pockets stops it moving, so it cannot carry energy by **convection**.

**Vacuum flask:** the **vacuum** between the double walls stops **conduction and convection**; the **silvered walls** reflect **radiation**; the **stopper** stops warm air escaping (**convection**) and is an insulator.

**In the home:** **loft insulation**, **cavity wall insulation**, **double glazing**, **carpets**, **curtains** and **draught excluders** cut conduction and convection. **Shiny foil** behind a radiator reflects infrared back into the room.
Less energy lost means lower heating bills and less fuel burned — good for the climate too (Year 7: energy costs).

**Clothing:** several thin layers trap more air than one thick one. Wool and fleece trap air between their fibres. A **shiny 'space blanket'** reflects infrared back to the body, so it is given to runners after a marathon.
In hot countries houses are often painted **white** to reflect the Sun's radiation and keep cool.

**Testing a claim** ('this coat keeps you twice as warm'): wrap identical containers of hot water in different materials, keep the **same** starting temperature, volume and thickness, and measure the **temperature drop over time**. Ask who made the claim and whether the test was fair and repeated.

air held in small pockets — a poor conductor that cannot form convection currents
a container with a vacuum between double walls, to keep drinks hot or cold
windows with two panes and a gap of air, gas or vacuum between them

a thick layer of wool laid above the ceiling
bounce radiation back instead of absorbing it — shiny surfaces do this

topics.title: How sound travels
topics.summary: Sound is a vibration passed on by particles, so it needs a material to travel through and can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted.

images.caption: A loudspeaker pushes and pulls on the air: the particles crowd together (compressions) and spread apart (rarefactions) as the wave moves on.

facts: Every sound starts with something **vibrating**: moving back and forth again and again (a guitar string, a drum skin, your vocal cords).

The vibration is passed from particle to particle as a **longitudinal wave**: the particles vibrate **in the same direction** as the wave travels. Where they crowd together is a **compression**; where they spread out is a **rarefaction**.
Sound needs **particles** to carry it, so it **cannot travel through a vacuum** (empty space with no particles). In space, nobody can hear you shout.
Sound travels **faster in denser materials**: fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases. In air it travels at about **330 m/s**.
Light is about **a million times faster** than sound. That is why you see lightning before you hear the thunder.
When sound meets a surface it can be **reflected** (bounce back), **absorbed** (its energy goes into the material) or **transmitted** (pass through).
An **echo** is sound reflected back to the listener. Hard, flat surfaces give strong echoes; soft materials like foam, curtains and carpet **absorb** sound.
**Distance = speed × time.** For an echo, the sound goes there **and back**, so halve the total distance to find how far away the wall is.
keywords: a back and forth movement that repeats
a wave where the particles vibrate in the same direction as the wave travels
part of a sound wave where particles are squashed together
part of a sound wave where particles are spread apart
the material a wave travels through
a space with no particles at all
a sound reflected from a surface back to the listener
when a material takes in the energy of the sound
when sound passes through a material

questions.stem: Every sound is made by something moving quickly back and forth. What is this movement called?
questions.explain: A sound source vibrates: it moves back and forth again and again, pushing on the particles around it.

questions.stem: Sound travels as which type of wave?
questions.explain: In a sound wave the particles vibrate along the same line the wave travels, so it is a longitudinal wave.

questions.stem: In a longitudinal wave, the particles vibrate in which direction compared with the way the wave travels?
questions.explain: Longitudinal means the vibration is in the same direction as the wave moves: the particles move back and forth along it.

questions.stem: In a sound wave, what is a region where the particles are squashed close together called?
questions.explain: Compressions are where the particles crowd together; rarefactions are where they are spread apart.

questions.stem: Sound can travel through a vacuum.
questions.explain: A vacuum has no particles, so there is nothing to pass the vibrations on. Sound cannot travel through it.

questions.stem: What is a space with no particles of matter in it called?
questions.explain: A vacuum is completely empty: no particles at all, so sound cannot cross it (but light can).

questions.stem: Two astronauts on a spacewalk cannot hear each other shout, even when close together. Why?
questions.answer: space is a vacuum, so there are no particles to pass the vibrations on
choices: it is too cold in space for sound to form
sound travels too fast in space to be heard
their voices are too high-pitched in space
questions.explain: Sound needs a medium. With no particles between them, the vibrations from one astronaut cannot reach the other (they use radio, which can cross a vacuum).

questions.stem: Through which of these does sound travel fastest?
questions.explain: Sound is fastest in solids, where the particles are packed closely and pass vibrations on quickly. It cannot travel through a vacuum at all.

questions.stem: Sound travels faster through water than through air.
questions.explain: Water is denser than air: sound travels at about 1500 m/s in water and about 330 m/s in air.

questions.stem: Roughly how fast does sound travel in air, in metres per second?
questions.explain: Sound travels at about 330 m/s in air (some books say 340 m/s). Light is about a million times faster.

questions.stem: In a storm, why do you see the lightning before you hear the thunder?
questions.answer: light travels much faster than sound
choices: the lightning happens first and the thunder later
your eyes work faster than your ears
questions.explain: Both are made at the same moment, but light arrives almost instantly while sound takes about 3 seconds to travel 1 km.

questions.stem: You hear thunder 3 seconds after you see the lightning. Sound travels at 330 m/s. How far away is the storm, in metres?
questions.explain: Distance = speed × time = 330 × 3 = 990 m (the light reaches you almost instantly).

questions.stem: What is a sound reflected from a surface back to the listener called?
questions.explain: An echo is reflected sound. You hear it a moment later because the sound has travelled to the surface and back.

questions.stem: You shout towards a cliff and hear the echo 2 seconds later. Sound travels at 330 m/s. How far away is the cliff, in metres?
questions.explain: In 2 s the sound travels 330 × 2 = 660 m, but that is there and back, so the cliff is 660 ÷ 2 = 330 m away.

questions.stem: Which surface would give the clearest echo?
questions.explain: Hard, smooth surfaces reflect most of the sound. Soft materials absorb it, so there is little echo.

questions.stem: A music studio has foam on its walls. The sound's energy goes into the foam instead of bouncing back. The sound is…
questions.explain: Absorption: the sound's energy is transferred to the material, so less is reflected and the room has fewer echoes.

questions.stem: You can hear music from the next room through the wall. The sound has been…
questions.explain: Sound that passes through a material is transmitted. Walls transmit some sound, reflect some and absorb some.

questions.stem: A ringing electric bell is put inside a sealed glass jar. A pump slowly takes the air out of the jar. Describe and explain what you hear.

acceptablePoints.point: the sound gets quieter (and quieter) until it can hardly / no longer be heard
sound needs a medium / particles to travel through
as air is removed there are fewer particles to pass on the vibrations
sound cannot travel through a vacuum (when the jar is empty)
you can still see the bell's hammer moving because light can travel through a vacuum

markScheme.modelAnswer: The ringing gets quieter and quieter until you can hardly hear it. Sound is a vibration passed on by particles. As the air is pumped out there are fewer particles to carry the vibrations, and sound cannot travel through a vacuum. You can still see the hammer hitting the bell because light does not need particles.

questions.stem: Explain why sound travels faster through a solid than through a gas.

acceptablePoints.point: the particles in a solid are closer together / packed tightly (it is denser)
so each particle passes the vibration on to the next more quickly
in a gas the particles are far apart, so the vibration takes longer to pass on

award.2: two points, linked (closer particles → vibrations passed on faster)

markScheme.modelAnswer: In a solid the particles are packed closely together, so a vibrating particle quickly bumps into the next one and passes the vibration on. In a gas the particles are far apart, so the vibrations are passed on more slowly.

topics.title: Loudness, pitch and oscilloscopes
topics.summary: The height of a sound wave shows how loud it is, and how many waves arrive each second shows its pitch.

images.caption: The parts of a wave: amplitude is measured from the middle line, wavelength from one crest to the next.
Oscilloscope traces with the same settings: taller waves are louder, more waves across the screen are higher in pitch.

facts: An **oscilloscope** shows a sound as a wavy line (a **trace**). A microphone first turns the sound into an electrical signal.
The **amplitude** is the biggest distance the wave moves from its **middle (rest) position**. **Bigger amplitude = louder sound.**
**Volume** (loudness) is measured in **decibels (dB)**.
The **frequency** is the number of waves each second, measured in **hertz (Hz)**. **Higher frequency = higher pitch.**
The **wavelength** is the distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave, such as **crest to crest**. A higher frequency means a **shorter wavelength**.
Loudness and pitch are separate: a sound can be **loud and low**, or **quiet and high**.
Comparing traces only works if the oscilloscope settings are the same. Count the waves across the screen for pitch; look at the height for loudness.
On an instrument: plucking or hitting **harder** makes a louder note (bigger amplitude); a **shorter, tighter or thinner** string makes a higher note (higher frequency).
keywords: the biggest distance a wave moves from its middle position
the distance between two matching points on neighbouring waves
the number of waves each second, in hertz (Hz)
how high or low a sound is; set by the frequency
how loud or quiet a sound is, in decibels (dB)
a device that shows sound waves as a trace on a screen

questions.stem: What is the biggest distance a wave moves from its middle position called?
questions.explain: Amplitude is measured from the middle (rest) line to a crest or trough. A bigger amplitude means a louder sound.

questions.stem: What is the number of waves produced each second called?
questions.explain: Frequency is how many waves pass each second. It sets the pitch.

questions.stem: What unit is frequency measured in?
questions.explain: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz): 1 Hz is one wave each second.

questions.stem: What unit is the loudness (volume) of a sound measured in?
questions.explain: Loudness is measured in decibels (dB). Frequency is the one measured in hertz.

questions.stem: What is the distance from one crest of a wave to the next crest called?
questions.explain: Wavelength is the distance between two matching points on neighbouring waves, such as crest to crest.

questions.stem: The pitch of a sound depends on which property of its wave?
questions.explain: Higher frequency means higher pitch. The amplitude sets the loudness, not the pitch.

questions.stem: A sound gets louder but stays the same pitch. What happens to its wave?
questions.explain: Louder means more energy and a bigger amplitude. The same pitch means the frequency has not changed.

questions.stem: A sound gets higher in pitch. What happens to its wave?
questions.answer: its frequency increases and its wavelength gets shorter
choices: its frequency decreases and its wavelength gets longer
questions.explain: Higher pitch means more waves each second, so each wave is shorter. Sound still travels at the same speed in air.

questions.stem: Which device shows a sound as a wavy trace on a screen (after a microphone has turned it into an electrical signal)?
questions.explain: An oscilloscope draws the electrical signal from a microphone, so you can see the sound's amplitude and frequency.

questions.stem: A high-pitched sound has a longer wavelength than a low-pitched sound.
questions.explain: It is the other way round: a higher pitch means a higher frequency and a shorter wavelength.

questions.stem: Two sounds can have the same pitch but different loudness.
questions.explain: Pitch depends on frequency and loudness on amplitude, so they can change separately (like a note played softly or loudly).

questions.stem: The four oscilloscope traces use the same settings. Which trace shows the highest-pitched sound?
questions.explain: C has the most waves across the screen, so it has the highest frequency and the highest pitch (even though it is quiet).

questions.stem: Which trace has the same pitch as A but is louder?
questions.explain: B has the same number of waves as A (same frequency) but they are much taller (bigger amplitude), so it is louder.

questions.stem: Which trace shows the quietest, lowest-pitched sound?
questions.explain: A has small waves (small amplitude, quiet) and only two waves across the screen (low frequency, low pitch).

questions.stem: Which trace is loud and has a higher pitch than B?
questions.explain: D is as tall as B (just as loud) but has more waves across the screen, so it has a higher frequency.

questions.stem: A guitarist plucks the same string again, but harder. How does the oscilloscope trace change?
questions.answer: the waves get taller, but the number of waves stays the same
choices: more waves fit across the screen
the waves get shorter and closer together
the trace does not change at all
questions.explain: Plucking harder gives a bigger amplitude (louder). The same string gives the same frequency, so the pitch stays the same.

questions.stem: Which part of the wave is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The crest (or peak) is the highest point of a wave.

questions.stem: Which part of the wave is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The trough is the lowest point of a wave.

questions.stem: What does the arrow labelled {L} show?
questions.explain: The amplitude is measured from the middle line up to a crest (or down to a trough).

questions.stem: What does the arrow labelled {L} show?
questions.explain: The wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next (or between any two matching points).

questions.stem: What is the dashed line labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The middle (rest) position is where the particles would be with no wave. The amplitude is measured from this line.

questions.stem: On the same oscilloscope settings, a quiet, low note and a loud, high note are shown. Describe how the two traces are different, and say what each difference tells you.

acceptablePoints.point: the loud note has taller waves / a bigger amplitude
a bigger amplitude means a louder sound
the high note has more waves across the screen / a higher frequency
a higher frequency means a higher pitch
the high note's waves are closer together / shorter wavelength

award.4: four points, covering both amplitude and frequency

markScheme.modelAnswer: The loud, high note has taller waves than the quiet note: a bigger amplitude, which means it is louder. It also has more waves across the screen, closer together: a higher frequency and shorter wavelength, which means a higher pitch. The quiet, low note has small waves that are spread out.

topics.title: Hearing and the ear
topics.summary: How the parts of the ear pass a sound on to the brain, what different animals can hear, and what can go wrong.

images.caption: Inside the ear: the vibration goes from the eardrum through three tiny bones to the cochlea, then the auditory nerve carries a signal to the brain.

table.title: The journey of a sound through the ear
head: Part
What it does
rows: collects sound and directs it into the ear canal
carries the sound to the eardrum
a thin skin that vibrates when sound hits it
three tiny bones that pass on the vibrations and make them bigger
a fluid-filled coil with tiny hairs that turn vibrations into electrical signals
carries the electrical signals to the brain

facts: The **outer ear (pinna)** collects sound waves and funnels them down the **ear canal**.
The sound makes the **eardrum** vibrate. Three tiny bones, the **ossicles**, pass the vibrations on and make them bigger.
In the **cochlea**, tiny **hair cells** turn the vibrations into **electrical signals**. The **auditory nerve** carries them to the **brain**, which makes sense of the sound.
The **auditory range** is the lowest to highest frequency an animal can hear. For a young human it is about **20 Hz to 20 000 Hz**.
Sound too high for humans to hear is **ultrasound**. Dogs, cats and bats can hear some ultrasound; bats use it to find their way.
As people get older they usually **stop hearing the highest frequencies**.
**Very loud sounds** (over about 85 dB for a long time) can damage the hair cells in the cochlea. This **hearing loss is permanent**.
Other problems: a **perforated (burst) eardrum** cannot vibrate properly; **wax** blocking the ear canal stops sound reaching the eardrum. Both make sounds seem quieter.
**Ear defenders** and ear plugs protect hearing by **absorbing** sound energy, so less reaches the eardrum.
keywords: the part outside the head that collects sound
a thin skin that vibrates when sound reaches it
three tiny bones that pass vibrations to the cochlea
coiled part of the inner ear where hair cells make electrical signals
carries signals from the cochlea to the brain
the lowest and highest frequencies an animal can hear
sound too high-pitched for humans to hear (above 20 000 Hz)

questions.stem: Which part of the ear is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The outer ear (pinna) is the part you can see. Its shape collects sound and funnels it into the ear canal.

questions.stem: Which part of the ear is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The ear canal is the tube that carries sound from the outer ear to the eardrum.

questions.stem: Which part of the ear is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The eardrum is a thin skin across the end of the ear canal. It vibrates when sound reaches it.

questions.stem: Which part of the ear is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The ossicles are three tiny bones (hammer, anvil and stirrup) that pass the vibrations from the eardrum to the cochlea.

questions.stem: Which part of the ear is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The cochlea is the snail-shaped coil. Its hair cells turn vibrations into electrical signals.

questions.stem: Which part of the ear is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The auditory nerve carries electrical signals from the cochlea to the brain. (The optic nerve belongs to the eye.)

questions.stem: Which thin skin inside the ear vibrates when sound waves reach it?
questions.explain: Sound travels down the ear canal and makes the eardrum vibrate; the ossicles then pass the vibrations on.

questions.stem: Which part of the ear contains tiny hair cells that turn vibrations into electrical signals?
questions.explain: The hair cells in the fluid-filled cochlea move with the vibrations and send electrical signals along the auditory nerve.

questions.stem: In which order does a sound pass through the ear?
questions.answer: ear canal → eardrum → ossicles → cochlea → auditory nerve
choices: ear canal → cochlea → ossicles → eardrum → auditory nerve
eardrum → ear canal → cochlea → ossicles → auditory nerve
ear canal → ossicles → eardrum → auditory nerve → cochlea
questions.explain: Outside to inside: ear canal, eardrum, the three tiny bones, the cochlea, and then the nerve to the brain.

questions.stem: What is the name for the range from the lowest to the highest frequency an animal can hear?
questions.explain: The auditory range is different for different animals: dogs and bats can hear much higher frequencies than humans.

questions.stem: A young person can hear from about 20 Hz up to about how many hertz?
questions.explain: The human auditory range is about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz, and the top end drops as people get older.

questions.stem: What is sound with a frequency too high for humans to hear called?
questions.explain: Ultrasound is above 20 000 Hz. (Infrasound is the opposite: below 20 Hz, too low for us.)

questions.stem: A dog can hear some high-pitched sounds that humans cannot.
questions.explain: A dog's auditory range goes much higher than ours, which is why dog whistles work even though we hear nothing.

questions.stem: As people get older, they usually lose the ability to hear the lowest-pitched sounds first.
questions.explain: It is the highest frequencies that go first as people age.

questions.stem: Years of very loud music can damage the tiny hair cells in the cochlea. What is the most likely effect?
questions.answer: permanent hearing loss, often of high-pitched sounds
choices: hearing gets better at high pitches
a short loss that always heals within a day
questions.explain: Damaged hair cells do not grow back, so the hearing loss is permanent. The cells for high frequencies are often damaged first.

questions.stem: A person has a perforated (burst) eardrum. Why can they not hear as well?
questions.answer: the eardrum cannot vibrate properly, so less vibration reaches the ossicles
choices: sound travels faster through the hole
the cochlea makes extra electrical signals
questions.explain: A hole in the eardrum means it does not vibrate properly, so sounds seem quieter. It usually heals by itself.

questions.stem: Ear defenders protect a road worker's hearing. How do they work?
questions.answer: they absorb sound energy, so less reaches the eardrum
choices: they change the sound into ultrasound
they make the sound travel faster
they reflect the sound back into the ear canal
questions.explain: Soft, thick materials absorb sound. Less sound reaches the eardrum, so the hair cells in the cochlea are not damaged.

questions.stem: Describe how the sound of a drum reaches your brain. Start with the drum skin being hit.

acceptablePoints.point: the drum skin vibrates
it makes the air particles next to it vibrate
the vibrations pass from particle to particle through the air as a longitudinal wave (compressions and rarefactions)
the outer ear collects the sound and it travels down the ear canal
the eardrum vibrates
the ossicles / tiny bones pass on (and make bigger) the vibrations
hair cells in the cochlea turn the vibrations into electrical signals
the auditory nerve carries the signals to the brain

award.6: six points in a sensible order, from drum to brain
award.4: four points

markScheme.modelAnswer: When the drum is hit, its skin vibrates. This pushes and pulls on the air particles next to it, which vibrate and pass the vibration on to the next particles, so a longitudinal sound wave travels through the air. The outer ear collects the sound and it travels down the ear canal to the eardrum, which vibrates. The ossicles pass these vibrations on and make them bigger. In the cochlea, tiny hair cells turn the vibrations into electrical signals, and the auditory nerve carries them to the brain.

questions.stem: A company says its new headphones "block out 95% of outside noise". Describe what evidence you would want to see before believing this claim.

acceptablePoints.point: measurements of the sound level in decibels with a sound meter, with and without the headphones
tests at a range of frequencies / both low- and high-pitched sounds (and different loudness)
a fair test: same sound source, same distance, only the headphones changed
repeated measurements / several pairs tested, so the results are reliable
tested by an independent group, not only by the company selling them

markScheme.modelAnswer: I would want measurements in decibels from a sound meter placed inside and outside the headphones, using the same sound source at the same distance. They should test low- and high-pitched sounds, because headphones often block high sounds better than low ones. The tests should be repeated and done by an independent group, not just the company.

topics.title: Light, shadows and mirrors
topics.summary: Light travels in straight lines, very fast; materials can transmit, absorb, reflect or scatter it, and mirrors reflect it at equal angles.

images.caption: Reflection in a plane mirror: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.
A periscope: two mirrors at 45° each turn the light through a right angle.
Eclipses are shadows: of the Moon on the Earth (solar) or of the Earth on the Moon (lunar).

table.title: How much light gets through?
head: Type of material
Light through it
Examples
rows: all (or nearly all); you can see clearly through it
some, but scattered; you cannot see clearly through it

facts: Light travels in **straight lines**, at **300 million m/s** in a vacuum: nothing is faster. Unlike sound, it **can travel through a vacuum**.
Light **sources** (the Sun, a lamp) give out light. We see everything else because light **reflects** off it **into our eyes**.
When light meets a material it can be **transmitted** (pass through), **absorbed** (energy goes into the material), **reflected** or **scattered**. Usually a mix happens.
**Transparent** materials let all light through, **translucent** ones let some through, **opaque** ones let none through.
A **shadow** forms because light travels in straight lines and an opaque object blocks it. **Eclipses** are giant shadows.
A **smooth, shiny surface** like a mirror reflects all the rays the same way, so you see an image. A **rough** surface **scatters** light in all directions.
**Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection.** Both are measured from the **normal**, a line at right angles (90°) to the mirror.
The image in a flat mirror is the **same size**, the **same distance behind** the mirror as the object is in front, and **left-right reversed**.
In a **periscope**, two mirrors at **45°** each turn the light through 90°, so you can see over a wall.
keywords: the ray of light going towards a surface
the ray of light coming away from a surface
a line at right angles to the surface, used to measure angles
the angle between the incident ray and the normal
the angle between the reflected ray and the normal
lets some light through, but scattered
when the energy of light is taken in by a material
when light bounces off a surface in all directions

questions.stem: What is the dashed line labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The normal is drawn at right angles to the mirror where the ray hits it. Angles are measured from it.

questions.stem: Which ray is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The incident ray is the one travelling towards the mirror (look at the arrow).

questions.stem: Which ray is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The reflected ray is the one travelling away from the mirror after bouncing off it.

questions.stem: Which angle is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The angle of incidence is between the incident ray and the normal (not the mirror).

questions.stem: Which angle is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The angle of reflection is between the reflected ray and the normal. It always equals the angle of incidence.

questions.stem: What is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The mirror is drawn as a line with short hatching on the back (the non-shiny side).

questions.stem: A ray of light hits a mirror with an angle of incidence of 35°. What is the angle of reflection, in degrees?
questions.explain: The law of reflection: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, so it is also 35°.

questions.stem: A ray hits a mirror at 30° to the mirror's surface. What is the angle of incidence, in degrees?
questions.explain: Angles are measured from the normal, which is at 90° to the mirror: 90° − 30° = 60°.

questions.stem: How fast does light travel in a vacuum, in metres per second?
questions.explain: Light travels at 300 million m/s in a vacuum, about a million times faster than sound in air.

questions.stem: Light, like sound, cannot travel through a vacuum.
questions.explain: Light does not need particles, so it crosses the vacuum of space: that is how sunlight reaches us.

questions.stem: Frosted glass lets some light through but you cannot see clearly through it. It is…
questions.explain: Translucent materials let some light through but scatter it, so things look blurred.

questions.stem: A material that lets no light through at all is…
questions.explain: Opaque materials absorb or reflect all the light, which is why they make shadows.

questions.stem: Clear window glass lets almost all light through, so you can see clearly through it. It is…
questions.explain: Transparent materials transmit nearly all the light without scattering it.

questions.stem: This page does not give out its own light. Why can you see it?
questions.answer: light from a source reflects off the page into your eyes
choices: light travels from your eyes to the page
the page absorbs all the light that hits it
the page is a light source
questions.explain: We see objects that are not light sources because light reflects (scatters) off them and enters our eyes.

questions.stem: When light hits a rough surface and bounces off in all directions, this is called…
questions.explain: A rough surface scatters light in all directions, so you see the surface but no clear image in it.

questions.stem: Light shines on a sheet of white paper. What happens to most of the light?
questions.answer: it is scattered in all directions
choices: it is reflected as a clear image, like a mirror
questions.explain: Paper is opaque and its surface is rough on a tiny scale, so it scatters light. That is why you see the paper but not your face in it.

questions.stem: Which describes your image in a flat (plane) mirror?
questions.answer: the same size, as far behind the mirror as you are in front, and left-right reversed
choices: smaller than you, and on the surface of the mirror
upside down, and the same size
bigger than you, and in front of the mirror
questions.explain: A plane mirror gives an upright image, the same size, the same distance behind the mirror, with left and right swapped.

questions.stem: You stand 2 m in front of a flat mirror. How far are you from your image, in metres?
questions.explain: The image is 2 m behind the mirror and you are 2 m in front of it, so you are 2 + 2 = 4 m from your image.

questions.stem: In a periscope, each of the two mirrors is tilted at what angle, in degrees?
questions.explain: A mirror at 45° turns the light through 90°: once down the tube and once back out towards your eye.

questions.stem: In a solar eclipse, which object is between the Sun and the Earth?
questions.explain: In a solar eclipse the Moon blocks the Sun's light and its shadow falls on part of the Earth.

questions.stem: During a solar eclipse, what do people standing in the darkest part of the Moon's shadow see?
questions.answer: a total eclipse: the Sun is completely blocked
choices: a partial eclipse: only part of the Sun is blocked
no eclipse: the Sun looks normal
a lunar eclipse: the Moon turns red
questions.explain: In the darkest shadow no direct sunlight arrives at all. Just outside it, in the paler shadow, people see part of the Sun covered (partial eclipse).

questions.stem: What happens in a lunar eclipse?
questions.answer: the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, so Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
choices: the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth, so the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth
the Sun moves behind the Moon
the Moon stops reflecting light because it is new moon
questions.explain: In a lunar eclipse the Moon passes through Earth's shadow, so it goes dark (often a reddish colour).

questions.stem: Explain how a periscope lets you see over a wall. You may use the idea of rays.

acceptablePoints.point: light from the object travels in a straight line into the top of the periscope
the top mirror (at 45°) reflects the light down the tube / turns it through 90°
the bottom mirror (at 45°) reflects the light out into your eye
at each mirror the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (45°)

markScheme.modelAnswer: Light from the object travels in a straight line into the top opening. It hits the top mirror, which is at 45°, so the angle of incidence and reflection are both 45° and the light turns through 90° down the tube. The bottom mirror, also at 45°, reflects it through 90° again, out into your eye.

questions.stem: Explain how a shadow is formed when you stand in sunlight.

acceptablePoints.point: light travels in straight lines
your body is opaque / blocks (absorbs or reflects) the light
so no light reaches the area behind you, which looks dark

markScheme.modelAnswer: Light travels in straight lines and cannot bend round you. Your body is opaque, so it blocks the light, and the ground behind you gets no direct sunlight: that dark area is your shadow.

topics.title: Refraction, lenses and the eye
topics.summary: Light bends when it passes between materials; lenses use this to focus light, as the eye does onto the retina.

images.caption: Light through a glass block bends towards the normal on the way in and away from it on the way out.
A convex lens brings rays together at a focus; a concave lens spreads them out.
The cornea and lens focus light onto the retina; the optic nerve carries signals to the brain.

table.title: Fixing blurred vision
head: Problem
What goes wrong
Lens that corrects it
rows: light focuses in front of the retina

facts: **Refraction** is the change in direction of light as it goes from one material into another. It happens because light **changes speed**.
Going into a **denser** material (air → glass or water), light slows down and bends **towards the normal**.
Going into a **less dense** material (glass or water → air), light speeds up and bends **away from the normal**.
A ray that hits the surface **along the normal** (at 90°) changes speed but **does not change direction**.
Refraction makes a pool look **shallower** than it is and a straw in a glass look **bent**: our brain assumes light travels in straight lines.
A **convex** lens is **thicker in the middle**. It brings rays together (**converges** them) at a point called the **focus**. Magnifying glasses are convex.
A **concave** lens is **thinner in the middle**. It spreads rays out (**diverges** them).

In the eye, the **cornea** and **lens** focus light onto the **retina**, which has light-detecting cells. The **optic nerve** carries signals to the **brain**. The **iris** changes the size of the **pupil** to let in more or less light.
**Short-sighted** eyes focus light in front of the retina: **concave** lenses fix it. **Long-sighted** eyes focus it behind the retina: **convex** lenses fix it.
keywords: the change of direction of light going from one material into another
a line at right angles to the surface
a lens thicker in the middle that brings light rays together
a lens thinner in the middle that spreads light rays out
the point where a convex lens brings parallel rays together
the clear front of the eye; it starts focusing the light
the coloured part of the eye; it controls the size of the pupil
the hole in the iris that lets light in
layer at the back of the eye with light-detecting cells, where the image forms
carries signals from the retina to the brain

questions.stem: What is the change in direction of light as it passes from one material into another called?
questions.explain: Refraction: light changes speed as it crosses into a new material, which makes it change direction.

questions.stem: A ray of light goes from air into glass at an angle. Which way does it bend?
questions.explain: Glass is denser than air, so light slows down and bends towards the normal.

questions.stem: A ray of light goes from water into air at an angle. Does it bend towards or away from the normal?
questions.explain: Going into a less dense material, light speeds up and bends away from the normal.

topics.title: Colour
topics.summary: White light is a mixture of colours; objects and filters look coloured because of which colours they reflect, absorb or let through.

images.caption: A prism splits white light into a spectrum: red is bent least, violet most.

facts: **White light** is a mixture of all the colours. A **prism** splits it into a **spectrum**: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. This is called **dispersion**.
Each colour is refracted by a different amount: **red the least, violet the most**, so the colours spread out.
Different colours of light have different **frequencies**: **red is the lowest**, **violet the highest**.
A coloured object **reflects** its own colour and **absorbs** the others. A red apple reflects red light and absorbs the rest.
**White** objects reflect all colours. **Black** objects absorb all colours.
In coloured light, an object looks its own colour only if that colour is in the light; otherwise it reflects nothing and looks **black**. A white object takes the colour of the light.
A **filter** **transmits** (lets through) only its own colour and **absorbs** the rest. A red filter does not add red: it takes the other colours away.
The **primary colours of light** are **red, green and blue**. Red + green = **yellow**, red + blue = **magenta**, green + blue = **cyan**, all three = **white**.

a triangular block of glass that splits white light into colours

topics.title: Waves carry energy
topics.summary: A wave passes energy along through a material while the particles only move to and fro; bigger and faster-vibrating waves carry more.

table.title: Ultrasound at work
head: Use
How it works
rows: vibrations shake the liquid and knock dirt off
vibrations massage and warm deep muscle
echoes from inside the body build a picture
echoes help them find their way and their food

facts: In Year 7 you met sound as a vibration passed from particle to particle. In any wave travelling through a substance, the **particles move to and fro** about one place, but **energy is transferred** in the direction the wave travels.
The material itself does **not** travel along with the wave: only the **energy** does.
Waves with a **bigger amplitude** carry **more energy**: a loud sound or a tall sea wave can do more than a quiet sound or a ripple.
Waves with a **higher frequency** also carry **more energy** (if the amplitude is the same).
**Ultrasound** is sound with a frequency **above 20 000 Hz**, too high for humans to hear. It is still a sound wave, so it needs a material to travel through.
Ultrasound can **clean** delicate things: in an ultrasonic bath, the vibrations shake the liquid so hard that dirt is knocked off jewellery, glasses and surgical instruments.
**Physiotherapists** use ultrasound to **massage** muscles deep under the skin: the vibrations warm and loosen the tissue. Doctors use its **echoes** for scans of unborn babies.

**Wave power** uses the energy of sea waves to make electricity. It is **renewable**, but it depends on the **weather and location**: a stormy, exposed coast gives far more energy than a sheltered bay on a calm day.
keywords: a vibration that transfers energy from place to place without transferring matter
the biggest distance a wave moves from its middle position; bigger amplitude = more energy
the number of waves each second, in hertz (Hz)
sound waves with frequencies higher than humans can hear (above 20 000 Hz)
the range of frequencies an animal can hear
using ultrasound to shake a liquid so it knocks dirt off objects

making electricity from the energy carried by sea waves

topics.title: Light, UV and living cells
topics.summary: The higher the frequency of a light-like wave, the more energy it carries and the more it can damage living cells.

images.caption: Light is one part of a family of waves. Going down, the frequency and the energy carried go up.

facts: Visible light is one member of a family of waves called the **electromagnetic spectrum**. All of them travel at the speed of light and **can travel through a vacuum**.
In order of **increasing frequency**: **radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet (UV), X-rays, gamma rays**.
**Higher frequency = more energy carried** by the wave = **more damage** it can do to living cells.
**Ultraviolet (UV)** has a frequency **higher than light**, so our eyes **cannot see it**. It comes from the Sun and from sunbeds.
UV carries enough energy to harm cells: it causes **sunburn**, can damage the **eyes**, and can damage the **DNA** in skin cells, which can lead to **skin cancer**.
Protect yourself with **sunscreen** (it absorbs or reflects UV), **clothes and hats**, **sunglasses** that block UV, and **shade** in the middle of the day.

**X-rays and gamma rays** have even higher frequencies and carry so much energy that they can damage DNA deep inside the body. Hospitals keep doses small, and radiographers stand behind **lead** screens.
Waves with **lower frequencies than light** (radio waves, most infrared) do not carry enough energy to damage DNA, although strong infrared can burn by heating.

waves with frequencies higher than light, which human eyes cannot detect
waves with frequencies just lower than red light; we feel them as heat
the number of waves each second; higher frequency means more energy

the highest-frequency waves in the spectrum, carrying the most energy

topics.title: Microphones and loudspeakers
topics.summary: A microphone turns the pressure wave of sound into a changing electric current, and a loudspeaker turns it back into sound.

images.caption: A microphone turns the high- and low-pressure pattern of sound into a current that rises and falls in the same pattern.
Inside a loudspeaker: the changing current makes the coil and cone vibrate, pushing the air into a sound wave.

facts: Sound is a **pressure wave**: a repeating pattern of **high-pressure** regions (compressions) and **low-pressure** regions (rarefactions) travelling through the air.
A **microphone** turns the pressure wave of sound into an **electrical signal**: a current that changes in the **same pattern** as the sound.
Inside the microphone, a thin **diaphragm** is pushed in by high pressure and pulled out by low pressure, so it **vibrates** with the sound. Its movement makes the **current change**.
**Higher frequency sound** gives a current that changes **more times each second**; **louder sound** gives **bigger changes** in current. That is why an oscilloscope can show sound.
An **amplifier** makes the small signal from the microphone **bigger**, so it can drive a loudspeaker.
A **loudspeaker** does the opposite: it turns an **electrical signal** back into a **pressure wave** of sound.
In a loudspeaker, the changing current flows through a **coil** next to a **permanent magnet**. The coil is pushed and pulled back and forth, moving the **cone**, which pushes the air to make sound.
The cone vibrates at the **same frequency** as the current, so the sound has the same pitch as the original.
keywords: a wave, like sound, made of repeating high-pressure and low-pressure regions
turns the pressure wave of sound hitting it into an electrical signal
