markScheme.modelAnswer: Her voice is a pressure wave: a pattern of high- and low-pressure regions in the air. These pressure changes push and pull the thin diaphragm in the microphone, so it vibrates. The microphone turns this movement into an electric current that changes in the same pattern as the sound: more often for a higher note, by more for a louder one. An amplifier makes this signal bigger. The current then flows through a coil in the loudspeaker, which sits next to a permanent magnet. As the current changes, the coil is pushed and pulled back and forth, and it moves the cone. The cone pushes on the air, making a pressure wave with the same frequency as the signal, so we hear her voice.

questions.tip: Go in order: voice → microphone → signal → amplifier → loudspeaker → sound.

topics.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves
topics.summary: In every wave the energy moves on while the material stays put; how the material vibrates makes it transverse or longitudinal.

images.caption: A slinky can show both kinds of wave: shake it side to side for a transverse wave, push and pull it for a longitudinal wave.

facts: **Waves** are vibrations that **transport energy** from place to place **without transporting matter**.
A slinky or rope is a **physical model** of a wave: a pulse travels from one end to the other, but each coil only moves about its own place and ends up where it started.

In a **transverse wave** the vibrations are **at right angles (perpendicular)** to the direction the wave travels. Examples: **light** (and all the electromagnetic spectrum), **ripples on water**, a wave on a **rope** or **guitar string**.
In a **longitudinal wave** the vibrations are **parallel** to (along) the direction the wave travels, making **compressions** and **rarefactions**. Example: **sound** (Year 7) and ultrasound.
Transverse waves have **crests** (peaks) and **troughs**. Longitudinal waves have **compressions** and **rarefactions**. Both have a **wavelength**, **frequency** and **amplitude**.
**Wave speed = distance ÷ time.** A wave that travels 30 m in 6 s has a speed of 5 m/s.
**Wave speed = frequency × wavelength.** A wave with frequency 4 Hz and wavelength 2 m travels at 8 m/s.
Earthquakes send both kinds through the Earth: **P-waves** are longitudinal and **S-waves** are transverse.
keywords: a vibration that transports energy from place to place without transporting matter
the direction of vibration is perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction the wave travels
the direction of vibration is parallel to the direction the wave travels
in the same line, side by side
the highest point of a transverse wave
the lowest point of a transverse wave
a region in a longitudinal wave where particles are close together
a region in a longitudinal wave where particles are spread out
how far a wave travels each second, in m/s

questions.stem: Which part of the wave is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: A crest is the top of a transverse wave.

questions.stem: Which part of the wave is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: A trough is the bottom of a transverse wave.

questions.stem: Which part of the wave is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: In a compression the coils (or particles) are squashed close together.

questions.stem: Which part of the wave is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: In a rarefaction the coils (or particles) are spread out.

questions.stem: In which type of wave are the vibrations at right angles to the direction the wave travels?
questions.explain: Transverse means 'across': the material moves across the direction the energy travels.

questions.stem: In which type of wave are the vibrations parallel to the direction the wave travels?
questions.explain: In a longitudinal wave the material moves back and forth along the line the wave travels.

questions.stem: What word means 'at right angles to'?
questions.explain: Perpendicular lines meet at 90°. In a transverse wave the vibration is perpendicular to the wave's direction.

questions.stem: Which of these is a longitudinal wave?
choices: a wave on a guitar string
questions.explain: Sound travels as compressions and rarefactions, with the particles moving back and forth along the wave's direction.

questions.stem: Which of these is a transverse wave?
choices: a slinky pushed and pulled along its length
questions.explain: Light, and every wave in the electromagnetic spectrum, is transverse.

questions.stem: You want to make a longitudinal wave on a slinky lying on the floor. What should you do?
questions.answer: push and pull one end along the slinky's length
choices: move one end from side to side
stretch it and let go of both ends
questions.explain: Pushing and pulling makes the coils vibrate along the slinky, making compressions and rarefactions.

questions.stem: When a wave travels along a rope, bits of the rope move from one end to the other.
questions.explain: Each bit of rope only moves up and down about its own place. The energy travels along the rope, not the rope itself.

questions.stem: A transverse wave has crests and troughs. What do longitudinal waves have instead?
questions.explain: A longitudinal wave has regions where the particles are squashed (compressions) and spread out (rarefactions).

questions.stem: A water wave travels 30 m in 6 s. What is its speed, in m/s?
questions.explain: Speed = distance ÷ time = 30 ÷ 6 = 5 m/s.

questions.stem: A wave has a frequency of 4 Hz and a wavelength of 2 m. What is its speed, in m/s?
questions.explain: Wave speed = frequency × wavelength = 4 × 2 = 8 m/s.

questions.stem: A sound wave has a frequency of 110 Hz and a wavelength of 3 m. What is its speed, in m/s?
questions.explain: Wave speed = frequency × wavelength = 110 × 3 = 330 m/s, the speed of sound in air.

questions.stem: Which statement is true for BOTH transverse and longitudinal waves?
questions.answer: they transfer energy without transferring matter
choices: they can travel through a vacuum
they vibrate at right angles to their direction
questions.explain: All waves carry energy from place to place while the material only vibrates about one position.

questions.stem: Earthquake S-waves are transverse and P-waves are longitudinal.
questions.explain: P-waves push and pull the rock along the direction they travel; S-waves shake it from side to side.

questions.stem: Describe the similarities and differences between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave. Give an example of each.

acceptablePoints.point: both transfer energy without transferring matter / the material only vibrates about one place
in a transverse wave the vibrations are at right angles (perpendicular) to the direction of travel
in a longitudinal wave the vibrations are parallel to / along the direction of travel
transverse waves have crests and troughs; longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions
example of a transverse wave: light / water ripples / wave on a rope or string / S-wave
example of a longitudinal wave: sound / ultrasound / P-wave

award.4: four points, including at least one similarity, one difference and an example

markScheme.modelAnswer: Both kinds of wave transfer energy from place to place without moving the material along with them. In a transverse wave, such as light or a ripple on water, the material vibrates at right angles to the direction the wave travels, making crests and troughs. In a longitudinal wave, such as sound, the material vibrates back and forth along the direction of travel, making compressions and rarefactions.

topics.title: Reflection, absorption and transmission
topics.summary: When a wave reaches a new material, its energy can bounce back, be taken in, or pass through, and usually a mix of all three happens.

images.caption: A wave meeting a material: some energy is reflected, some absorbed and some transmitted, so the wave that gets through is smaller.

facts: When a wave reaches the boundary of a new material, three things can happen: it can be **reflected** (bounce back), **absorbed** (its energy is taken in by the material) or **transmitted** (pass through).
**Usually all three happen at once**, in different amounts. The energy of the incoming wave is shared between them.
**Reflection:** the wave bounces back. For a flat surface the **angle of incidence = angle of reflection** (Year 7). Echoes and mirror images are reflections.
**Absorption:** the energy goes into the material, usually **warming it up**. Dark, matt surfaces absorb most light; soft foam and curtains absorb sound.
**Transmission:** the wave travels **through** the material. The transmitted wave has a **smaller amplitude** if some energy was reflected or absorbed.
A **ripple tank** models this with water waves: a barrier reflects them, and a beach of sponge absorbs them so they do not bounce back.
Reflection and transmission do **not change the frequency** of a wave: a reflected sound has the same pitch, and green light through clear glass stays green.
Examples: **glass** transmits light; **water in food** absorbs microwaves and gets hot; **X-rays** are transmitted by soft tissue but absorbed by **bone**, which is why bones show up on an X-ray.
keywords: a wave bouncing back from a surface
a material taking in a wave's energy, usually warming up
where waves travel through a medium rather than being absorbed or reflected
the material a wave travels through
a shallow tank of water used to model how waves behave
transmits light so you can see clearly through it

questions.stem: What has happened to the wave labelled {L}?
questions.explain: This part of the wave has bounced back from the surface of the material.

questions.stem: What is happening to the wave's energy at {L}?
questions.explain: This energy is taken in by the material and warms it up.

questions.stem: What has happened to the wave labelled {L}?
questions.explain: This part of the wave has passed through the material. It is smaller because some energy was reflected or absorbed.

questions.stem: What is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The incoming (incident) wave carries energy towards the material.

questions.stem: When a wave travels through a material rather than being absorbed or reflected, what is this called?
questions.explain: Transmission means the wave passes through the material and comes out the other side.

questions.stem: When a material takes in the energy of a wave and warms up, the wave has been…
questions.explain: Absorbed energy goes into the material, usually as a store of thermal energy, so it warms up.

questions.stem: A wave bounces back from a surface. What is this called?
questions.explain: Reflection is a wave bouncing back. Echoes are reflected sound.

questions.stem: When a wave meets a new material, only one of reflection, absorption and transmission can happen.
questions.explain: Usually all three happen at once: the wave's energy is split between them.

questions.stem: Light passes through a sheet of tinted glass. Why is the light that comes out dimmer?
questions.answer: some of the light energy was reflected or absorbed by the glass
choices: the glass changed the light into sound
the light slowed down and stopped
questions.explain: Only part of the energy is transmitted; the rest was reflected or absorbed, so the transmitted light has a smaller amplitude.

questions.stem: In a ripple tank, why is a sloping sponge 'beach' put at one end?
questions.answer: it absorbs the waves so they do not reflect back and confuse the pattern
choices: it reflects the waves back more strongly
it makes the waves travel faster
questions.explain: The sponge takes in the waves' energy, so few waves bounce back from that end.

questions.stem: Why do bones show up white on an X-ray picture?
questions.answer: bone absorbs X-rays, but soft tissue transmits them
choices: bone reflects X-rays, while soft tissue absorbs them
bone gives out its own X-rays
soft tissue absorbs X-rays, while bone transmits them
questions.explain: X-rays pass through soft tissue to the detector, but bone absorbs them, leaving a pale shadow of the bone.

questions.stem: A microwave oven heats a bowl of soup. What happens to the microwaves in the soup?
questions.answer: the water in the soup absorbs them and warms up
choices: the soup reflects them all back
the soup transmits them without warming
questions.explain: Water absorbs microwave energy, so its particles move faster and the soup gets hot.

questions.stem: On a sunny day, a black car gets hotter than a white car. Why?
questions.answer: the black surface absorbs more light, while the white surface reflects more
choices: the black surface reflects more light
the white car transmits light through its body
questions.explain: Absorbed light energy warms the car. White surfaces reflect most of the light, so less is absorbed.

questions.stem: When a sound is reflected as an echo, its frequency (pitch) stays the same.
questions.explain: Reflection changes the direction of a wave, not its frequency, so an echo has the same pitch.

questions.stem: A recording studio has soft foam on the walls so the sound does not echo. What happens to the sound's energy at the foam?
questions.explain: Soft, uneven materials absorb sound energy instead of reflecting it, so there are fewer echoes.

questions.stem: Clear window glass lets light through. Is most of the light reflected, absorbed or transmitted?
questions.explain: Glass is transparent: most of the light passes through. A little is reflected, which is why you can see faint reflections in a window.

questions.stem: A sound wave meets a brick wall. Some of it can still be heard, more quietly, on the other side. Use the ideas of reflection, absorption and transmission to explain why.

acceptablePoints.point: some of the sound energy is reflected by the wall / bounces back as an echo
some of the energy is absorbed by the wall / warms the wall
the rest is transmitted through the wall
the transmitted wave has less energy / a smaller amplitude, so it is quieter

markScheme.modelAnswer: When the sound reaches the wall, some of its energy is reflected back into the first room, and some is absorbed by the bricks, warming them very slightly. Only the rest is transmitted through the wall. The transmitted sound carries less energy, so it has a smaller amplitude and sounds quieter on the other side.

topics.title: Sound and light compared; waves combining
topics.summary: Sound and light are both waves but behave very differently, and when two waves meet they can add up or cancel out.

images.caption: When two waves meet in step they add up to a bigger wave; when they meet out of step they cancel out.

facts: Sound and light are both **waves** that **transfer energy**, and both can be **reflected, absorbed and transmitted**.

**Sound** is **longitudinal** and needs a **medium** (particles); it **cannot** cross a vacuum. **Light** is **transverse** and **can travel through a vacuum**: sunlight crosses empty space to reach us.
**Light is much faster:** about **300 000 000 m/s**, while sound in air is about **330 m/s**.
Sound travels **fastest in solids**; light travels **fastest in a vacuum** and slows down in glass and water (which is why it refracts).
When two waves meet, they **combine**: their effects **add up**. This is called **superposition**.
If two waves meet **in step** (crest on crest), they make a **bigger wave**: louder sound, or a taller water wave.
If they meet **out of step** (crest on trough), they **cancel out**: quiet sound or flat water.
**Noise-cancelling headphones** use this: a microphone picks up outside noise and the headphones play the **opposite** wave, so the two cancel.
keywords: a material a wave travels through
two waves meeting and their effects adding together
crests meet crests and troughs meet troughs; the waves add up
crests meet troughs; the waves cancel out
making an opposite sound wave so that unwanted noise cancels out

questions.stem: Which can travel through a vacuum: sound or light?
questions.explain: Light does not need particles to carry it. Sound does, so it cannot cross a vacuum.

questions.stem: Is sound a transverse or a longitudinal wave?
questions.explain: Sound particles vibrate back and forth along the direction the sound travels.

questions.stem: Is light a transverse or a longitudinal wave?
questions.explain: Light, like every wave in the electromagnetic spectrum, is transverse.

questions.stem: Which is a property that sound and light SHARE?
choices: both need a medium to travel
questions.explain: Both are waves, so both can be reflected, absorbed and transmitted. Echoes reflect sound; mirrors reflect light.

questions.stem: In which material does sound travel fastest?
questions.explain: Sound is passed on by particles, and in solids they are packed closely and strongly linked, so sound travels fastest.

questions.stem: In which does light travel fastest?
questions.explain: Light is fastest in a vacuum, about 300 000 000 m/s. It slows down in glass and water.

questions.stem: About how many times faster than sound in air is light: a hundred, a thousand or a million?
questions.explain: Light: about 300 000 000 m/s. Sound: about 330 m/s. That is roughly a million times slower.

questions.stem: We can see the Sun but cannot hear it, because sound cannot cross the vacuum of space.
questions.explain: Light crosses empty space; sound has no particles to travel through there.

questions.stem: Two waves meet with crest on crest. Do they make a bigger wave or cancel out?
questions.explain: In step, the waves add up: the crests add to a bigger crest and the troughs to a deeper trough.

questions.stem: Two waves of the same size meet with crest on trough. What happens?
questions.explain: Out of step, the crest of one fills the trough of the other, so the waves cancel.

questions.stem: What is the name for two waves meeting and their effects adding together?
questions.explain: Superposition: at each point, the two waves' displacements add (a crest plus a trough gives zero).

questions.stem: How do noise-cancelling headphones work?
questions.answer: they play a sound wave that is out of step with the noise, so the two cancel
choices: they play the same noise louder
they reflect the noise back with mirrors
they absorb all sound, including music
questions.explain: The headphones make the opposite wave to the noise: its crests line up with the noise's troughs, so they cancel.

questions.stem: Two loudspeakers play the same note. As you walk across the room, the sound gets loud, then quiet, then loud. Why?
questions.answer: the waves from the two speakers meet in step in some places and out of step in others
choices: sound travels faster in some parts of the room
your ears stop working for a moment
questions.explain: Where the waves arrive in step they add up (loud); where they arrive out of step they cancel (quiet).

questions.stem: When two waves combine in step, the new wave has a bigger amplitude than either wave alone.
questions.explain: Crest adds to crest, so the combined wave is taller: twice as tall if the waves are the same size.

questions.stem: Compare sound waves and light waves. Give similarities and differences.

acceptablePoints.point: both are waves that transfer energy
both can be reflected / absorbed / transmitted
sound is longitudinal, light is transverse
sound needs a medium / cannot travel through a vacuum; light can travel through a vacuum
light is much faster (about 300 000 000 m/s) than sound (about 330 m/s in air)
sound travels fastest in solids; light travels fastest in a vacuum

award.4: four points, including at least one similarity and one difference

markScheme.modelAnswer: Sound and light are both waves that transfer energy, and both can be reflected, absorbed and transmitted. But sound is a longitudinal wave that needs particles to travel, so it cannot cross a vacuum, while light is a transverse wave that can travel through a vacuum. Light is also far faster: about 300 000 000 m/s, compared with about 330 m/s for sound in air. Sound travels fastest in solids, but light travels fastest in a vacuum.

topics.title: Checkpoint: particles and solutions (Tue 24 Nov)
topics.source: The checkpoint’s topic list on Arbor (lessons 1–9). The notes and questions are ours, not the school’s.
topics.summary: All nine lessons on one page, plus checkpoint-style questions. “Practise all of it” mixes these with the questions from the topic notes.

links.title: Solids, liquids and gases: the particle model
links.note: lessons 1–2 (a GCSE page, more than you need)

links.title: What is the process of diffusion?

images.caption: Lessons 1–2: the same particles as a solid, a liquid and a gas.
Lessons 3–4: the temperature stays flat while ice melts and while water boils.

table.title: The nine lessons in one line each
head: Lesson
Remember
rows: everything is made of tiny particles that are always moving
solid: touching, pattern, vibrate · liquid: touching, no pattern, slide · gas: far apart, fast, all directions
same temperature (melting point); heat in to melt, heat out to freeze
at the boiling point, bubbles all through the liquid; temperature stays flat
evaporating (surface, any temperature), condensing (gas → liquid), subliming (solid → gas)
particles spread from many to few by themselves; fastest in gases and when warm
particles hitting the walls; more particles, smaller space or hotter = more pressure
atoms and molecules; same particles in every state; particles don't grow or melt
solute + solvent = solution; mass is conserved; saturated = no more dissolves

facts: **Changes of state:** melting (solid → liquid), freezing (liquid → solid), boiling and evaporating (liquid → gas), condensing (gas → liquid), subliming (solid → gas). They are **physical changes**: reversible, no new substance, **mass stays the same**.
**Heating** gives particles **energy**: they move or vibrate faster. Melting and boiling **take in** energy; freezing and condensing **give out** energy.
**Melting point = freezing point.** Water melts and freezes at **0 °C** and boils at **100 °C**. Solid below the melting point, liquid between, gas above the boiling point.
**Flat parts of a heating curve:** while a substance melts or boils its temperature does not rise; the energy goes into breaking the particles out of their arrangement.

**Boiling vs evaporating:** boiling happens **at the boiling point**, **all through** the liquid (bubbles); evaporating happens at **any temperature**, only at the **surface**. Evaporation is faster when it's **warm, windy** or the liquid is **spread out**.
**Diffusion** needs no stirring: particles move randomly from **high to low concentration**. Faster in **gases** than liquids, faster when **hotter**; not in solids.
**Gas pressure** comes from particles **colliding with the walls**. Heating makes them hit **harder and more often**, so the pressure rises.

**Pressure** is a force pushing on an area. Gas particles fly in **straight lines** until they hit something, so they keep hitting every wall. A pumped-up tyre is hard because **more particles push inside than outside**; squash a gas (smaller volume) and the walls are hit **more often**, so its pressure rises.

**Solutions:** the **solute** dissolves in the **solvent** to make a **solution**. Its particles spread out between the solvent particles: they don't disappear (you can still taste sugar). **Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent.**

**Physical or chemical?** Changes of state and dissolving are **physical changes**: no new substance, easy to reverse. A **chemical change** makes a **new substance** (iron + sulfur heated → iron sulfide). **Dissolving is not diffusion**: a solid first dissolves, then its particles diffuse through the liquid. Diffusion also moves substances **into and out of cells**.

**Why melting points differ:** particles attract each other. The **stronger the attraction**, the more energy is needed to separate them, so the **higher** the melting and boiling points (ice 0 °C, chocolate about 35 °C).

**Solubility depends on** the **solute**, the **solvent** (water isn't the only one: polystyrene dissolves in propanone) and the **temperature**. Most **solids** dissolve **more** when hotter, so cooling a saturated solution makes **crystals**; most **gases** dissolve **less** when hotter.
**Exam tip:** for “explain using particles”, always say what the particles **do** (move faster, hit the walls, spread out) and **why** that causes what you see. Count the marks: 3 marks = 3 points.
keywords: the temperature at which a solid melts (and its liquid freezes)
the temperature at which a liquid boils
a solid turning straight into a gas
particles spreading out by themselves from high to low concentration
the push of gas particles colliding with the walls of their container
the liquid it dissolves in (e.g. water)
a solution in which no more solute can dissolve

questions.stem: What is the change of state from liquid to solid called?
questions.explain: Freezing is the reverse of melting, and happens at the same temperature.

questions.stem: What is the change of state from gas to liquid called?
questions.explain: Gas particles cool, slow down and come close together again as a liquid.

questions.stem: What is the change of state from solid straight to gas called?
questions.explain: Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) sublimes: it never becomes a liquid.

questions.stem: At what temperature, in °C, does pure water freeze?
questions.explain: Water's melting point and freezing point are the same: 0 °C.

questions.stem: At what temperature, in °C, does pure water boil?
questions.explain: Pure water boils at 100 °C (at normal air pressure).

questions.stem: Butter melts at about 35 °C. At what temperature does liquid butter freeze?
questions.explain: A substance freezes at the same temperature as it melts.

questions.stem: A substance melts at 80 °C and boils at 220 °C. What state is it in at 150 °C?
questions.explain: 150 °C is above its melting point but below its boiling point, so it is a liquid.

questions.stem: Water is boiling in a kettle at 100 °C. The kettle keeps heating. What happens to the water's temperature?
questions.answer: it stays at 100 °C until all the water has boiled
questions.explain: While a liquid boils, the energy goes into freeing particles from the liquid, not into making it hotter.

questions.stem: Which change of state gives out energy to the surroundings?
questions.explain: Freezing and condensing give out energy as particles settle back together. Melting, boiling and evaporating take energy in.

questions.stem: Where in a liquid does evaporation happen?
questions.explain: Only particles at the surface with enough energy can escape. Boiling happens all through the liquid.

questions.stem: Water can evaporate at room temperature.
questions.explain: Evaporation happens at any temperature. That is how puddles dry without boiling.

questions.stem: What are the bubbles that appear all through boiling water made of?
questions.explain: At the boiling point, liquid water turns to gas inside the liquid, making bubbles of steam.

questions.stem: Which of these will make a puddle dry fastest?
choices: a warm day with no wind
questions.explain: Warmth gives particles more energy to escape, and wind carries away the particles that have escaped.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign that diffusion is happening?
questions.answer: the smell of a bin spreads through the kitchen
choices: steam turns to water on a window
a ball bounces off a wall
questions.explain: Smell particles spread out from the bin by themselves, from where there are many to where there are few.

questions.stem: Why is diffusion faster in a gas than in a liquid?
questions.answer: gas particles move faster and have more space
questions.explain: Fast particles with lots of space between them spread out quickly.

questions.stem: Why doesn't diffusion happen in a solid?
questions.answer: the particles are held in place and can only vibrate
choices: solid particles don't move at all
questions.explain: Solid particles vibrate on the spot but can't move about, so they can't spread out.

questions.stem: A tea bag is put in hot water and another in cold water. In which will the colour spread faster: hot or cold?
questions.explain: In hot water the particles move faster, so diffusion is faster.

questions.stem: A tyre is pumped up with more air. Why does the pressure inside go up?
questions.answer: more particles hit the inside walls more often
choices: the air gets heavier and pushes down
questions.explain: More particles in the same space means more collisions with the walls each second.

questions.stem: Gas particles push on every wall of a sealed container, not just the bottom.
questions.explain: Gas particles move in all directions, so they hit every wall, top and sides included.

questions.stem: A sealed bottle of air is warmed in the sun. Does the pressure inside go up or down?
questions.explain: Warmer particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often, so the pressure rises.

questions.stem: Sugar dissolves in tea. Which is the solute?
questions.explain: The solute is what dissolves (the sugar); the solvent is the liquid it dissolves in.

questions.stem: Sugar dissolves in tea. What is the sweet tea called?
questions.explain: Solute + solvent = solution.

questions.stem: 5 g of salt dissolves completely in 95 g of water. What is the mass of the solution, in grams?
questions.explain: Mass is conserved: 5 g + 95 g = 100 g. The salt particles are still there, just spread out.

questions.stem: Salt seems to disappear when stirred into water. What has really happened to the salt particles?
questions.answer: they have spread out between the water particles
questions.explain: Dissolving isn't melting or destroying: the solute particles mix in between the solvent particles. You can still taste the salt.

questions.stem: What word describes a solution in which no more solute can dissolve?
questions.explain: Once a solution is saturated, any extra solute just sits at the bottom.

questions.stem: How can you usually get more sugar to dissolve in the same amount of water?
questions.explain: For most solids, solubility rises as the temperature rises.

questions.stem: Which is the correct difference between dissolving and melting?
questions.answer: dissolving needs a solvent; melting needs only one substance and heat
choices: melting needs a solvent; dissolving needs heat
questions.explain: Sugar dissolving in water involves two substances. Ice melting involves just one, heated up.

questions.stem: A particle diagram shows particles touching, in rows, all the same. What does it show?
questions.explain: Touching + regular pattern = a solid.

questions.stem: A particle diagram shows a few particles far apart, with arrows pointing in different directions. What does it show?
questions.explain: Far apart, moving fast in all directions = a gas.

questions.stem: When 100 g of water freezes, you get less than 100 g of ice.
questions.explain: Changes of state conserve mass: the same particles are there, so it's still 100 g.

questions.stem: Pressure is…
questions.answer: a force pushing on a certain area
choices: the number of particles in a container
questions.explain: Pressure is how much force pushes on each bit of area. Gas pressure is the force of the particles hitting the walls.

questions.stem: A sealed syringe of air is squashed into a smaller volume. Why does the pressure go up?
questions.answer: the particles hit the walls more often
choices: the particles get hotter and bigger
questions.explain: Same particles, less space: each part of the wall gets hit more often, so the pressure rises.

questions.stem: How do gas particles move?
questions.answer: quickly, in straight lines, in random directions, until they hit something
questions.explain: Gas particles fly in straight lines until they bump into another particle or a wall, then change direction — so their movement is random.

questions.stem: Why is a pumped-up tyre hard?
questions.answer: more air particles push on the inside of the tyre than on the outside
choices: the rubber gets harder when air is added
the air inside is a solid
there are no particles outside the tyre
questions.explain: The tyre has more particles packed inside, so the push from inside is bigger than the push from the air outside.

questions.stem: If you sit on an exercise ball, it squashes until the air pressure inside is big enough to hold you up.
questions.explain: Squashing makes the volume smaller, so the pressure rises until it balances your weight.

questions.stem: A pumped-up beach ball is left in a freezer for 30 minutes. What will it be like?
questions.answer: softer, because the pressure inside has dropped
choices: harder, because cold makes the pressure rise
questions.explain: The cold gas particles have less energy, so they hit the inside of the ball less often and less hard: lower pressure, softer ball.

questions.stem: What is the word for a prediction you can test, with a scientific reason, like “the ball will go soft in the freezer because the gas particles slow down”?
questions.explain: A hypothesis is a testable idea with a reason. You test it by doing the investigation.

questions.stem: Which state has a fixed volume but no fixed shape?

topics.title: Solids, liquids and gases
topics.summary: How the arrangement and movement of particles explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases.

images.caption: The same particles arranged as a solid, a liquid and a gas.

table.title: Comparing the three states
head: Solid
Liquid
Gas
rows: takes the shape of its container

facts: Everything is made of **particles** (atoms or molecules). They are far too small to see, even with a light microscope.

The **particle model** explains how a substance behaves from how its particles are **arranged** and how they **move**. A substance has the **same particles** in all three states — only the arrangement and movement change.
**Solid:** particles **touching** in a **regular pattern**, held in place, **vibrating on the spot**. So a solid keeps its shape, cannot flow and cannot be squashed.

**Liquid:** particles still **touching** but in **no pattern**, and they **slide past each other**. So a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container, but hardly squashes — there are no gaps to push the particles into.
**Gas:** particles **far apart**, in no pattern, moving **fast in all directions**. So a gas spreads out to fill any container, flows, and is easy to **compress** (squash) because of the big spaces.

**Density** is how much mass there is in a certain volume — how closely packed the particles are. Solids and liquids are dense; gases have a very low density. (Ice is unusual: it is less dense than water, so it floats.)
When something is heated its particles **move or vibrate faster** and get a little **further apart**, so it **expands**. The particles themselves never get bigger, melt or change shape.

Some materials are tricky to classify. **Sand** pours like a liquid, but every grain is a solid with a fixed shape. **Toothpaste** and **jelly** keep their shape until pushed. Decide by asking what the particles of each part are doing.

the idea that everything is made of tiny moving particles, used to explain how substances behave
move quickly backwards and forwards on the spot
how much mass there is in a certain volume; how close together the particles are
get bigger in volume (the particles move further apart)

squashing pushes the gas particles closer together into the spaces

topics.title: Changes of state
topics.summary: Melting, freezing, evaporating, boiling, condensing and subliming explained by particles gaining or losing energy.

images.caption: The changes of state. Red arrows: particles gain energy. Blue arrows: they lose energy.
Heating ice at a steady rate: the line is flat while the state changes.

table.title: The changes of state
head: Change
From → to
Particles
rows: liquid → gas, at the surface, any temperature
liquid → gas, all through the liquid, at the boiling point

facts: Changes of state are **physical changes**: the particles stay the same, no new substance is made, they can be reversed, and the **mass stays the same**.
**Heating** gives the particles more **energy**, so they move or vibrate faster. **Cooling** takes energy away, so they slow down.

**Melting** happens at the **melting point**: the particles vibrate so much that they break out of their fixed pattern. **Freezing** happens at the **same temperature**, when the particles lose energy and settle back into a pattern.

**Boiling** happens at the **boiling point**, with bubbles of gas forming all through the liquid. **Evaporating** happens only at the **surface**, at **any temperature** — the fastest particles escape. That is how puddles and washing dry.
**Condensing** is gas turning back into liquid when it cools — like mist on a cold bathroom mirror.
**Subliming** is a solid turning straight into a gas, e.g. **dry ice** (solid carbon dioxide) or iodine.

A substance is a **solid below its melting point**, a **liquid between** its melting and boiling points, and a **gas above its boiling point**. Water: melting point **0 °C**, boiling point **100 °C**.
On a **heating curve** the temperature stays **flat** while the substance melts or boils: the energy goes into freeing the particles, not into making them hotter.
keywords: change from solid to liquid at the melting point
change from liquid to solid at the melting point
change from liquid to gas at the surface, at any temperature
change from liquid to gas all through the liquid, at the boiling point
change from gas to liquid when it cools

the temperature at which a solid melts (and a liquid freezes)
the temperature at which a liquid boils

topics.title: Diffusion and gas pressure
topics.summary: How moving particles spread out by themselves, and how their collisions with walls make gas pressure.

images.caption: Diffusion: perfume particles spread out among the air particles by themselves.
Gas pressure comes from particles hitting the walls of the container.

facts: **Diffusion**: particles of a liquid or gas spread out by their own **random movement**, from where there are **lots** of them (high concentration) to where there are **fewer** (low concentration). No stirring is needed.
Examples: the smell of perfume or cooking spreads across a room; a drop of ink slowly colours a glass of water; tea spreading from a tea bag.
Diffusion is **faster in gases** than in liquids (the particles move faster and have more space) and **faster when it is warmer**. It does not happen in solids, where particles cannot move about.
**Gas pressure** is caused by gas particles **colliding with the walls** of their container. Each hit gives a tiny push; all the pushes together make the pressure.

The pressure goes **up** when there are **more particles** in the same space (pumping up a tyre), when the gas is **squashed** into a smaller volume, or when it is **heated** (the particles move faster, so they hit the walls **harder and more often**).

That is why a balloon grows when you blow more air in, why an aerosol can must never be heated, and why a sealed crisp packet puffs up high on a mountain, where fewer air particles push on the outside.

**Evidence for particles:** smells spread (diffusion); gases can be squashed (there are spaces); sugar "disappears" in tea but the tea tastes sweet; under a microscope, specks of smoke or pollen **jiggle randomly** (**Brownian motion**) because invisible particles keep bumping into them.

topics.title: Inside particles
topics.summary: What particles really are: atoms and molecules, why each substance has its own particles, and what changes (and what doesn't) when a substance changes state.

images.caption: Some particles are single atoms; many are molecules: atoms joined together. Each colour is a different kind of atom.

table.title: What changes when a substance changes state?
head: Changes?
Why
rows: the same particles are there in every state
particles never grow, shrink or melt
nothing is added or taken away, so mass is conserved
pattern in a solid, no pattern in a liquid or gas
faster when heated, slower when cooled
big spaces in a gas, tiny gaps in a solid or liquid

facts: Particles are the tiny pieces that every substance is made of. The smallest are **atoms**. An **atom** is the smallest part of an element that can exist.

Many particles are **molecules**: **two or more atoms joined together**. A water particle is a molecule of **2 hydrogen atoms + 1 oxygen atom** (H₂O). An oxygen particle in the air is **2 oxygen atoms** joined (O₂).

**Each substance has its own particles.** All the particles in pure water are water molecules; all the particles in pure oxygen are oxygen molecules. Different substances have particles that differ in **size, mass and shape**, which is why they have different properties (different melting points, colours, densities).
A substance keeps the **same particles in every state.** Ice, liquid water and steam are all made of water molecules. Only the **arrangement**, **movement** and **spaces** between them change.

Particles themselves **do not change**: they don't get bigger when heated, they don't melt, and they have no colour or smell of their own. A single particle of copper isn't shiny; shininess belongs to lots of particles together. These are **properties of the substance, not of one particle**.
**Between the particles is empty space**, not air. In a gas the particles are far apart with nothing in between.
Atoms are incredibly small: about **10 million** side by side would fit across a millimetre. Even the best light microscope can't show them.

The particle model is a **model**: a simple picture that explains a lot (states, changes of state, diffusion, pressure). Drawing particles as hard balls leaves things out: real particles are not coloured balls and the forces between them aren't shown.
keywords: the smallest part of an element that can exist
two or more atoms joined together
one kind of matter, made of one kind of particle (e.g. water, oxygen, copper)
what a substance is like or does, e.g. its melting point, colour or density
a simple way of picturing something that helps explain what we see

questions.stem: What is the name for the smallest part of an element that can exist?

questions.stem: What is the name for two or more atoms joined together?

questions.stem: Ice is heated until it becomes steam. What happens to the water particles themselves?
questions.answer: they stay the same; only their arrangement and movement change

questions.explain: Ice, water and steam are all made of the same water molecules. Heating changes how they are arranged and how fast they move, never the particles themselves.

questions.stem: When a metal bar is heated, each of its particles gets bigger.
questions.explain: The bar expands because the particles vibrate more and move a little further apart. Each particle stays the same size.

questions.stem: One single particle of copper is shiny and orange-brown, just like a copper coin.
questions.explain: Colour and shininess are properties of lots of particles together, not of one particle on its own.

questions.stem: What is between the particles in a gas?
questions.explain: The spaces between particles are empty. 'Air' would be wrong: air is itself made of particles.

questions.stem: Why do water and oxygen have different melting and boiling points?
questions.answer: they are made of different particles
choices: they have the same particles arranged differently
questions.explain: Each substance has its own particles, with their own size, mass and shape, so each substance has its own properties.

questions.stem: All the particles in a sample of pure water are the same.
questions.explain: A pure substance contains only one kind of particle: here, water molecules.

questions.stem: Steam, liquid water and ice are three states of one substance. Which substance's particles are in all three?
questions.explain: All three are water: the same water molecules, just arranged and moving differently.

questions.stem: Why can't we see atoms with a light microscope?
choices: they move too fast to see
questions.explain: Atoms are so tiny that about 10 million side by side fit across one millimetre, far below what light microscopes can show.

questions.stem: A particle diagram shows particles as coloured balls. What does this model leave out?
questions.answer: real particles are not coloured balls, and the forces between them aren't shown
choices: it leaves out the arrangement of the particles
it leaves out that there are three states
nothing: particles really are coloured balls
questions.explain: A model is a simple picture. It explains a lot, but real particles have no colour and the forces holding them together are invisible in the drawing.

questions.stem: An oxygen particle (O₂) is made of how many atoms?
questions.explain: The small 2 after O shows two oxygen atoms joined: an oxygen molecule.

questions.stem: When water boils, the number of water particles stays the same, so the mass is conserved (if no steam escapes).
questions.explain: Changing state doesn't create or destroy particles. If you trap all the steam, its mass equals the mass of the water you started with.

questions.stem: A student says: “When ice melts, the ice particles melt into water particles.” Explain what is wrong with this, using the particle model.

acceptablePoints.point: the particles do not melt / particles themselves do not change
ice and water are made of the same (water) particles / molecules
the particles gain energy and vibrate faster
they break out of their fixed pattern / arrangement changes / they can slide past each other

award.3: one mark per point, up to 3

markScheme.modelAnswer: The particles themselves don't melt or change: ice and liquid water are made of the same water molecules. When ice is heated the particles gain energy and vibrate faster until they break out of their fixed pattern and can slide past each other. Only the arrangement and movement change.

topics.title: Pure substances, mixtures and solutions
topics.summary: What makes a substance pure, how things dissolve, how to read a solubility curve, and how to get a solid back by evaporating.

images.caption: A solubility curve: how much of solid X dissolves in 100 g of water at each temperature.
Evaporating the water from a salt solution.

facts: A **pure substance** is just one element or one compound, with nothing mixed in. It melts and boils at **fixed temperatures** (pure water: 0 °C and 100 °C).

A **mixture** is two or more substances mixed but not joined, so it can be separated using differences in their **physical properties**. It melts or boils over a **range** of temperatures. **Air, fruit juice, sea water and milk are all mixtures.** ("Pure orange juice" on a carton only means nothing was added.)

**Dissolving:** a **solute** (like sugar) mixes completely with a **solvent** (like water) to make a **solution**. The solvent particles pull the solute particles apart and they spread out in between. The solute is still there — you can taste it.
**Mass is conserved:** mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent. 10 g of salt in 100 g of water makes 110 g of solution.

**Soluble** substances dissolve (salt, sugar in water); **insoluble** ones do not (sand, chalk). A solution is see-through, though it may be coloured. Dissolving is not melting: melting needs one substance and heat.
**Solubility** is the most solute that dissolves in a certain amount of solvent, often given in **g per 100 g of water**. When no more can dissolve, the solution is **saturated**.
For most solids, solubility **rises as the temperature rises**. A **solubility curve** shows this. Cool a hot saturated solution and the solid that no longer fits comes out as **crystals**.

**Evaporation** gets a dissolved solid back: heat the solution in an **evaporating basin** so the water turns to gas and the solid is left. For bigger crystals (**crystallisation**), heat until about half the water has gone, then leave it to cool.

two or more substances mixed together but not joined
the substance (usually a liquid) that does the dissolving

questions.stem: Use the particle model to explain how salt dissolves in water, and why the mass of the salty water equals the mass of the salt plus the water.

acceptablePoints.point: water particles collide with / surround the salt particles and pull them away from the solid

the salt is still there (you can taste it), in particles too small to see
no particles are made or lost, so the total mass stays the same (mass is conserved)

topics.title: Filtration and distillation
topics.summary: Choosing a method to separate a mixture: filtering, evaporating, distilling or using a magnet.

images.caption: Filtration: the insoluble solid stays in the paper.
Simple distillation: boil, then condense the gas back into a pure liquid.

table.title: Which method?
head: Mixture
Method
Why it works
rows: insoluble solid in a liquid (sand and water)
the solid grains are too big to pass through the paper
dissolved solid in a liquid (salt from salt water)
the water turns to gas; the salt does not
pure liquid from a solution (water from sea water)
the water boils off, then condenses in the condenser
the liquid with the lower boiling point boils off first
the dyes travel up the paper at different speeds
a magnetic metal and something else (iron and sulfur)

facts: Choose the method from **how the substances are different**: grain size and solubility (filter), boiling point (evaporate, distil), how well they dissolve in a solvent (chromatography), magnetism (magnet).

**Filtration:** pour the mixture through **filter paper** in a **funnel**. The liquid and anything dissolved in it pass through as the **filtrate**; the insoluble solid stays behind as the **residue**.
Filtration cannot remove a **dissolved** solid: its particles are spread out among the water particles and pass straight through the paper.

**Simple distillation:** heat the solution until the liquid **boils**. The gas goes into the **condenser**, where cold water cools it so it **condenses**. The pure liquid (the **distillate**) drips into the collecting flask; dissolved solids stay in the flask.

**Cold water goes in at the bottom** of the condenser and out at the top, so the cooling jacket stays completely full. The **thermometer bulb** sits level with the side arm to measure the temperature of the gas leaving.
Liquids have **different boiling points** (ethanol 78 °C, water 100 °C), so distillation can also separate two liquids: the one with the **lower boiling point** boils off first.

Complicated mixtures need **several steps**. **Rock salt** (salt + sand and grit): crush it, stir it into warm water so the salt dissolves, **filter** off the sand, then **evaporate** the filtrate to get salt crystals.
**Safety:** wear eye protection, heat gently, and don't boil a solution dry — the solid can spit out.

the liquid that passes through the filter paper
the solid left behind in the filter paper
separating substances by boiling a liquid and condensing the gas
a cooled tube that turns a gas back into a liquid

questions.stem: Rock salt is a mixture of salt and sand. Describe how you would get pure, dry salt crystals from rock salt, explaining why each step works.

acceptablePoints.point: crush the rock salt (pestle and mortar) so the salt dissolves faster / more easily
add (warm) water and stir
the salt dissolves but the sand does not / sand is insoluble
filter the mixture (filter paper and funnel)
the sand stays in the filter paper as the residue because its grains are too big to pass through; the salt solution passes through as the filtrate
heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin so the water evaporates
the salt is left behind as crystals (heat until about half has gone, then leave to crystallise / dry)
a safety point: eye protection / don't heat to dryness because it spits

award.6: one mark per point, up to 6; for full marks at least two steps must say why they work

markScheme.modelAnswer: First crush the rock salt so the salt dissolves more quickly. Add warm water and stir: the salt dissolves but the sand is insoluble. Filter the mixture through filter paper in a funnel. The sand grains are too big to go through, so they stay behind as the residue, while the salt solution passes through as the filtrate. Pour the filtrate into an evaporating basin and heat it gently so the water evaporates. When about half has gone, leave it to cool and dry: salt crystals form. Wear eye protection, because hot salt can spit.

questions.tip: Think in three main steps: dissolve, filter, evaporate — and give a reason for each.

questions.stem: Explain how simple distillation gets pure water from sea water.

the salt stays behind in the flask (it does not boil at 100 °C)
the steam goes into the condenser and is cooled
it condenses back into liquid water, which is collected (the distillate)

award.3: one mark per point, up to 3

markScheme.modelAnswer: The sea water is heated until the water boils. The salt does not turn to gas, so it stays in the flask. The steam passes into the condenser, where cold water cools it, so it condenses back into pure liquid water that drips into the collecting flask.

topics.title: Chromatography
topics.summary: Separating the coloured substances in inks and dyes, and using the results to identify unknown substances.

images.caption: Paper chromatography: the solvent carries the dyes up the paper.
A chromatogram: three known dyes (A, B, C) and two unknown inks (X, Y).

facts: **Chromatography** separates the different **coloured substances** in a mixture, such as the dyes in an ink or a food colouring.

**Method:** draw a **baseline in pencil** about 1–2 cm from the bottom of the paper. Put a small spot of each sample on it. Stand the paper in a beaker with a little **solvent** (water or ethanol), with the solvent **below the baseline**. When the solvent has nearly reached the top, take the paper out, mark the **solvent front** and let it dry. The result is a **chromatogram**.
**How it works:** the solvent soaks up the paper and carries the dyes with it. Dyes that **dissolve better** in the solvent travel **further**, so the dyes spread out.
**Pencil**, because it does not dissolve — pen ink would run up the paper too. **Solvent below the baseline**, or the spots would wash off into the solvent instead of moving up.
A **pure** substance gives **one spot**; a mixture gives two or more. A spot that stays on the baseline is **insoluble** in that solvent.

**Identifying unknowns:** run known substances next to the unknown on the same paper. A spot at the **same height** as a known one is probably that substance. A spot that matches nothing is a substance you did not test.
**How sure can you be?** Two different substances can travel the same distance in one solvent. Repeating with a **different solvent** — and still getting a match — gives much stronger evidence.
keywords: separating coloured substances by letting a solvent carry them up paper
the dried paper showing the separated spots
the pencil line where the samples are spotted
how far the solvent has travelled up the paper
a coloured substance; inks are often mixtures of dyes
made of only one substance, giving one spot

topics.title: The periodic table
topics.summary: How the elements are arranged in groups and periods, where the metals and non-metals are, and how to use patterns in data.

images.caption: A simplified periodic table (periods 1–6). Blue: metals (darker blue: transition metals). Yellow: non-metals. The thick staircase line separates them.

facts: The **periodic table** shows every element (about 118) in one chart. Elements with **similar properties** end up lined up underneath each other.
The columns are **groups** and the rows are **periods**. The main groups are numbered **1 to 7**, then **0** for the last column.
Elements in the **same group react in a similar way**, and their properties often change in a steady **pattern (trend)** as you go down the group.

**Metals** are on the **left** and in the middle; **non-metals** are on the **right**, past the staircase line. (Year 7: the properties of metals and non-metals.) **Hydrogen** sits on its own at the top — it is a non-metal gas.
Some groups have names: **Group 1 = alkali metals**, **Group 7 = halogens**, **Group 0 = noble gases**. The wide middle block holds the **transition metals**, such as iron, copper and gold.

**Physical properties** can be seen or measured **without changing** the substance: melting point, boiling point, density, colour, state, whether it conducts. **Chemical properties** are about how it **reacts** — with water, oxygen or acids.
Going **across a period** the elements change from **metals to non-metals**: sodium and magnesium are shiny metals, sulfur and chlorine are non-metals, argon is an unreactive gas.
**Using data:** if a property rises or falls steadily down a group, a missing value lies **between** its neighbours. A value that does not fit the pattern is an **anomaly**.

In 1869 **Dmitri Mendeleev** arranged the known elements by their properties and left **gaps** for elements nobody had found yet — and predicted what they would be like. Later discoveries matched his predictions.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between a group and a period in the periodic table, and why elements in the same group are put together.

a period is a row (going across)
elements in the same group react in a similar way / have similar (chemical) properties
properties change in a pattern (trend) down a group

markScheme.modelAnswer: A group is a column of the periodic table and a period is a row. Elements in the same group are put together because they have similar properties and react in a similar way; their properties also change in a steady pattern down the group.

topics.title: Groups 1, 7 and 0
topics.summary: The alkali metals, the halogens and the noble gases: how they react, the trends down each group, and predicting the elements you have not met.

images.caption: The melting points of the alkali metals fall steadily going down group 1.

table.title: Group 1 metals with water
head: Metal
Melting point
What you see in water
rows: fizzes fast, melts into a ball and whizzes around
very fast; the hydrogen catches fire with a lilac flame

facts: **Group 1 — alkali metals** (lithium, sodium, potassium…): **soft** enough to cut with a knife, shiny when freshly cut but **tarnish** quickly in air, and very **low density** — lithium, sodium and potassium **float** on water. They are kept **under oil** to stop them reacting with air and water.
With water: **metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen**. The solution left is **alkaline** — that is where the name comes from. Sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen.
Going **down group 1**, the metals get **more reactive** and their **melting points fall**.

**Group 7 — halogens** (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine): **non-metals**, **poisonous**, made of molecules of **two atoms** (Cl₂, Br₂). Chlorine is a pale green **gas**, bromine a red-brown **liquid**, iodine a grey-black **solid** that gives a purple vapour.
Going **down group 7**, melting and boiling points **rise** (gas → liquid → solid), the colours get **darker**, and the halogens get **less reactive**.

Halogens react with metals to make **salts** called **halides**: sodium + chlorine → sodium **chloride**. A **more reactive halogen displaces** a less reactive one from its compound: chlorine + potassium bromide → potassium chloride + bromine.
**Group 0 — noble gases** (helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon): colourless gases that are **very unreactive**, so they exist as **single atoms**. Their boiling points **rise** down the group.
Noble gases are used where nothing must react or burn: **helium** in balloons (less dense than air, does not burn), **argon** inside light bulbs, **neon** in glowing signs.

**Predicting:** an element you have not met follows its group's trend. Rubidium (below potassium) reacts even more violently with water; astatine (below iodine) is a dark solid and the least reactive halogen.
keywords: a group 1 element: soft, reactive, makes alkalis with water
a group 7 element: a reactive, poisonous non-metal
a group 0 element: a very unreactive gas
what a group 1 metal makes with water (e.g. sodium hydroxide)
a compound of a halogen with a metal, e.g. a chloride or bromide
a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive one in a compound
a shiny surface going dull because it reacts with the air

questions.stem: A group 1 metal reacts with water. It makes a metal hydroxide and which gas?
questions.explain: Metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen. The hydrogen is what makes the fizzing.

questions.stem: What happens to the reactivity of the halogens as you go down group 7?
questions.explain: The halogens get less reactive down the group — the opposite trend to group 1. Fluorine is the most reactive.

questions.stem: Why are the alkali metals stored under oil?
questions.answer: to stop them reacting with air and water

because oil makes them less dense

questions.stem: The alkali metals are so hard that you need a saw to cut them.
questions.explain: Alkali metals are soft — you can cut them with a knife, and they get softer down the group.

questions.stem: Which halogen is a red-brown liquid at room temperature?
questions.explain: Bromine is the red-brown liquid. Chlorine above it is a gas; iodine below it is a solid.

questions.stem: What state is chlorine in at room temperature?
questions.explain: Chlorine is a pale green gas: the halogens near the top of the group have low boiling points.

questions.stem: How does the colour of the halogens change as you go down group 7?
questions.explain: Pale green chlorine, red-brown bromine, grey-black iodine: the colours get darker down the group.

questions.stem: Astatine is below iodine in group 7. What is astatine most likely to be like?
questions.answer: a dark solid, less reactive than iodine

a colourless liquid, more reactive than iodine
a dark solid, more reactive than fluorine

questions.stem: Rubidium is below potassium in group 1. What will happen when it is put in water?
questions.answer: it reacts even more violently than potassium, giving off hydrogen
choices: it does not react at all
it reacts more slowly than lithium
questions.explain: Reactivity increases down group 1, so rubidium reacts faster than potassium — it can explode.

questions.stem: Melting points of group 1 (°C): lithium 181, sodium 98, potassium 63, rubidium ?, caesium 28. What is the best estimate for rubidium?
questions.explain: Rubidium lies between potassium (63 °C) and caesium (28 °C), so about 40 °C. (It is really 39 °C.)

questions.stem: Chlorine water is added to colourless potassium iodide solution. What happens?
questions.answer: chlorine displaces iodine, so the solution turns brown
choices: nothing, because iodine is more reactive than chlorine
iodine displaces chlorine, which bubbles off
potassium is displaced as a shiny metal
questions.explain: Chlorine is more reactive than iodine, so it takes iodine's place: chlorine + potassium iodide → potassium chloride + iodine.

questions.stem: Bromine can displace chlorine from sodium chloride solution.
questions.explain: Bromine is less reactive than chlorine, so it cannot push chlorine out of its compound. Nothing happens.

questions.stem: Sodium burns in chlorine gas. Name the white solid that is made.
questions.explain: Sodium + chlorine → sodium chloride. The halogen's name changes to '-ide' in the compound.

questions.stem: Which noble gas fills party balloons, because it is less dense than air and does not burn?
questions.explain: Helium is light and unreactive. Hydrogen is also light but it burns explosively.

questions.stem: Why do the noble gases exist as single atoms instead of molecules?
questions.answer: they are so unreactive that their atoms do not even join to each other
choices: their atoms are too heavy to join
their atoms are too far apart to see each other
questions.explain: The noble gases hardly react with anything — not even with another atom of themselves.

questions.stem: Small pieces of lithium, sodium and potassium are each dropped into water with a few drops of universal indicator. Describe what you would see, and explain what this shows about reactivity in group 1.

acceptablePoints.point: all three fizz / give off bubbles of (hydrogen) gas / float
lithium fizzes steadily / most slowly
sodium melts into a ball and whizzes around (faster than lithium)
potassium reacts most violently / catches fire with a lilac flame
the indicator turns purple / blue — an alkaline solution (metal hydroxide) forms
reactivity increases down the group (lithium least, potassium most reactive)

award.4: any four points

markScheme.modelAnswer: All three float and fizz, giving off hydrogen, and the indicator turns purple because an alkaline metal hydroxide forms. Lithium fizzes steadily; sodium reacts faster, melting into a ball that whizzes around; potassium is the most violent and its hydrogen catches fire with a lilac flame. This shows that reactivity increases down group 1.

questions.tip: Say what you see for each metal, in order, then name the trend.

topics.title: Elements, atoms and molecules
topics.summary: Atoms, molecules and chemical symbols, and how to tell an element, a compound and a mixture apart in a particle diagram.

images.caption: Eight particle diagrams. Each circle is an atom; each colour is a different element.

facts: Everything is made from **elements**. An element contains **only one type of atom**. An **atom** is the **smallest particle of an element** that can exist.
Every element has a **chemical symbol** of one or two letters. The **first letter is a capital**, any second letter is small: Co is cobalt, but CO is carbon and oxygen together.
Some symbols come from old Latin names: **Fe** iron (ferrum), **Cu** copper (cuprum), **Na** sodium (natrium), **K** potassium (kalium).
A **molecule** is **two or more atoms joined together**. Some elements are made of molecules of the same atom: oxygen **O₂**, hydrogen **H₂**, nitrogen **N₂**, chlorine **Cl₂**.
Most **non-metals** exist as **molecules** — small ones like O₂, or **giant** ones like diamond (carbon). **Metals** are giant, regular lattices of atoms. **Noble gases** are single atoms.
A **compound** is two or more **different elements chemically joined**. A **mixture** has two or more substances that are **not joined**. (Year 7: pure substances and mixtures.)

**Reading a particle diagram:** only one kind of atom → **element**. Every particle the same, but each made of **different atoms joined** → **compound**. **Two or more different kinds of particle** → **mixture**.

**Element or compound?** An element cannot be broken down into anything simpler. If heating a substance splits it into **new substances** (copper carbonate → copper oxide + carbon dioxide), it must be a **compound**.

**Predicting properties:** small separate molecules with weak pulls between them → low melting and boiling points (often a gas, like oxygen). A **giant structure** with every atom held strongly → **high melting point** (metals, diamond).
keywords: a substance made of only one type of atom
the smallest particle of an element that can exist
two or more atoms joined together
two or more different elements chemically joined
two or more substances mixed but not joined
one or two letters standing for an element, e.g. Fe
a huge number of atoms joined in a regular pattern
a picture of the atoms or molecules in a substance

questions.stem: What is the chemical symbol for iron?

questions.stem: What is the chemical symbol for potassium?

questions.stem: What is the chemical symbol for chlorine?

questions.explain: S is sulfur. Sodium is Na, silicon Si and tin Sn.

questions.stem: Which element has the symbol Al?
questions.explain: Al is aluminium. Argon is Ar, silver Ag and gold Au.

questions.explain: An atom is the smallest particle of an element. Atoms can join together to make molecules.

questions.stem: Two or more atoms joined together make a…
questions.explain: A molecule is atoms joined together — they can be the same atoms (O₂) or different ones (H₂O).

questions.stem: Look at box B. Is it an element, a compound or a mixture?
questions.explain: Every atom in B is the same kind, so it is an element — even though the atoms are joined in pairs (molecules), like oxygen O₂.

questions.stem: Look at box D. Is it an element, a compound or a mixture?
questions.explain: All the particles in D are the same, and each is made of two different kinds of atom joined together — a compound, like water.

questions.stem: Look at box E. Is it an element, a compound or a mixture?
questions.explain: Two kinds of atom joined in one regular pattern: a compound with a giant structure, like sodium chloride.

questions.stem: Look at box G. Is it an element, a compound or a mixture?
questions.explain: G has two different kinds of particle — molecules of an element and molecules of a compound — not joined to each other. That is a mixture.

questions.explain: In A every atom is the same and none are joined — like a noble gas such as neon.

questions.stem: Which box shows an element with a giant structure, like a metal?
questions.explain: C has only one kind of atom, packed in a regular pattern — like the atoms in a metal.

questions.stem: Oxygen gas is a compound because each of its molecules contains two atoms.
questions.explain: Both atoms in O₂ are oxygen, so it is an element. A compound needs two or more different elements.

questions.stem: Why is Co the symbol for cobalt, but CO the formula of carbon monoxide?
questions.answer: each capital letter starts a new element, so CO means carbon and oxygen

CO is used when cobalt is a gas

questions.stem: A green powder is heated. It turns black and gives off a gas that turns limewater milky. What does this tell you about the green powder?
questions.answer: it is a compound, because it broke down into new substances
choices: it is a mixture of two gases
questions.explain: Elements cannot be broken down into simpler substances. The powder (copper carbonate) split into copper oxide and carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: A substance is made of small, separate molecules that are only weakly attracted to each other. What is it most likely to be like?
questions.answer: a gas or liquid with a low boiling point
choices: a hard solid with a very high melting point
a shiny metal that conducts electricity
questions.explain: Little energy is needed to pull small molecules apart, so the melting and boiling points are low — oxygen is a gas.

questions.stem: Explain how you can use a particle diagram to decide whether a substance is an element, a compound or a mixture.

acceptablePoints.point: element: only one type of atom (the atoms may be single or joined in molecules)
compound: different types of atom chemically joined together
in a compound all the particles are the same (fixed ratio of atoms)
mixture: two or more different kinds of particle, not joined to each other

markScheme.modelAnswer: In an element every atom is the same kind, whether the atoms are on their own or joined in molecules. In a compound each particle contains different kinds of atom joined together, and all the particles are the same. A mixture contains two or more different kinds of particle that are not joined to each other.

topics.title: Compounds and their formulae
topics.summary: Why a compound is different from its elements, how to read a chemical formula, and the rules for naming compounds.

images.caption: Some small molecules and their formulae. Each colour is a different element.

table.title: Naming compounds
head: Rule
Example
rows: oxygen → oxide, chlorine → chloride, sulfur → sulfide
carbon monoxide CO, carbon dioxide CO₂, sulfur trioxide SO₃

facts: Most substances around us are **compounds or mixtures**, not pure elements.

A compound has **different properties** from the elements it is made of. **Sodium** (a metal that fizzes in water) + **chlorine** (a poisonous green gas) → **sodium chloride**, the salt you eat. Hydrogen and oxygen are gases, but water is a liquid.
The elements in a compound are **strongly joined**, so you cannot separate them by filtering or distilling — it takes a **chemical reaction**.

A **chemical formula** shows which elements are in a compound and **in what proportion**. A small number after a symbol counts the atoms of **that element only**: H₂O = **2 hydrogen + 1 oxygen**. No number means one.
**Naming:** the **metal** comes first and keeps its name; the **non-metal's** ending changes to **-ide**: magnesium oxide (MgO), iron sulfide (FeS), potassium bromide (KBr).
**Prefixes** count atoms: **mono = 1, di = 2, tri = 3**. CO is carbon **mon**oxide, CO₂ carbon **di**oxide, SO₃ sulfur **tri**oxide.
Some groups of atoms have their own names: **hydroxide OH**, **nitrate NO₃**, **sulfate SO₄**, **carbonate CO₃**. A name ending in **-ate** means **oxygen** is in it too.
A **bracket** multiplies everything inside it: Mg(OH)₂ has 1 magnesium, **2** oxygen and **2** hydrogen atoms.
**Patterns:** elements in the same group make similar formulae. NaCl and KCl, so lithium chloride is **LiCl**. Water is H₂O and sulfur is in oxygen's group, so hydrogen sulfide is **H₂S**.
keywords: two or more different elements chemically joined
shows the elements in a compound and their proportions
ending for a compound of a metal with one non-metal, e.g. chloride
ending that means oxygen is also present, e.g. sulfate
prefixes meaning one / two / three atoms

questions.stem: Name the compound with the formula NaCl.
questions.explain: Na is sodium, Cl is chlorine. The non-metal ending changes to -ide: sodium chloride.

questions.explain: One carbon and two oxygens: 'di' means two, so carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: How many hydrogen atoms are there in Mg(OH)₂?
questions.explain: The 2 outside the bracket doubles everything inside it: 2 oxygen and 2 hydrogen.

questions.explain: One carbon for every two oxygens: 1:2.

questions.stem: What is the formula of carbon dioxide?

questions.explain: Elements in the same group make similar formulae, so lithium chloride follows the pattern: LiCl.

questions.explain: Sulfur behaves like oxygen, so it joins with two hydrogens: H₂S.

questions.stem: Iron is magnetic and sulfur is yellow. They are heated together to make iron sulfide. What is iron sulfide like?
questions.answer: a new substance with different properties: not magnetic and not yellow
choices: magnetic and yellow, like both elements
easy to separate with a magnet
questions.explain: In a compound the elements are joined, so it has its own new properties.

questions.stem: A compound has the same properties as the elements it is made from.
questions.explain: A compound is a new substance. Sodium is reactive and chlorine poisonous, but sodium chloride is safe to eat.

questions.stem: A name ending in '-ate', such as sulfate, tells you that oxygen is in the compound.
questions.explain: Sulfate SO₄, nitrate NO₃ and carbonate CO₃ all contain oxygen.

questions.stem: Iron filings and sulfur powder are stirred together. Then the mixture is heated strongly and glows, leaving a black solid, iron sulfide. Compare the mixture of iron and sulfur with the compound iron sulfide.

acceptablePoints.point: the mixture: iron and sulfur are not joined / just mixed
the mixture keeps the properties of each element (iron is still magnetic, yellow sulfur can be seen)
the mixture can be separated easily, e.g. with a magnet
heating causes a chemical reaction / a new substance is made (it glows: energy given out)
in the compound the iron and sulfur atoms are chemically joined, in a fixed ratio (FeS, 1:1)
the compound has different properties: it is not magnetic / black, not yellow
the compound cannot be separated with a magnet / needs a chemical reaction to split it

award.6: one mark for each point, up to 6

markScheme.modelAnswer: In the mixture the iron and sulfur are only mixed, not joined, so each keeps its own properties: the iron is still magnetic and the yellow sulfur can be seen. A magnet will pull the iron out, separating them. When the mixture is heated, a chemical reaction happens and it glows as energy is given out. A new substance, iron sulfide, forms, in which iron and sulfur atoms are chemically joined in a fixed ratio (FeS). It has different properties: it is a black solid that is not attracted to a magnet, and it cannot be separated by a magnet — only by another chemical reaction.

questions.tip: Six marks: give three points about the mixture and three about the compound, and compare them.

topics.title: Polymers, ceramics and composites
topics.summary: Long-chain molecules called polymers, and two other families of materials: ceramics and composites.

images.caption: Small molecules (monomers) join into a very long chain: a polymer.
Two composites: each combines materials so the whole has the best of both.

facts: A **polymer** is a **very long molecule** made of **thousands of small molecules** (**monomers**) joined in a **repeating pattern**. 'Poly' means many.
**Natural polymers:** **starch** and **cellulose** (in plants, wood and cotton), **proteins**, wool, silk and natural rubber.
**Plastics** are **man-made (synthetic) polymers**: poly(ethene) for carrier bags and bottles, PVC for pipes and window frames, nylon for clothes and ropes, polystyrene for packaging.

Plastics are usually **light**, **flexible or tough**, **electrical insulators**, easy to **mould** and do **not rot or corrode**. The downside: most are **not biodegradable**, so litter lasts for hundreds of years.
**Ceramics** are made by **heating clay** or similar materials to a very high temperature: pottery, bricks, tiles, china and glass.

Ceramics are **hard**, **strong when squashed**, have **very high melting points**, are good **insulators** of heat and electricity and are **unreactive** — but they are **brittle**, so they shatter when hit or dropped.
A **composite** combines **two or more materials** so the result has the **best properties of each**. Usually fibres or pieces of one material are held in another (the **matrix**).

**Reinforced concrete:** concrete is strong when squashed but cracks when stretched or bent; **steel rods** inside take the stretching. **Fibreglass:** glass fibres in plastic resin — light, strong and waterproof, for boats and car bodies.
**Carbon fibre** (carbon fibres in resin) is very **strong and light**, for racing bikes and tennis rackets. **Wood** is a natural composite: cellulose fibres in a tough natural glue.
keywords: a very long molecule of thousands of small molecules joined in a repeating pattern
a small molecule that joins up with others to make a polymer
a polymer made by living things, e.g. starch, cellulose
a hard, brittle material made by heating clay or similar
breaks or shatters easily when hit
two or more materials combined to get the best properties of each
the material that holds the fibres or pieces in a composite
can be broken down by microorganisms

questions.stem: Plastics are man-made polymers.

questions.stem: Why is plastic used to cover electrical wires?
