questions.explain: Plastic is an electrical insulator and bends without breaking — ideal around a cable.

questions.stem: Why is plastic litter a problem?
questions.answer: most plastics are not biodegradable, so they last for hundreds of years
choices: plastics dissolve in rain and poison rivers
plastics are too heavy to collect
questions.explain: Microorganisms cannot break most plastics down, so they build up in the environment and the sea.

questions.stem: What type of material is made by heating clay to a very high temperature, like a brick or a plate?
questions.explain: Pottery, bricks, tiles and china are all ceramics.

questions.stem: Which of these describes most ceramics?

topics.title: Metals and non-metals
topics.summary: How to tell a metal from a non-metal by its properties, the odd ones out, and why we choose certain metals for certain jobs.

table.title: Typical properties
head: Property
Metals
Non-metals
rows: bromine is a liquid; graphite conducts

facts: **Metals** are usually **shiny**, **good conductors** of electricity and heat, **malleable** (hammer them into shape) and **ductile** (pull them into wires). Most are solid at room temperature with high melting points.
**Non-metals** are usually **dull**, **poor conductors** (insulators) and, if solid, **brittle** — they shatter when hit. Many are **gases** at room temperature, such as oxygen and nitrogen.
Only three elements are **magnetic**: **iron, nickel and cobalt**. Steel is magnetic because it is mostly iron. Most metals, like copper and aluminium, are **not** magnetic.
**Mercury** is the only metal that is a **liquid** at room temperature. **Bromine** is the only non-metal that is a **liquid** at room temperature.
**Graphite** (a form of carbon) is an unusual non-metal: it **conducts electricity**.
To identify an **unknown element**, look at several properties together: shiny + conducts + malleable → a metal; dull + brittle + does not conduct → a non-metal.

We choose a material for its properties: **copper** for wires (conducts well, ductile), **aluminium** for aircraft (light, does not corrode), **gold** for jewellery (shiny, unreactive), **iron/steel** for bridges (strong).
Most elements in the periodic table are metals. Metals are on the **left** and middle; non-metals are on the **right**.

topics.title: Reactions with oxygen
topics.summary: Oxidation: metals and non-metals join with oxygen to make oxides — metal oxides are bases, non-metal oxides are acidic.

images.caption: Particle pictures: the atoms are rearranged, never made or destroyed.

facts: **Oxidation** is a reaction where a substance **combines with oxygen**. **Burning** (combustion) is fast oxidation that gives out heat and light.
**Metal + oxygen → metal oxide.** Magnesium burns with a dazzling **white flame** and leaves a white powder, **magnesium oxide**.
**Non-metal + oxygen → non-metal oxide**, often a gas: carbon makes **carbon dioxide**, sulfur makes **sulfur dioxide**.
**Metal oxides are bases** — they neutralise acids. Those that dissolve in water make **alkaline** solutions.
**Non-metal oxides are acidic** — they dissolve in water to make **acidic** solutions. Sulfur dioxide from burning fuels causes **acid rain**.
Oxidation can be **slow**: **rusting** is iron reacting with oxygen and water. A shiny metal that turns **dull** or dark on the surface (tarnishing) has reacted with oxygen — a **chemical change**.
In a **particle diagram** the atoms are **rearranged**: none are made or destroyed. The oxide has **more mass** than the metal because oxygen atoms have joined it.
To write a **word equation**: reactants on the left, an arrow (→, meaning 'makes'), products on the right.
keywords: a reaction in which a substance combines with oxygen
a compound of an element with oxygen
burning: fast oxidation that gives out heat and light
a substance that neutralises an acid
slow oxidation of iron, which needs oxygen and water
a change that makes a new substance

topics.title: The reactivity series and displacement
topics.summary: Metals in order of how readily they react: metals with acids make a salt and hydrogen, and a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one.

images.caption: The reactivity series: the higher up, the more readily the metal reacts.
Testing for hydrogen: a lit splint at the mouth of the tube gives a squeaky pop.

table.title: Metals in dilute hydrochloric acid
head: Metal
What you see
Reactivity
rows: fizzes fast, gets warm, metal soon disappears

facts: **Reactivity** is how readily a substance reacts. The **reactivity series** lists metals from most to least reactive: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold.
**Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen.** For example: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen.
**Test for hydrogen:** hold a **lit splint** at the mouth of the tube — hydrogen burns with a **squeaky pop**.
The more reactive the metal, the **faster** it fizzes and the **warmer** the mixture gets. **Copper, silver and gold do not react** with dilute acids.
**Displacement:** a **more reactive** metal takes the place of a **less reactive** metal in its compound. zinc + copper sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper.
If the metal added is **less reactive** than the one in the compound, **nothing happens** — copper in magnesium sulfate solution does not react.
To **order metals** by experiment: use the same size pieces and the same volume and concentration of acid, then compare how fast they bubble or how much the temperature rises.
An **unfamiliar metal** goes in the series by comparing it: if it reacts faster than zinc but slower than magnesium, it goes between them.
**Gold** is so unreactive that it is found in the ground as the pure metal, and it stays shiny for thousands of years.

topics.title: pH and indicators
topics.summary: The pH scale from 0 to 14, strong and weak acids, concentration, hazards, and indicators that tell acids from alkalis.

images.caption: The pH scale with the colours of universal indicator.

facts: The **pH scale** runs from **0 to 14**. **Acids** have a pH **below 7**, **neutral** solutions (like pure water) are **pH 7**, **alkalis** have a pH **above 7**.
The **lower** the pH, the **stronger** the acid. The **higher** the pH, the stronger the alkali.

**Strong acids:** hydrochloric, sulfuric and nitric acid. **Weak acids:** acetic acid (also called ethanoic acid, in vinegar) and citric acid (in lemons). At the same concentration, a strong acid has a lower pH than a weak acid.

**Indicators** change colour to show whether a solution is acidic or alkaline. **Litmus** turns **red** in acid and **blue** in alkali. **Universal indicator** has many colours, so it shows the **pH number** (match it to a colour chart). A **pH probe** gives an exact reading.
To tell two solutions apart, choose an indicator that **changes colour between** their two pH values.
**Concentration** is how many particles are in a given volume. **Concentrated** means lots of acid particles in the water; **dilute** means few. Concentrated is **not** the same as strong.
Acids and alkalis can be **corrosive** (destroy skin and eyes) or **irritant** (make skin red and sore). Very low or very high pH, and high concentration, mean more danger: wear **eye protection**.

topics.title: Neutralisation
topics.summary: Acids and bases cancel each other out to make a salt and water — how to name the salt, make a neutral solution, and where we use it.

images.caption: Neutralising an acid: add alkali a little at a time and stir until the indicator turns green.

facts: A **base** is a substance that **neutralises** an acid. A base that **dissolves in water** is called an **alkali** (e.g. sodium hydroxide).
**Acid + alkali → salt + water.** This reaction is called **neutralisation**.

**Naming the salt:** the first word comes from the **metal** in the alkali or base; the second from the **acid** — hydrochloric → **chloride**, sulfuric → **sulfate**, nitric → **nitrate**. Potassium hydroxide + nitric acid → potassium nitrate + water.

**Making a neutral solution:** put a measured volume of acid in a beaker with a few drops of universal indicator; add alkali **a little at a time**, stirring; stop when the indicator turns **green** (pH 7). A **pH probe** makes this more accurate.
**Indigestion tablets** contain a base that neutralises extra **stomach acid**.
Farmers spread **lime** (a base) on **acidic soil**; lime is also added to lakes damaged by acid rain. Factory **acid waste** is neutralised before it goes into rivers.
**Toothpaste** is slightly alkaline: it neutralises acids made by bacteria in your mouth, which would damage your teeth.
To **compare indigestion remedies**, use the same volume of the same acid each time and find how much of each remedy it takes to reach pH 7 — the less needed, the better it works.

a substance that neutralises an acid

questions.stem: Describe how to make a neutral solution from dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution.

acceptablePoints.point: measure a set volume of the acid (measuring cylinder) into a beaker or conical flask
add a few drops of universal indicator (or use a pH probe)
add the sodium hydroxide a little at a time / drop by drop (dropping pipette or burette)
stir or swirl after each addition
stop when the indicator turns green / the pH is 7

award.4: any four points in a sensible order

markScheme.modelAnswer: Wearing eye protection, measure 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid into a beaker and add a few drops of universal indicator, which turns red. Add sodium hydroxide solution a few drops at a time with a dropping pipette, stirring after each addition. Stop as soon as the indicator turns green, which shows pH 7 — the solution is now neutral (sodium chloride and water).

questions.stem: Plan an investigation to find out which of three indigestion remedies neutralises acid best.

acceptablePoints.point: use the same volume of the same acid (dilute hydrochloric acid, like stomach acid) for each remedy, measured with a measuring cylinder

add the remedy in equal small amounts (e.g. one spatula or a weighed mass, crushed to powder) and stir after each
count how many amounts / what mass is needed to reach pH 7 (green) — or measure the pH after adding the same mass of each remedy
the remedy that needs the least to neutralise the acid (or raises the pH most) works best
repeat for each remedy and calculate a mean to make the results more reliable
safety: wear eye protection; do not taste the remedies

award.5-6: a clear, logical method: what is measured, how the best remedy is decided, at least two control variables, and repeats
award.3-4: a method that would work, with what is measured and at least one control variable
award.1-2: a few relevant steps, e.g. 'add the remedy to acid and see the colour'

markScheme.modelAnswer: Measure 25 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid into a beaker and add a few drops of universal indicator (or put in a pH probe). Crush one remedy into powder and add it one spatula (or 0.5 g) at a time, stirring after each, until the indicator turns green, pH 7. Record how many spatulas (or what mass) were needed. Repeat with the other two remedies, using the same volume and concentration of acid at the same temperature. Do each test three times and take a mean. The remedy that needs the smallest amount to neutralise the acid works best. Wear eye protection throughout.

questions.tip: Six marks: say what you change, what you measure, what you keep the same, how you decide the winner, and repeats.

topics.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
topics.summary: Reactions that give out energy and reactions that take it in — how to tell them apart, and how we use them.

images.caption: Energy level diagrams: an exothermic reaction ends lower, an endothermic one ends higher.

table.title: Test results: four mixtures in a cup (starting at 20 °C)
head: Mixture
Start (°C)
End (°C)
Change
rows: A: iron powder + air (with salt water)
D: ammonium nitrate dissolving in water

facts: An **exothermic** reaction **gives out** energy to the surroundings, usually as **heat** (sometimes light too). The thermometer reading **goes up**.
An **endothermic** reaction **takes in** energy from the surroundings, usually as heat. The surroundings get **colder** — the thermometer reading **goes down**.

To find out which kind a reaction is: measure the **temperature at the start**, mix, then measure the **highest or lowest** temperature reached. A rise means exothermic; a fall means endothermic. Use an **insulated cup** with a lid so less heat escapes.
**Exothermic examples:** burning (combustion), **neutralisation**, **respiration**, metals reacting with acids (Year 7), iron rusting.
**Endothermic examples:** **thermal decomposition**, **photosynthesis** (takes in light energy), citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate (the fizz of sherbet feels cold).
An **energy level diagram** shows the energy stored in the reactants and products. Exothermic: products **lower** than reactants. Endothermic: products **higher**.

**Uses:** a **hand warmer** needs a large **temperature rise** (iron powder slowly reacting with oxygen); a **cool pack** for sports injuries needs a large **temperature fall**. Choose using the data — and check the chemicals are safe to seal in a pack.

A **catalyst** **speeds up** a reaction but is **not used up** — it is unchanged at the end, so a little can be used again and again. **Enzymes** are biological catalysts; a car's **catalytic converter** uses metals as catalysts.
keywords: gives out energy, usually as heat — surroundings warm up
takes in energy, usually as heat — surroundings cool down
everything around the reaction: the container, the air, the solution
graph comparing the energy stored in reactants and products
speeds up a reaction and is unchanged at the end
a catalyst made by living things
wrapped so heat does not easily get in or out

topics.title: Bonds, energy and changes of state
topics.summary: Why reactions give out or take in energy (breaking and making bonds), and the energy changes when a substance changes state.

images.caption: Melting and boiling take energy in; condensing and freezing give energy out.

facts: A **chemical bond** is the force that holds atoms together in a molecule.
In a reaction, the bonds in the reactants are **broken** and new bonds are **made** in the products.
**Breaking bonds takes in energy. Making bonds gives out energy.** (Remember: you have to pull hard to break something apart.)
If **more energy is given out** making the new bonds than was taken in breaking the old ones, the reaction is **exothermic**. If **more is taken in** than given out, it is **endothermic**.

Working it out from data: **energy change = energy to break bonds − energy given out making bonds**. Breaking 1,370 kJ and making 1,650 kJ: 1,370 − 1,650 = −280 kJ, so **280 kJ is given out** → exothermic.
Changes of state also involve energy. **Melting** and **boiling** (and evaporating) **take in** energy: particles gain energy and overcome the forces holding them together.
**Condensing** and **freezing** **give out** energy: the particles lose energy and come closer together. Steam condensing on your skin gives out a lot of energy — why steam burns are so bad.
While a substance is **changing state**, its **temperature stays the same** — the energy goes into separating (or is released by bringing together) the particles, not into making them faster.
A change of state is a **physical change** — no new substance is made, and no chemical bonds inside the molecules break. Year 7: the particle model of solids, liquids and gases.

1,000 joules — the unit used for bond energies

markScheme.modelAnswer: When methane burns, the bonds in the methane and oxygen molecules are broken, which takes in energy. topics.title: Combustion and fuels
topics.summary: Burning is a fast reaction with oxygen: how to predict the products, test for them, and compare fuels.

images.caption: Testing the products of a burning candle: water collects in the cold U-tube and limewater turns milky.
Methane burning: the atoms are rearranged, none are made or lost.

facts: **Combustion** is a reaction with **oxygen** that transfers energy to the surroundings as **heat and light**. It is **exothermic**. (Year 7: oxidation and metal oxides.)
A **fuel** stores energy in a **chemical store** that is released as heat when it burns. Examples: methane (natural gas), petrol, coal, wood, hydrogen.
Most fuels are **hydrocarbons** — compounds of **hydrogen and carbon only**. **Hydrocarbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.** methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
**Predicting products:** each element in the fuel joins with oxygen. Carbon → **carbon dioxide**, hydrogen → **water**, sulfur → **sulfur dioxide**. Hydrogen + oxygen → water (its only product).
**Testing the products:** **carbon dioxide** turns **limewater milky** (cloudy). **Water** turns blue **cobalt chloride paper pink**, or white anhydrous copper sulfate blue.
The **fire triangle**: a fire needs **fuel**, **oxygen** and **heat**. Take away any one and it goes out — e.g. a fire blanket cuts off the oxygen.
With too little oxygen, burning is **incomplete**: it makes poisonous **carbon monoxide** and **soot** (carbon), and less energy is released.

**Comparing fuels:** carbon dioxide adds to **global warming**; **sulfur dioxide** (from coal) causes **acid rain**; **hydrogen** makes only water, but it is hard to store safely and is usually made using other energy sources.

stores energy in a chemical store, released as heat when burnt
compound made of hydrogen and carbon only
blue paper that turns pink with water

topics.title: Thermal decomposition
topics.summary: Breaking one substance down into simpler ones by heating it — especially metal carbonates.

images.caption: Heating copper carbonate: the gas given off turns limewater milky.

facts: **Thermal decomposition** is a reaction where **one reactant** is **broken down** into **simpler products** by **heating**. 'Thermal' = heat, 'decomposition' = breaking down.
It needs **no oxygen** — that is how it differs from **combustion**. There is only **one substance before the arrow**.
It is **endothermic**: heat must keep being taken in for it to happen.
**Metal carbonate → metal oxide + carbon dioxide.** copper carbonate → copper oxide + carbon dioxide.
**Copper carbonate** is a **green** powder; it turns into **black** copper oxide. The gas turns **limewater milky**, showing it is carbon dioxide.
**Calcium carbonate** (limestone) → **calcium oxide** (quicklime) + carbon dioxide — done in **lime kilns** to make lime for farming and cement.
**Sodium hydrogencarbonate** (baking soda) decomposes when heated, giving off carbon dioxide — the bubbles make **cakes rise**.
In an **open** tube the solid gets **lighter**: the carbon dioxide **escapes into the air**. No atoms are lost — they are just somewhere else.

**A general rule:** the **more reactive** the metal, the **harder** its carbonate is to decompose. Sodium and potassium carbonates do not break down in a Bunsen flame; copper carbonate breaks down easily.

topics.title: Conservation of mass and equations
topics.summary: Atoms are rearranged, not made or destroyed — so mass is conserved. Using that to explain and calculate masses, and to write and balance equations.

images.caption: Count the atoms: the same number of each on both sides.

table.title: Physical change or chemical reaction?
head: Physical change
Chemical reaction
rows: Stays the same (if nothing escapes or gets in)

facts: In a **chemical reaction** a **new substance** is made. In a **physical change** (melting, boiling, dissolving) **no new substance** is made — it is usually easy to reverse.
**Reactants** go **before** the arrow, **products** **after** it. The arrow means 'react to make'.
In a reaction the atoms are **rearranged** into new substances. **No atoms are made or destroyed**, so the **total mass is conserved** (stays the same).
**Mass seems to go down** when a **gas escapes** — e.g. marble chips fizzing in acid in an open flask, or heating a carbonate.
**Mass seems to go up** when a **gas from the air joins** a substance — e.g. magnesium burning gains mass as oxygen combines with it.
In a **sealed (closed) container** nothing can get in or out, so the mass on a balance **stays the same**.
**Calculating masses:** total mass of reactants = total mass of products. 2.4 g magnesium + 1.6 g oxygen → **4.0 g** magnesium oxide.
A **word equation** names the substances: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide. A **symbol equation** uses formulae: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
**Balancing:** put big numbers **in front of** formulae (never change the small numbers) until there are the **same number of each atom on both sides**. CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.

topics.title: Inside the Earth
topics.summary: The layers the Earth is made of, from the thin rocky crust to the solid inner core, and what rocks are made of.

images.caption: The layers of the Earth (not to scale).
images.title: Layers of the Earth

facts: The Earth is built in layers. The three rock layers are the **crust**, the **mantle** and the **core**.
**Crust** — the thin, solid, rocky outside that we live on. It is thinnest under the oceans (about 6 km) and thickest under mountains (up to about 70 km).
**Mantle** — the thickest layer, nearly 3000 km deep. It is very hot rock that is mostly solid but can **flow very slowly**, like extremely thick toffee.
**Core** — made mostly of the metals **iron and nickel**. The **outer core is liquid**; the **inner core is solid**, because the pressure there is so huge, even though it is the hottest part.
The deeper you go, the **hotter** it gets and the **higher the pressure**.
**Atmosphere** — the layer of gases around the Earth: about **78 % nitrogen**, **21 % oxygen**, and small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Rocks are made of **minerals** — natural chemicals, usually in the form of grains or crystals. Quartz and calcite are two common minerals.
Nobody has dug deeper than the crust. Scientists work out what is inside the Earth from the way **earthquake waves** travel through it.
keywords: the thin, solid, rocky outer layer of the Earth
hot rock under the crust that can flow very slowly

topics.title: Igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
topics.summary: The three kinds of rock, how each one forms, and how the way it forms explains what it is like.

images.caption: Close up: how the crystals or grains fit together in each kind of rock.

table.title: The three kinds of rock
head: Kind
How it forms
What it is like
Examples
rows: magma or lava cools and crystallises
interlocking crystals; hard; no gaps; no fossils
layers of sediment are compacted and cemented
rounded grains with gaps (porous); often crumbly; layers (strata); may have fossils
existing rock is changed by heat and pressure, without melting
hard; crystals often in bands; no gaps; fossils usually destroyed

facts: **Igneous rocks** form when **magma** (melted rock underground) or **lava** (melted rock at the surface) **cools and crystallises**. Examples: **granite, basalt, obsidian**.

**Cooling speed sets crystal size.** Magma cooling **slowly** deep underground gives crystals time to grow **large** (granite). Lava cooling **quickly** at the surface makes **small** crystals (basalt). Very fast cooling makes a **glass with no crystals** (obsidian).
Igneous crystals **interlock** with no gaps, so the rock is **hard** and does not soak up water.

**Sedimentary rocks** form from **layers of sediment** (bits of rock, sand, mud or shells). The layers are **compacted** (squeezed by the weight above) and **cemented** (glued by minerals left by water). Examples: **limestone, chalk, sandstone**.

Sedimentary rocks have **rounded grains with gaps**, so they are often **porous** (soak up water) and **crumbly**. They lie in layers called **strata** and can contain **fossils**. The **oldest layer is usually at the bottom** — it was laid down first.

**Metamorphic rocks** form when existing rock is changed by **heat and pressure** over a long time, **without melting**. **Limestone or chalk → marble**; **mudstone or shale → slate**; **schist** forms at even higher heat and pressure.
Metamorphic rocks are **hard**, with crystals often lined up in **bands**. Any fossils are squashed and usually destroyed.
Rocks are clues: rounded pebbles cemented in layers on **Mars** suggest **water once flowed** there; **basalt** means there were **volcanoes**.
**Pottery and bricks** are made by heating clay in a very hot kiln. Like a metamorphic rock, the clay **changes and hardens without melting**.

topics.title: Weathering, erosion and the rock cycle
topics.summary: How rocks are broken down, carried away and laid down, and how the rock cycle turns one kind of rock into another.

images.caption: The rock cycle: how one kind of rock becomes another.
images.title: The rock cycle

facts: **Weathering** is rock breaking down **where it is**. It can be **physical**, **chemical** or **biological**.

**Freeze–thaw** (physical weathering): rainwater gets into a crack, **freezes and expands**, and pushes the crack wider. The ice melts, more water gets in, and it happens again and again until bits break off. Hot days and cold nights can crack rock too.
**Chemical weathering:** rain is slightly **acidic**. It **reacts** with rocks like **limestone, chalk and marble** and slowly dissolves them.
**Biological weathering:** **plant roots** grow into cracks and force them apart; burrowing animals break rock up too.
**Erosion** is the **movement** (transport) of the broken bits by **water, wind, ice** or gravity. As they are carried they bash together and become **smaller and rounder**.
**Deposition:** where the water slows down (a lake or the sea), the bits settle in layers of **sediment**. Over time they are **compacted** and **cemented** into **sedimentary rock**.

**The rock cycle:** heat and pressure turn rock into **metamorphic** rock; **melting** makes **magma**; **cooling** turns magma into **igneous** rock; **weathering and erosion** start it all again. The cycle takes **millions of years**.
Some changes are **fast**: a volcanic eruption, earthquake, landslide or flood can change the land in hours. Others are **very slow**: sediment builds up only millimetres a year.

Many rock-cycle changes are **physical changes** like everyday ones — melting and setting (like candle wax), mud settling out of water. **Chemical weathering** is different: it is a **chemical reaction** that makes new substances.

markScheme.modelAnswer: The igneous rock is weathered, for example by freeze–thaw, into small pieces. These are eroded — carried away by rivers — and become smaller and rounder. The layers are buried and compacted by the weight above, and minerals in the water cement the grains together, making sedimentary rock. Over millions of years this rock is buried deeper, where heat and pressure change it into metamorphic rock without melting it.

topics.title: The Solar System and the Moon
topics.summary: The Sun, the eight planets and their moons, why we can see them, and why the Moon seems to change shape.

head: Planet
Kind
Remember

facts: The **Sun** is a **star** at the centre of our **Solar System**. Its **gravity** keeps eight **planets** in **orbit** around it.
In order from the Sun: **Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune**. A way to remember: **M**y **V**ery **E**asy **M**ethod **J**ust **S**peeds **U**p **N**aming.
The four **inner planets** are small and **rocky**. The four **outer planets** are **giants** made mostly of gas and ice. Pluto is now called a **dwarf planet**.
An **orbit** is the path an object takes around a larger one. Earth takes **one year** to orbit the Sun; planets further out take **longer**.
A **moon** is a **natural satellite** — it orbits a planet. Our Moon orbits the Earth about once a month.
Only stars give out their own light. We see **planets and moons** because they **reflect sunlight**.

The Sun always lights **half** of the Moon. As the Moon orbits, we see **different amounts of the lit half**: **new moon → crescent → first quarter → gibbous → full moon → gibbous → last quarter → crescent → new moon**, about every 29½ days.

Long ago most people thought the **Earth was at the centre** and everything moved round it (the **geocentric** model). In the 1500s **Copernicus** put the **Sun at the centre** (the **heliocentric** model); **Galileo**'s telescope then showed moons orbiting Jupiter, which backed him up.

topics.title: Day, night, years and seasons
topics.summary: How the spinning, tilted Earth orbiting the Sun gives us day and night, years, seasons and changing day length.

images.caption: The half of the Earth facing the Sun has day; the other half has night.
The tilted Earth in June and December. The axis always points the same way, so in June the UK leans towards the Sun.
images.title: The seasons

facts: The Earth **spins on its axis** once every **24 hours**. The half facing the Sun has **day**; the half facing away has **night**.
The Earth spins from **west to east**, so the Sun appears to **rise in the east** and **set in the west**. The Sun isn't moving across the sky — we are turning.
The Earth **orbits the Sun** once a **year** — 365¼ days. The extra quarters add up to a **leap day** every 4 years.

The Earth's axis is **tilted** (about 23½°) and always points the same way in space. The **tilt** causes the **seasons** — **not** how close we are to the Sun (the Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January).

**UK summer (June):** the northern hemisphere tilts **towards** the Sun. The Sun is **higher** in the sky, the **days are longer**, and the sunlight is **more concentrated** (less spread out), so it is warmer.
**UK winter (December):** the northern hemisphere tilts **away** from the Sun. The Sun stays **low**, the **days are short**, and the same sunlight is **spread over a bigger area**, so it is colder.
The **southern hemisphere** has the **opposite** seasons: when it is summer in the UK, it is winter in Australia.
Day length hardly changes at the **equator** (about 12 hours all year). Near the **poles** it changes the most: **24 hours of daylight** in summer and **24 hours of darkness** in winter.
The higher the Sun, the **shorter the shadows**: midday shadows are shortest in summer and longest in winter.

topics.title: Stars, galaxies and light years
topics.summary: How huge the Universe is: stars, exoplanets and galaxies, the light year, and why the scale matters for exploring space.

table.title: How long light takes to reach us
head: From

rows: the nearest star after the Sun (Proxima Centauri)

facts: A **star** is a huge ball of very hot gas that **gives out its own light**. The Sun is our nearest star. Many stars have planets orbiting them.
An **exoplanet** is a planet that orbits a star **other than the Sun**. Astronomers have found thousands.
A **galaxy** is an enormous collection of **billions of stars** held together by **gravity**. Ours is the **Milky Way**; the whole Solar System is a tiny part of it.
The **Universe** contains **billions of galaxies**. From smallest to biggest: **planet → solar system → galaxy → Universe**.

Light is the fastest thing there is — about **300 000 km every second**. Even so, sunlight takes about **8 minutes** to reach us, light from the nearest other star about **4 years**, and light from other galaxies **millions or billions of years**.
A **light year** is a **distance**, not a time: how far light travels in one year — over **9 million million km** (about 9.5 million million km).

Choose a **unit that fits the distance**: **kilometres** on Earth; **astronomical units** (1 AU = the average Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km) in the Solar System; **light years** for stars and galaxies, so the numbers stay sensible.
Because light takes time to travel, we see distant stars and galaxies **as they were in the past**.

Space is so big that people have only travelled as far as the **Moon**. Robot **probes** take years to reach the outer planets and would take tens of thousands of years to reach the nearest star — so we learn about stars by studying their **light** with **telescopes**.

topics.title: The carbon cycle
topics.summary: How carbon moves between the air, living things, the oceans and the rocks, and how people have upset the balance.

images.caption: The carbon cycle: green arrows take carbon dioxide out of the air, grey arrows put it back.

facts: Carbon is in every living thing. The same carbon atoms are used again and again: they move between the **air**, **living things**, the **oceans** and the **rocks**. This is the **carbon cycle**.
**Photosynthesis** takes carbon dioxide **out of** the air: plants and algae use it to make glucose. **Respiration** puts carbon dioxide **back** — plants, animals and decomposers all respire.
**Feeding** passes carbon along food chains: when an animal eats a plant, the carbon in the plant's sugars, fats and proteins becomes part of the animal.
When plants and animals die, **decomposers** (bacteria and fungi) feed on them. As the decomposers respire, the carbon goes back into the air as carbon dioxide.
Sometimes dead things are buried before they rot. Over **millions of years**, heat and pressure turn them into **fossil fuels** — coal, oil and natural gas — which lock the carbon away underground.
**Combustion** (burning) of fossil fuels and wood releases their carbon as **carbon dioxide** very quickly — carbon that took millions of years to store.
The **oceans** dissolve carbon dioxide from the air. Sea creatures use carbon to build **shells**; when they die, their shells pile up and can become **limestone** — so rocks store carbon too.
A **carbon sink** is something that takes in and stores more carbon than it gives out: forests, the oceans and soil.

For thousands of years the carbon going into the air roughly **balanced** the carbon coming out. People have upset this by **burning fossil fuels** and **cutting down forests** (deforestation), so the amount of carbon dioxide in the air is **rising**.

topics.title: The greenhouse effect and global warming
topics.summary: How some gases in the air keep the Earth warm, and why adding more of them is heating the planet.

images.caption: The greenhouse effect: greenhouse gases stop some of the Earth's heat escaping to space.
As carbon dioxide in the air has risen, the Earth's average temperature has risen too.

facts: You met the air's make-up in Year 7: about **78 % nitrogen** and **21 % oxygen**. **Carbon dioxide** is **less than 1 %** — about 0.04 % — but it matters a lot.
Light from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and **warms the Earth's surface**. The warm surface then gives off energy as **infrared radiation**.

**Greenhouse gases** — mainly **carbon dioxide**, **methane** and **water vapour** — absorb some of this infrared and send it back out in all directions, some back towards the ground. So **less energy escapes to space** and the Earth stays warmer. This is the **greenhouse effect**.
The greenhouse effect is **natural and needed**: without it the Earth's average temperature would be about **−18 °C** instead of about **15 °C**, too cold for most life.
Adding **more** greenhouse gas makes the effect **stronger**, so even less energy escapes and the Earth warms. This gradual rise in the Earth's average surface temperature is **global warming**.

Since the mid-1800s carbon dioxide in the air has risen from about **280 to over 420 parts per million**, mostly from **burning fossil fuels**. Over the same time the Earth has warmed by **more than 1 °C**.
**Methane** is a stronger greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide, but there is much less of it. It comes from **cattle and sheep**, **rice paddies**, **landfill** sites and leaks from gas wells.

**Correlation is not enough on its own:** two things rising together does not prove one causes the other. Scientists are sure carbon dioxide causes warming because they also understand **how** it traps energy, and they can measure it doing so.

topics.title: Climate change: evidence, effects and what we can do
topics.summary: The evidence that people are changing the climate, what global warming does to weather and places, and how to cut emissions.

table.title: Effects of global warming
head: What changes
Why
What it means
rows: ice on land melts; sea water expands as it warms
flooding of coasts and low islands

facts: **Weather** is what happens day to day (rain today, sunny tomorrow). **Climate** is the average weather of a place over many years — usually **30 years or more**. One cold winter doesn't disprove global warming.
**Climate change** is a long-term change in climate patterns. Global warming is making climates change around the world.

**Evidence of warming:** thermometer records since about 1850; **glaciers shrinking**; **Arctic sea ice** getting smaller; **sea levels rising**; spring arriving earlier (birds nesting, flowers opening sooner).

**Ice cores** drilled from Antarctica hold tiny **bubbles of ancient air**. They show how much carbon dioxide there was in the past — and that today's level is far higher than at any time in the last 800 000 years.

**Natural causes** change climate too — changes in the **Sun's output**, big **volcanic eruptions**, and slow changes in the **Earth's orbit** (which caused the ice ages). But the Sun's output hasn't risen since the 1950s, and natural causes **can't explain** the fast warming of the last 70 years. Human greenhouse gases can.
Almost all climate scientists agree that **human activity is the main cause** of recent warming. Their conclusions are checked by other scientists (**peer review**).

**Effects:** rising **sea levels**, more **extreme weather** (heatwaves, droughts, floods, storms), **changing rainfall**, habitats lost and **species dying out**, harder farming in some places. In the UK: hotter, drier summers and wetter winters.

**Cutting emissions:** generate electricity from **renewable** sources (wind, solar), **insulate** homes, use **public transport**, cycle or **electric** cars, waste less energy, eat **less meat**, **plant trees** and protect forests.

**Weighing up a plan** to cut emissions: how much carbon dioxide does it save? What does it cost, and who pays? Does it create or lose jobs? Is it reliable? Does it cause other harm (e.g. new land for wind farms)?

topics.title: Earth's resources and recycling
topics.summary: Why the Earth's materials will run out, how recycling works, and why it matters more for some materials than others.

table.title: Recycling: for and against
head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: less mining and quarrying, so less damage to land and habitats
collecting, sorting and transporting waste uses energy and costs money
materials must be sorted and cleaned first
usually uses much less energy than making new material
some materials get weaker each time (paper fibres get shorter)
some mixtures are hard to separate (e.g. plastics stuck to metal)

facts: **Natural resources** are materials from the Earth that we use to make things: **metal ores**, rock, sand, **crude oil**, natural gas, wood, water.
Most resources are **finite** — there is only a certain amount. The **faster** we extract them, the **sooner they run out**. Metal ores and fossil fuels are finite.
Rocks you met in Year 7 are resources too: **limestone** for cement and building, **sand** for glass, **clay** for bricks and pottery.
**Recycling** is processing used materials so they can be made into new products. **Steps:** collect → **sort** (e.g. magnets pull out steel cans) → clean → melt or pulp → make new products.
Recycling means **less extraction**: fewer mines and quarries, so less damage to habitats, less noise and dust, and **less waste** in landfill.
**Aluminium** is the star example: recycling it uses only about **5 % of the energy** needed to extract new aluminium from its ore, because extraction needs huge amounts of electricity.

Recycling is **especially important** for materials that are **rare** (gold and other metals in phones), that need **lots of energy** to extract (aluminium), or that **don't break down** in landfill (plastics, glass).

Even better than recycling: **reduce** (use less), **reuse** (use again, e.g. refillable bottles), **repair**, and choose **alternative materials** (e.g. paper or plant-based packaging instead of plastic from crude oil).
Factories can cut **waste** too: sell or use **by-products** (blast furnace slag goes into roads and cement), reuse **waste heat**, recycle water, and design products that are easy to take apart.
keywords: a material from the Earth used to make products
there is only a limited amount — it will run out
processing a used material so it can be used again
getting a resource out of the ground, or a metal out of its compound
a large hole where rubbish is buried

meeting our needs now without leaving too little for the future

topics.title: Extracting metals from ores
topics.summary: How a metal's place in the reactivity series decides whether it is found pure, heated with carbon or extracted by electrolysis.

images.caption: Where carbon fits in the reactivity series decides how each metal is extracted.

table.title: Choosing an extraction method
head: Metal's place
Method
Examples
rows: found as the metal itself; just separate it from the rock

facts: Most metals are found in the ground **joined to other elements**, as **compounds** — often oxides. A rock with enough metal compound in it to be worth extracting is an **ore**. The metal compounds in rocks are **minerals**.
**Extraction** means separating the metal from its compound. The **more reactive** the metal, the more tightly it holds on to the other elements, and the **harder** it is to extract.
In Year 7 you met the **reactivity series** and **displacement**. **Carbon** isn't a metal, but it fits into the series **between aluminium and zinc**.

**Metals less reactive than carbon** (zinc, iron, copper) are extracted by **heating their oxide with carbon**. Carbon **displaces** the metal — it takes the oxygen: **iron oxide + carbon → iron + carbon dioxide**. Taking oxygen away is called **reduction**.
Iron is made this way in a **blast furnace**, using coke (almost pure carbon). In the lab you can heat copper oxide with carbon powder and get copper.

**Metals more reactive than carbon** (potassium to aluminium) can't be displaced by carbon. They are extracted by **electrolysis**: electricity is passed through the **molten** (melted) compound to split it into its elements. This uses **lots of energy**, so these metals cost more to make.
**Gold** is so unreactive that it is found as the **pure metal**. It only has to be separated from the rock around it.

**Is extraction worth it?** Think about: how much metal the ore contains, the cost of extraction (especially energy), the price the metal sells for, how much is needed, transport, and the damage mining does to land, water and wildlife.
Unreactive metals like gold and copper were the first metals people used; aluminium wasn't produced in large amounts until electricity could be used to extract it, in the late 1800s.

topics.title: The skeleton
topics.summary: The names of the main bones and the five jobs the skeleton does.

images.caption: The main bones of the human skeleton. An adult has 206 bones.

facts: The skeleton has **five jobs**: **support** (holds the body up), **protection** (skull protects the brain, ribs protect the heart and lungs), **movement** (muscles pull on bones), **making blood cells** (in the bone marrow) and **storing minerals** such as calcium.
**Skull** — protects the brain. **Vertebrae** (backbone / spine) — protect the spinal cord. **Ribs** — protect the heart and lungs.
Arm: **humerus** (upper arm), **radius** and **ulna** (forearm — the ulna is on the little-finger side).
Leg: **femur** (thigh — the longest and strongest bone), **patella** (kneecap), **tibia** (shin) and **fibula** (the thinner bone beside the tibia).
Shoulder and chest: **clavicle** (collarbone), **scapula** (shoulder blade), **sternum** (breastbone). Hip: **pelvis**.
An adult has **206 bones**. Bones are living tissue: they grow, repair and contain blood vessels and nerves.

Use the exam words for the jobs: **support**, **protection**, **movement** and **making blood cells** (in the bone marrow). “Keeps us together” or “holds us up” won't get the mark — write **support**.

A bird's **wing** and your **arm** have the **same bones** (humerus, radius, ulna) but **different jobs**: the wing is for **flying** (flapping pushes air down and lifts the bird), the arm and hand are for **lifting, carrying, holding and gripping** things.

topics.title: Movement at joints
topics.summary: Where bones meet: the types of joint, and the tissues that hold them together and keep them moving smoothly.

images.caption: The main types of joint and where you find them.

facts: A **joint** is where two or more bones meet. Without joints the skeleton couldn't bend.
**Hinge joint** — moves in one direction, like a door hinge: the **knee** and the **elbow**.
**Ball-and-socket joint** — moves in all directions: the **hip** and the **shoulder**.
**Pivot joint** — lets one bone turn on another: the **neck** (turning your head). **Fixed joints** don't move at all: the plates of the **skull**.
**Ligaments** are tough, slightly stretchy bands that join **bone to bone** and hold the joint together.
**Cartilage** is a smooth, rubbery layer on the ends of bones that stops them rubbing and absorbs shocks. **Synovial fluid** oils the joint so it moves smoothly.
**Tendons** join **muscle to bone** — that's how a muscle pulls on a bone to move it (more in the next topic).

smooth cushion on the ends of bones

topics.title: Muscles and antagonistic pairs
topics.summary: How muscles move bones by pulling, why they come in pairs, and the names and places of the main muscles.

images.caption: The biceps and triceps are an antagonistic pair. When one contracts, the other relaxes.
The main muscles of the body.
The leg from the revision sheet: D quadriceps, A hamstrings, C tibialis anterior, B gastrocnemius (with the soleus underneath).

facts: Muscles move bones by **contracting** (getting shorter and pulling). Muscles can only **pull — they can never push**.
Because they can't push, muscles work in **antagonistic pairs**: one contracts while the other **relaxes**. They pull the bone in opposite directions.
To **bend** (flex) the arm, the **biceps contracts** and the triceps relaxes. To **straighten** (extend) it, the **triceps contracts** and the biceps relaxes.

Other antagonistic pairs: **quadriceps** (front of thigh) and **hamstrings** (back of thigh) at the knee; **tibialis anterior** (front of shin) and **gastrocnemius** (calf) at the ankle; **abdominals** and back muscles.
Muscles are attached to bones by **tendons**.

Names to know: **deltoids** (shoulders), **pectorals** (chest), **biceps/triceps** (upper arm), **abdominals** (stomach), **trapezius** (upper back/neck), **latissimus dorsi** (back), **gluteals** (bottom), **quadriceps** and **hamstrings** (thigh), **tibialis anterior** (front of shin), **gastrocnemius** and **soleus** (calf).

The calf has two muscles: the **gastrocnemius** on the outside and the **soleus** underneath it. Both join the **Achilles tendon** and point the toes. The **tibialis anterior** on the front of the shin does the opposite: it lifts the toes.
**Use the scientific names** in tests: gastrocnemius, not "calf muscle"; tibia, not "shin bone". The everyday name in brackets is only there to help you remember.

a muscle gets longer and stops pulling
two muscles that pull a bone in opposite directions

topics.title: Levels of organisation
topics.summary: How living things are built up: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism — and what the main organ systems and plant organs do.

images.caption: From one cell to a whole organism. Each level is made of the one before it.

facts: A **cell** is the smallest building block of a living thing. Every living thing is made of cells.
A **tissue** is a group of similar cells working together — muscle tissue, nerve tissue, the lining of your stomach.
An **organ** is made of different tissues working together to do a job — the heart, the stomach, a leaf.
An **organ system** is a group of organs working together — the digestive system (mouth, stomach, intestines), the circulatory system (heart and blood vessels).
An **organism** is a complete living thing, made of organ systems working together — you, a cat, an oak tree.
The order, smallest first: **cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism**. A trick: Cats Taste Of Old Socks.
**Digestive system** (mouth, stomach, intestines) — breaks food down into small molecules and **absorbs** them into the blood.
**Circulatory system** (heart, blood vessels, blood) — **transports** substances such as oxygen and food molecules **around the body**.
**Respiratory system** — also called the **gas exchange system** (lungs, windpipe) — takes **oxygen** into the blood and removes **carbon dioxide**.
**Reproductive system** — produces **sex cells** (sperm in males, eggs in females) so that new humans can be made.
**Skeletal** and **muscular systems** work together for support and movement; the **nervous system** (brain, spinal cord, nerves) carries messages.

Plants have organs too: the **root** anchors the plant in the soil and absorbs **water** (and minerals); the **stem** holds the plant **upright** and carries water up; the **leaf** absorbs **sunlight** to make food by **photosynthesis**; the **flower** is for reproduction.

a group of similar cells doing the same job
different tissues working together (heart, lung, leaf)

topics.title: The microscope
topics.summary: The parts of a light microscope, how to use it, and how to work out magnification.

images.caption: The parts of a light microscope.

facts: **Eyepiece lens** — the lens you look through (usually ×10). **Objective lenses** — the lenses just above the specimen, on a turning **nosepiece** (usually ×4, ×10, ×40).
**Stage** — the flat platform the slide sits on, held by **stage clips**. **Light** (lamp or mirror) under the stage shines through the specimen.
**Coarse focusing wheel** — big movements to get the image roughly sharp. **Fine focusing wheel** — small movements to make it clear.
**Arm** — carry the microscope by this (and support the **base**). The **tube** holds the eyepiece.

To use it: put the slide on the stage, start with the **lowest-power objective**, turn the **coarse** wheel until you see the image, then the **fine** wheel to sharpen it. Then switch to a higher power.
**Total magnification = eyepiece lens × objective lens.** Eyepiece ×10 with objective ×40 = ×400.
**Magnification = image size ÷ actual size.** A cell 0.1 mm wide that appears 40 mm wide is magnified ×400.
**Why a microscope?** Cells are **too small to see with the naked eye**. A microscope **magnifies** them (makes them look bigger) so you can see their parts.

**Preparing a slide:** the sample must be **very thin** (one layer of cells) so that **light can pass through it**. A **stain** is added to make cells and their parts (like the nucleus) **easier to see** — **iodine** for plant cells such as onion, **methylene blue** for cheek cells. A **cover slip** keeps the sample flat and stops it drying out.

**Using it step by step:** (1) put the slide on the stage and hold it with the clips; (2) choose the **lowest-power objective**; (3) **looking from the side**, turn the coarse wheel so the lens comes close to the slide without touching it; (4) look through the eyepiece and turn the **coarse wheel** the other way until the cells appear; (5) sharpen with the **fine wheel**; (6) turn to a **higher-power objective** (×10, ×20, ×40) and refocus with the **fine wheel** only.

topics.title: Plant and animal cells
topics.summary: The parts of a cell, what each one does, and the three extra parts only plant cells have.

images.caption: An animal cell and a plant cell. The plant cell has three extra parts.

facts: **Both** animal and plant cells have a **nucleus**, **cytoplasm**, a **cell membrane** and **mitochondria**.
**Nucleus** — controls the cell and contains the **genetic information** (DNA / chromosomes).
**Cytoplasm** — the jelly where the cell's **chemical reactions** happen.
**Cell membrane** — a thin skin that **controls what goes in and out** of the cell.
**Mitochondria** — where **respiration** happens, **releasing energy** from food (glucose).

**Only plant cells** have a **cell wall** (made of cellulose — gives support and shape), **chloroplasts** (contain green **chlorophyll** for **photosynthesis**) and a **permanent vacuole** (full of cell sap — keeps the cell firm).
Plant cells have a regular, box-like shape because of the cell wall. Animal cells are irregular and can change shape.

plant only — cell sap, keeps the cell firm

topics.title: Specialised cells
topics.summary: Cells with a special shape or extra parts to do one job well: nerve, sperm, leaf (palisade), root hair and red blood cells.

images.caption: Five specialised cells and the adaptations that suit them to their job.

facts: A **specialised cell** has a shape or special features (**adaptations**) that suit it to one particular job.
**Nerve cell** — very **long**, with **branched ends** to connect to other cells. Job: carries **electrical signals** (impulses) quickly around the body.
**Sperm cell** — a **tail** to swim to the egg, lots of **mitochondria** for energy, and a head with **enzymes** to get into the egg. Carries **half** the genetic information.
**Leaf (palisade) cell** — packed with **chloroplasts** for **photosynthesis**; tall and thin so lots fit at the top of the leaf where the light is.
**Root hair cell** — a **long, thin extension** that gives a **large surface area** to **absorb water and minerals** from the soil. No chloroplasts — it's underground, in the dark.
**Red blood cell** — a **biconcave disc** (dented both sides) for a big surface area, **no nucleus** so there is more room for **haemoglobin**, which carries **oxygen**.

topics.title: Unicellular organisms
topics.summary: Living things made of just one cell: amoeba, euglena, bacteria and yeast.

images.caption: Four unicellular organisms. Each single cell does everything the organism needs.

facts: A **unicellular** organism is made of **one cell only**. That single cell does everything — feeding, moving, getting rid of waste, reproducing. **Multicellular** organisms (like us) are made of many cells.
**Amoeba** — lives in pond water. It moves and feeds by pushing out **pseudopodia** ('false feet') and wrapping around its food. A **contractile vacuole** squeezes out extra water.
**Euglena** — also in ponds. Has **chloroplasts** so it can photosynthesise like a plant, but swims with a **flagellum** (a whip-like tail) like an animal. An **eyespot** senses light.

**Bacteria** — very small, with **no nucleus**: the DNA floats in a loop in the cytoplasm. They have a cell wall (not cellulose), and some have a **flagellum** to move. They reproduce by splitting in two.
**Yeast** — a single-celled **fungus**. It has a nucleus and a cell wall, and reproduces by **budding**. Used to make bread rise and to brew beer (it makes carbon dioxide).
Unicellular organisms are so small you need a **microscope** to see them.

topics.title: Diffusion
topics.summary: How particles spread out from where there are lots of them to where there are few — and why that matters for cells.

images.caption: Particles spread out from a high concentration to a low concentration until they are evenly mixed.

facts: **Diffusion** is the **net movement of particles** from an area of **high concentration** to an area of **low concentration** — from where there are lots to where there are few.
It happens because particles in liquids and gases are always **moving randomly**. Over time they spread out until they are **evenly mixed**.
Diffusion is **passive** — it needs **no energy** from the cell.
The difference in concentration is the **concentration gradient**. A **bigger** difference means **faster** diffusion.
Diffusion is also faster when it's **warmer** (particles move faster), over a **shorter distance**, and with a **larger surface area**.
Examples: **oxygen** diffuses from the lungs into the blood; **carbon dioxide** diffuses out of the blood into the lungs; glucose diffuses from the gut into the blood; a smell spreads across a room.
Cells get what they need (oxygen, glucose) and get rid of waste (carbon dioxide) by diffusion across the **cell membrane**.

One alveolus wrapped in a capillary: oxygen diffuses into the blood, carbon dioxide diffuses out.

table.title: Air breathed in and air breathed out (roughly)
head: Gas
Breathed in
Breathed out

facts: Air goes in through the nose or mouth, down the **trachea**, into two **bronchi** (one to each lung), then into smaller and smaller **bronchioles**, which end in tiny air sacs called **alveoli**.
The trachea has **rings of cartilage** that keep it open, so air can always get through.

**Gas exchange** happens in the alveoli: **oxygen** diffuses from the air into the blood, and **carbon dioxide** diffuses from the blood into the air. (Year 7: diffusion goes from high to low concentration.)

The blood carries oxygen to every cell for **aerobic respiration**: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (energy is released). Carbon dioxide is a **waste product** of respiration, so the blood brings it back to the lungs to be breathed out.

Alveoli are adapted for gas exchange: **millions of them** give a **huge surface area**; their walls are **one cell thick**, so gases only diffuse a **short distance**; each is wrapped in **capillaries** (a rich blood supply); the inside is **moist**, so gases dissolve.
Blood flowing past keeps taking oxygen away and bringing carbon dioxide, so the **concentration gradient** stays steep and diffusion stays fast.
The lungs sit inside the **ribcage**, which protects them. The **intercostal muscles** between the ribs and the **diaphragm** (a sheet of muscle under the lungs) do the work of breathing.
Breathed-out air has **less oxygen** and **more carbon dioxide** (and more water vapour) than breathed-in air. Nitrogen stays the same — the body doesn't use it.

the two tubes that branch off the trachea, one into each lung (one is a bronchus)
the small tubes that branch through each lung

the tiniest blood vessel, with a wall one cell thick

topics.title: Breathing in and out
topics.summary: How the ribs and diaphragm change the volume and pressure in the chest to move air, the bell jar model, and measuring lung volume.

images.caption: Breathing in and breathing out: what the ribs and diaphragm do.
The bell jar model of breathing. Each part of the model stands for a part of the body.

facts: **Breathing** is moving air in and out of the lungs. It is **not** the same as respiration, which is a chemical reaction in cells.

**Breathing in (inhaling):** the **intercostal muscles contract**, pulling the ribs **up and out**; the **diaphragm contracts** and **flattens**. The chest gets **bigger** (volume up), so the **pressure inside drops** below the air pressure outside, and air is pushed **in**.

**Breathing out (exhaling):** the intercostal muscles **relax**, the ribs move **down and in**; the diaphragm **relaxes** and goes back to a **dome**. The chest gets **smaller**, the pressure inside **rises**, and air is pushed **out**.
Gases always move from **higher pressure** to **lower pressure**.

**Bell jar model:** balloons = lungs, rubber sheet = diaphragm, bell jar = ribcage (chest wall), glass tube = trachea, Y-tube = bronchi. Pull the sheet down → volume up, pressure down → balloons inflate.

The model's limits: the jar **can't move** like ribs (no intercostal muscles), the sheet is pulled **down** while a real diaphragm **flattens**, and balloons have no alveoli, so there's **no gas exchange**.

**Lung volume** is how much air you breathe in or out. Measure it by breathing out fully through a tube into an **upside-down bottle full of water**: the volume of water pushed out = the volume of air.
Your **breathing rate** (breaths per minute) and **depth** depend on how much oxygen your cells need. More activity → more respiration → faster, deeper breathing.

To test a claim like "taller people have bigger lungs": height is the **independent variable**, lung volume the **dependent variable**; use lots of people of the same age, repeat each measurement and take a **mean**, then plot a **scatter graph** to look for a **correlation**.

topics.title: Exercise, smoking and asthma
topics.summary: How exercise changes breathing, and how smoking and asthma harm the gas exchange system.
facts: During **exercise**, muscle cells respire faster, so they need **more oxygen** and make **more carbon dioxide**. Breathing gets **faster** (higher rate) and **deeper** (more air per breath).
After exercise, breathing stays fast for a while until the extra carbon dioxide has been removed and the body has recovered. A **fitter** person recovers more quickly.
Regular exercise makes the **intercostal muscles and diaphragm stronger**, so more air can be moved with each breath.

**Smoking:** **tar** coats the airways and alveoli and contains chemicals that can cause **cancer**; it damages the **cilia** (tiny hairs) that sweep mucus and dirt out of the airways, so mucus builds up — **smoker's cough** and more chest infections.
Smoking also breaks down the walls of the **alveoli** (**emphysema**): fewer, bigger air sacs → **smaller surface area** → less oxygen gets into the blood, and the person gets breathless.
**Carbon monoxide** in smoke sticks to **red blood cells** instead of oxygen, so the blood carries **less oxygen**. **Nicotine** is the **addictive** drug.

**Asthma:** something (a **trigger** — dust, pollen, smoke, cold air, exercise) makes the muscles round the **bronchioles tighten**, the lining **swells** and makes extra **mucus**. The airways get **narrower**, so less air gets through: wheezing, coughing, a tight chest.
A **reliever inhaler** (often blue) relaxes the muscles round the bronchioles, opening them in minutes. A **preventer inhaler** (often brown) taken every day reduces the swelling over time.
Anything that cuts the oxygen getting into the blood affects the **whole body**: cells respire less, so the person tires quickly and struggles to exercise.

markScheme.modelAnswer: During an attack the muscles round the bronchioles tighten and the lining swells and makes extra mucus. This makes the airways narrower, so less air reaches the alveoli and less oxygen gets into the blood, which makes the person breathless.

topics.title: A balanced diet
topics.summary: The seven things a healthy diet needs, what each is for, what goes wrong without them, and working out energy needs.

table.title: What a balanced diet contains
head: Nutrient
What it's for
Found in
rows: the main source of energy (sugars and starch)
bread, pasta, rice, potatoes; sweets for sugar
energy (lots of it), a store of energy, keeping warm

facts: A **balanced diet** has the right amounts of **carbohydrates, lipids, protein, vitamins, minerals, dietary fibre and water** — for **energy**, **growth** and **repair** (maintenance) of cells.
**Carbohydrates** are the body's **main energy source**. There are two kinds: **simple** (sugars) and **complex** (starch).
**Lipids** (fats and oils) give **energy** too — about twice as much per gram as carbohydrate — and are stored under the skin, which keeps you warm.
**Protein** is used to build **new tissue** for **growth and repair**.

**Vitamins and minerals** are needed only in **small amounts**. **Iron** is needed for **red blood cells** (too little → **anaemia**, feeling tired). **Calcium** is needed for **strong bones and teeth**. Too little **vitamin C** → **scurvy** (bleeding gums); too little **vitamin D** → **rickets** (soft, bent bones).
**Dietary fibre** is the part of plants we **can't digest**. It helps food and waste move through the gut, preventing **constipation**.

An **unbalanced diet** causes problems: too much energy (fat and sugar) → stored as fat → **obesity**, which raises the risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes; too little food → **starvation** and being underweight; too little of one nutrient → a **deficiency disease**.
Energy in food is measured in **kilojoules (kJ)**. The energy you need depends on your **age, sex, size and how active you are**. If you take in more than you use, the extra is stored as fat.
**Food labels** give energy and nutrients **per 100 g** — scale it for your portion: a 30 g portion has 30 ÷ 100 = 0.3 times the amount.

topics.title: The digestive system
topics.summary: The organs of the digestive system, what each one does, and the journey of a meal from the mouth to your cells.

images.caption: The digestive system.

facts: **Digestion** breaks **large food molecules** into **small, soluble** ones that can pass into the **blood** and travel to every cell.
**Mouth:** **teeth** chew food into small pieces (bigger surface area); **saliva** wets it and contains an enzyme that starts digesting **starch**.
**Oesophagus:** a muscular tube; waves of muscle squeeze the food down to the stomach.
**Stomach:** a muscular bag that **churns** food with **acid** and enzymes. The acid **kills microorganisms** and helps start the digestion of **protein**.
**Liver** makes **bile**, which **neutralises** the stomach acid and breaks fat into small droplets. The **pancreas** makes **enzymes** that pour into the small intestine.
**Small intestine:** a long tube where digestion is **finished** and the small molecules are **absorbed** into the blood through the **villi**.

**Large intestine:** **water is absorbed** back into the body, leaving **faeces** (undigested food such as fibre, dead cells and bacteria). The **rectum** stores faeces until they leave through the **anus** (**egestion**).
The blood carries the small molecules to cells: **glucose** is used in **respiration** to release energy; **amino acids** are built into new **proteins** for growth and repair.
This is an **organ system** (Year 7: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems): muscle tissue moves food along, gland tissue makes enzymes, and the lining tissue absorbs.

topics.title: Enzymes, villi and gut bacteria
topics.summary: How enzymes cut big food molecules into small ones, how villi absorb them, and the helpful bacteria living in the gut.

images.caption: Each enzyme breaks one kind of large food molecule into small ones.
Villi lining the small intestine, each with a network of blood capillaries.

facts: **Enzymes** are substances that **speed up** the chemical reactions of digestion. They are **not used up**, so they work again and again.

Each enzyme works on **one kind** of molecule (like a key in a lock): **carbohydrase** breaks down **starch** into **sugars**; **protease** breaks down **protein** into **amino acids**; **lipase** breaks down **lipids** into **fatty acids and glycerol**.
Enzymes work best at **body temperature (about 37 °C)**. Each also has a best **pH**: stomach enzymes like **acid**, enzymes in the small intestine like **neutral to slightly alkaline**.
The **small intestine** is lined with millions of **villi** — tiny finger-like folds — that **absorb** small food molecules.

Villi are adapted: they give a **huge surface area**; their walls are **one cell thick** (short distance to diffuse); each has a **network of capillaries** (rich blood supply) that carries the food away, keeping the **concentration gradient** high. (Like the alveoli in the lungs!)

**Gut bacteria** live naturally in the intestines (trillions of them). They help **break down** some food we can't digest ourselves, such as some **fibre**, make some **vitamins** (like vitamin K), and crowd out harmful microbes.
**Antibiotics** can kill helpful gut bacteria too, which may cause an upset stomach or diarrhoea.
If the villi are damaged (as in **coeliac disease**), less food is absorbed, so the person may be tired, lose weight and lack nutrients, even when eating well.

topics.title: Food chains and food webs
topics.summary: Who eats whom: producers, consumers, and how food chains join up into a food web.

images.caption: A woodland food web. Each arrow points from the food to the animal that eats it.

facts: An **ecosystem** is all the living things in an area together with their non-living **environment** — the air, water and soil around them.
A **population** is all the organisms of **one species** living in an area, such as all the rabbits in a field.
**Producers** are green plants and algae. They make their own food by photosynthesis, using light energy from the **Sun**. Every food chain starts with a producer.
**Consumers** are animals: they get their energy by eating other living things. **Herbivores** eat plants, **carnivores** eat animals and **omnivores** eat both.
A **food chain** shows what eats what. The **arrows point from the food to the animal that eats it** — the direction the energy flows.
In grass → rabbit → fox, the rabbit is the **primary consumer** and the fox the **secondary consumer**. The animal at the end of a chain, which nothing else eats, is the **top predator**.
A **predator** hunts and eats other animals; the animals it eats are its **prey**.
A **food web** is several food chains joined together. Most animals eat more than one kind of food and are eaten by more than one predator.
To **combine food chains** into a web, write each organism only once, then draw every arrow from every chain.

topics.title: Changing populations
topics.summary: Why the number of one organism rises or falls, and how that change spreads through a food web.

images.caption: Predator and prey numbers rise and fall in turn. The foxes' peaks come after the rabbits' peaks.

facts: Organisms in a food web **depend on each other** for food and nutrients — this is **interdependence**. A change in one population changes others.
The size of a population depends on the number of **predators**, the amount of **food (prey)**, **disease**, **pollution** and **competition**.

**Competition**: there is not enough of everything for everyone. Animals compete for **food, water, space and mates**; plants compete for **light, water, space and minerals (nutrients)** from the soil.

**Predator and prey cycle**: lots of prey → more food, so more predators survive and breed → more prey are eaten and prey numbers fall → predators go hungry and fall → prey recover. The predator peaks come **after** the prey peaks.
If one population falls, look **both ways** in the web: its predators may fall (less food) and its food may rise (less is eaten). Other prey may be eaten more instead.
**Environmental changes** — a cold winter, a drought, a flood, a hedge or wood cut down — change the food, water and shelter available, so populations change.
**Toxic materials** such as pesticides or oil spills can kill organisms directly, or kill their food.

A **new species brought into an area** can upset a food web: it may eat the native species, compete with them, spread disease, and often has no predators of its own. Grey squirrels from North America have pushed out red squirrels across most of England.
With population **data**, look at what changed just **before** the rise or fall — a new predator, a hard winter, a disease — to work out the most likely cause.

topics.title: Decomposers, toxins and pollinators
topics.summary: How decomposers recycle nutrients, why poisons build up along food chains, and why we need pollinating insects.
facts: **Decomposers** — mostly **bacteria** and **fungi** — break down dead plants, dead animals and animal waste.
This **recycles nutrients** (minerals) back into the soil or water. Plants take them up through their roots and use them to grow — so the nutrients go round again.
Without decomposers, dead material would pile up and plants would run out of nutrients. Every level of a food web depends on them.
**Toxic materials** such as some **pesticides** or **mercury** can get into food chains. Some cannot be broken down or got rid of, so they **build up** in an animal's body.
Each animal eats **many** of the organisms below it, so the toxin gets **more concentrated at each step**. The **top predator** gets the biggest dose and may die or fail to breed.
In the 1950s–60s, the pesticide **DDT** built up in birds of prey such as peregrine falcons; their eggshells became so thin that numbers crashed. DDT is now banned in the UK.
Humans are at the top of many food chains, so toxins can end up in **our food** — large fish such as tuna can contain more mercury than small fish.

**Insects are needed to pollinate many food crops** — apples, strawberries, beans, oilseed rape. Without pollination, the fruits and seeds do not form. (Wheat, rice and maize are pollinated by the wind.)
**Bee numbers are falling** because of pesticides, disease and parasites, and the loss of wild flowers and hedgerows. Fewer pollinators means smaller harvests, dearer food and less choice.

minerals in soil or water that plants need to grow

a chemical sprayed to kill pests such as insects
an animal, often an insect, that carries pollen between flowers

facts: **Flowers** hold a plant's **reproductive organs**. Many flowers have both male and female parts.
The **stamen** is the **male** part. It is made of the **anther**, which makes **pollen**, and the **filament**, the stalk that holds the anther up.
**Pollen** grains contain the plant's **male sex cells**.
The **carpel** is the **female** part. It is made of the **stigma** (the sticky top where pollen lands), the **style** (the stalk) and the **ovary**.
Inside the ovary are the **ovules**. Each one contains a **female sex cell**, and after fertilisation it becomes a **seed**.
**Petals** are often brightly coloured and scented to **attract insects**. **Nectaries** at the base make sugary **nectar** as a reward.
**Sepals** are small, green, leaf-like parts under the petals. They **protect the flower while it is a bud**.
Watch the spelling: the **ovary** holds the **ovules** — the ovary becomes the fruit, each ovule becomes a seed.

topics.title: Pollination and fertilisation
topics.summary: How pollen gets from flower to flower, how the sex cells join, and how seeds and fruits form.

images.caption: After pollination a pollen tube grows down to an ovule.

table.title: Wind-pollinated and insect-pollinated flowers
head: Feature
Wind-pollinated
Insect-pollinated

facts: Flowering plants reproduce **sexually**: a male sex cell (from pollen) joins with a female sex cell (in an ovule).
**Pollination** is the **transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma**, on the same plant or another plant of the same kind.
Pollen is carried by the **wind**, by **insects**, or by other animals such as birds and bats.

**Fertilisation** comes after pollination: a **pollen tube** grows from the pollen grain down through the **style** to an ovule. The **male nucleus** moves down the tube and **joins the nucleus** of the female sex cell.
After fertilisation the **ovule becomes a seed** and the **ovary becomes the fruit**. The petals and stamens wither and drop off.
A **seed** contains the **embryo** (the tiny new plant) and a **food store**, inside a tough coat. A **fruit** is the ripened ovary with the seeds inside.

**Wind-pollinated** flowers are small and dull, with no scent or nectar; their anthers and feathery stigmas hang out in the wind, and they make **huge amounts** of light pollen because most of it is wasted.
**Insect-pollinated** flowers have bright petals, scent and nectar; the pollen is sticky or spiky so it clings to insects.

**Plant breeders** use pollination for **selective breeding**: they remove a flower's anthers, brush on pollen from a plant with a feature they want, then cover the flower with a bag so no other pollen gets in.

topics.title: Seed dispersal
topics.summary: How plants spread their seeds by wind, water and animals, and why it matters.

images.caption: Five ways seeds get away from the parent plant.

table.title: Ways of dispersing seeds
head: Method
Features of the fruit or seed
Examples
rows: light; wings that spin, or a parachute of hairs

facts: **Seed dispersal** means spreading seeds **away from the parent plant**.
Seeds that drop right under the parent would **compete** with it and with each other for **light, water, space and minerals**, and be shaded by its leaves. Spread out, more seedlings survive.
Dispersal also lets a species **reach new places**, so it survives even if one area is cleared, flooded or crowded.
**Wind**: light fruits with **wings** (sycamore spins and falls slowly) or a **parachute of hairs** (dandelion) are carried far by the wind.
**Water**: fruits that are light, waterproof and full of air **float** — a coconut can drift across an ocean.

**Animals**: **juicy, brightly coloured** fruits are eaten; the seeds have tough coats, pass through the gut unharmed and come out in **droppings**, far away. Fruits with **hooks** catch on fur and drop off later.
Some pods dry out and **burst open**, flinging the seeds away (peas, gorse).
To **work out** how a seed is dispersed, look at its features: wings or hairs → wind; floats → water; juicy and colourful → eaten; hooks → stuck on fur.
Plants make **many** seeds because most land where they cannot grow or are eaten — making lots means some will survive.

topics.title: Aerobic respiration
topics.summary: How every cell uses oxygen to break down glucose and release the energy it needs.

images.caption: The word equations for respiration: with oxygen (aerobic) and without (anaerobic).

facts: **Respiration** is a set of chemical reactions in **every living cell** that breaks down **glucose** to **release energy**. In Year 7 you met the **mitochondria** — that is where it happens.
**Aerobic respiration** uses **oxygen**: **glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water**. It releases **lots of energy**.
Glucose and oxygen are the **reactants**; carbon dioxide and water are the **products**.

Glucose comes from **digested food** (plants make their own by photosynthesis). Oxygen comes in through the **lungs**. The **blood** carries both to every cell, and carries the carbon dioxide back to the lungs to be breathed out.
The energy is used to **contract muscles** (move), **keep warm**, and **build new molecules** for growth and repair — for example proteins.
**Respiration is not breathing.** Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs; respiration is a chemical reaction inside cells.
Respiration goes on **all the time, day and night**, in plants, animals and microorganisms.
When you exercise, your muscles respire **faster**, so they need more glucose and oxygen: your **heart beats faster** and you **breathe faster and deeper**.
**Limewater** turns **cloudy (milky)** with carbon dioxide — you can show that breathed-out air contains more of it.
