topics.title: Anaerobic respiration in muscles
topics.summary: What cells do when oxygen runs short, and how aerobic and anaerobic respiration compare.

images.caption: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration side by side.

table.title: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration in muscles
head: Aerobic
Anaerobic (muscles)
rows: most of the time; long, steady activity
short bursts of very hard exercise

facts: When cells cannot get enough oxygen they switch to **anaerobic respiration** — respiration **without oxygen**.
In **muscles**: **glucose → lactic acid**. No carbon dioxide or water is made.
Anaerobic respiration releases **much less energy** from each glucose, because the glucose is only partly broken down.
In a **sprint**, your heart and lungs cannot deliver oxygen fast enough, so the muscles also respire anaerobically for a short burst of energy.
**Lactic acid** builds up in the muscles: they **ache**, get **tired (fatigue)** and may **cramp**.
After hard exercise you keep breathing hard: the extra oxygen, the **oxygen debt**, is needed to break down the lactic acid.
Long, steady activities (walking, jogging, a marathon) are mostly **aerobic**. Short, all-out efforts (a 100 m sprint, a heavy lift, a jump) use **anaerobic** respiration too.
**Same:** both break down glucose and release energy, in cells. **Different:** oxygen or not, the products, and how much energy.
Some organisms live where there is little or no oxygen — bacteria deep in mud, worms in the gut, roots in waterlogged soil — and rely on anaerobic respiration.

topics.title: Fermentation: yeast, bread and brewing
topics.summary: How yeast respires without oxygen, why that makes bread rise, and how to investigate it.

images.caption: Investigating fermentation: yeast in sugar solution, with the gas bubbled through limewater.

facts: **Yeast** is a **single-celled fungus**. Without oxygen it respires anaerobically: **glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide**. This is **fermentation**.
**Plant cells** do the same when short of oxygen (for example roots in waterlogged soil): they make **ethanol and carbon dioxide**, not lactic acid.
**Bread-making:** yeast in the dough ferments the sugar. Bubbles of **carbon dioxide** get trapped and make the dough **rise**. In the hot oven the ethanol **evaporates** and the yeast is killed.
**Brewing** (beer and wine): yeast ferments the sugar from grain or grapes. The **ethanol** is the alcohol in the drink; carbon dioxide can make it fizzy.

**Investigating:** yeast in sugar solution in a **water bath**. The gas turns **limewater cloudy**, so it is carbon dioxide. **Count the bubbles per minute** (or collect the gas) to compare how fast the yeast is respiring.
A layer of **oil** on top of the mixture keeps air out, so the yeast has to respire anaerobically.
**Temperature:** cold → slow; warm (about 30–40 °C) → fastest; very hot (above about 50 °C) → the yeast is damaged and killed, so the bubbling stops.
**No sugar → hardly any bubbles**: the yeast has nothing to respire. A tube like this is a useful **control**.
**Fair test:** change one thing (for example temperature) and keep the rest the same — the amount of yeast, sugar and water, and the time you count for.

topics.title: Photosynthesis: how plants make food
topics.summary: How plants and algae use light to make glucose, what they do with it, and how to test a leaf for starch.

images.caption: The word equation for photosynthesis, and where each substance comes from or goes.
A variegated leaf before and after the starch test: only the green parts made starch.

facts: Plants and algae **do not eat**. They make their own food, **glucose**, by **photosynthesis** — that is why they are the **producers** at the start of food chains (Year 7).
**carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen**, using **light energy**.
Light is absorbed by **chlorophyll**, the green pigment inside the **chloroplasts**.
Carbon dioxide comes from the **air**, in through the **stomata**; water comes from the **soil**, up through the **roots**. The oxygen goes out into the air.

Plants use the glucose in three ways: **respire** it for energy; **build new tissue** (cellulose for cell walls, and proteins using minerals); or **store** it as **starch** (in leaves, roots, seeds, potatoes).
**Starch test:** **iodine solution** turns from **orange-brown** to **blue-black** where there is starch.
A **variegated leaf** is green with white patches. After the starch test only the **green** parts go blue-black: **chlorophyll is needed** for photosynthesis.
Before an experiment, keep the plant in the **dark for two days** to **destarch** it, so any starch you find later was made during the experiment.
**Other organisms depend on photosynthesis**: it makes the food at the base of almost every food chain, and it releases the **oxygen** they need for aerobic respiration.
Photosynthesis is the **reverse** of aerobic respiration: in daylight a plant photosynthesises faster than it respires, so overall it takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen.

topics.title: Leaves, roots and stems
topics.summary: How leaves, roots and stems are adapted to get light, carbon dioxide, water and minerals.

images.caption: A slice through a leaf, seen under a microscope.

facts: Leaves are **broad and flat**: a **large surface area** to absorb light. They are **thin**, so gases only travel a short way.
The **waxy cuticle** is waterproof and cuts water loss. The **upper epidermis** is clear, so light passes through.
The **palisade layer** is just under the top surface, where the light is brightest. Its cells are packed with **chloroplasts**.
The **spongy layer** has **air spaces**, so carbon dioxide can spread (**diffuse**) to every cell, and oxygen can get out.
**Stomata** (one is a **stoma**) are tiny pores, mostly on the **underside** of the leaf. Each is opened and closed by two **guard cells**.
Stomata let **carbon dioxide in** and **oxygen and water vapour out**. They close at night and in hot, dry weather to save water.
**Day:** photosynthesis is faster than respiration, so carbon dioxide goes in and oxygen comes out. **Night:** only respiration, so oxygen goes in and carbon dioxide comes out.
**Roots** anchor the plant. **Root hair cells** have a long, thin part that gives a **large surface area** to absorb **water and minerals** from the soil.
The **stem** holds the leaves up to the light. Tubes called **xylem** carry water and minerals up from the roots to the leaves.
**Minerals** (such as **nitrates** for making proteins and **magnesium** for chlorophyll) are not food. **Fertilisers** add minerals to the soil so crops grow well.

topics.title: The rate of photosynthesis
topics.summary: How light, carbon dioxide and temperature change how fast a plant photosynthesises, and how growers use this.

images.caption: How light, carbon dioxide and temperature change the rate of photosynthesis.

facts: The **rate** of photosynthesis is how fast it happens. With **pondweed** in water, **count the oxygen bubbles per minute** (or collect the gas) — more bubbles means a faster rate.
**Light intensity:** more light → faster, until the graph **levels off**. Then something else (carbon dioxide or temperature) is holding it back.
**Carbon dioxide:** more carbon dioxide → faster, up to a point, then it levels off.
**Temperature:** warmer → faster, up to a **best (optimum) temperature**. Hotter than that, the cells are damaged and the rate **falls quickly**.
Moving the lamp **closer** makes the light brighter. A lamp also gives out heat, so use an **LED** or a beaker of water as a **heat shield** to keep the temperature the same.
In the investigation, light intensity (lamp distance) is the **independent variable** (what you change) and the number of bubbles is the **dependent variable** (what you measure).
To **sketch** a line graph: put what you change on the **x-axis**, the rate on the **y-axis**, and draw a smooth curve. Describe it: 'as … increases, the rate increases, then levels off'.
Plants also need **water** and **minerals** to grow. Short of water, the stomata close, so less carbon dioxide gets in.
**Greenhouses** help crops grow faster: lamps add **light**, heaters add **warmth**, and burning paraffin or gas adds **carbon dioxide**.

topics.title: Variation and species
topics.summary: Why living things differ, and whether a difference comes from genes, the environment or both.
facts: A **species** is a group of living things that have more in common with each other than with any other group. Members of a species can breed together.
**Variation** means the differences between living things. There is variation **between species** (a zebra and a horse) and **within a species** (two people).
**Inherited variation** comes from the **genes** passed on by your parents — for example blood group and natural eye colour.
**Environmental variation** comes from your surroundings and the way you live — for example a scar, the language you speak or dyed hair.
Many characteristics are affected by **both** genes and the environment. Your genes set a possible height, but **diet** and health affect how tall you actually grow.
**Identical twins** have the same genes, so any differences between them are caused by the **environment**.
To decide what causes a characteristic, ask: could it be changed by the way you live? If not, it is probably inherited; if it is also passed on in families, it is probably both.

the differences within and between species

topics.title: Continuous and discontinuous variation
topics.summary: Two kinds of variation, and which graph to draw for each.

images.caption: Blood group (discontinuous) as a bar chart with gaps; height (continuous) as a histogram with a line through it.

table.title: The two kinds of variation
head: Continuous
Discontinuous
rows: height, body mass, arm span, foot length, leaf length
blood group, eye colour, tongue rolling, earlobes free or attached
histogram or line graph — bars touch

facts: **Continuous variation:** the characteristic can have **any value** within a range — you measure it. Height, body mass and hand span are examples.
**Discontinuous variation:** the characteristic can only be sorted into **categories** — you count how many are in each. Blood group (A, B, AB, O) and whether you can roll your tongue are examples.
Show **discontinuous** data in a **bar chart**: one bar per category, with **gaps** between the bars.
Show **continuous** data in a **histogram** (bars touching) or a **line graph**. First group the measurements into equal ranges, such as 140–144 cm, 145–149 cm.
On both graphs the **y-axis** shows the **number of people** (or plants, animals) in each group.
A graph of continuous variation, such as height, usually makes a **hump shape**: most people are near the middle and few are very short or very tall.
Continuous characteristics are usually affected by **genes and the environment**; discontinuous ones are usually controlled by **genes only**.

topics.title: Variation, adaptation and survival
topics.summary: How adaptations and variation help a species survive in a changing environment.
facts: An **adaptation** is a feature that helps an organism **survive** in its environment. Adaptations are **inherited** — an animal cannot choose to grow one.

Examples: a **polar bear** has thick fur and a layer of fat to keep warm; an **arctic hare** has white fur for **camouflage** in the snow; a **camel** has wide feet that do not sink into sand and stores fat in its hump; a **cactus** has spines instead of leaves to lose less water and stop animals eating it.
Environments are **always changing**: the climate warms or cools, a new **disease** or **predator** arrives, or food runs short.
Because of **variation**, some individuals in a species have features that suit the new conditions better. They are **more likely to survive and reproduce**.
Their young **inherit** those helpful features, so over many generations the features become **more common**.
A species with **lots of variation** is more likely to survive a change. A species with **very little variation** could be wiped out — it may become **extinct**.
**Extinct** means every member of the species has died out, so it can never come back.

topics.title: The reproductive systems
topics.summary: The organs of the female and male reproductive systems and what each one does.

images.caption: The female reproductive system (front view).
The male reproductive system (front view).

facts: The **reproductive system** is all the organs involved in reproduction.
**Ovaries** contain the eggs. About once a month, one egg is released.
The **oviduct** (fallopian tube) carries the egg from the ovary to the uterus. **Fertilisation happens in the oviduct.**
The **uterus** (womb) is where a baby develops. Its **lining** builds up each month, ready for a fertilised egg.
The **cervix** is a ring of muscle at the entrance to the uterus; it holds the baby in during pregnancy. The **vagina** is where sperm are received and the baby leaves the body at birth.
The **testes** (one: testis) make sperm. They hang outside the body in the **scrotum**, where it is a little cooler — best for making sperm.
The **sperm duct** carries sperm from a testis to the urethra. **Glands** add a fluid that gives sperm nutrients; sperm plus fluid is **semen**.
The **urethra** carries semen (or urine — never both at once) through the **penis**, which carries sperm out of the male's body.

topics.title: Sex cells, the menstrual cycle and fertility
topics.summary: Sperm and egg cells, the 28-day menstrual cycle, and what can make it hard to have a baby.

images.caption: A sperm cell and an egg cell (not to scale).
What happens in the uterus during one menstrual cycle.

facts: A **gamete** is a sex cell. The male gamete is the **sperm**; the female gamete is the **egg** (ovum).
**Sperm** are adapted to swim to the egg: a **tail** to swim, lots of **mitochondria** to release energy, and a **head** holding the nucleus.
The **egg** is much bigger: its **cytoplasm** is a food store for the early embryo, and its **jelly coat** changes after fertilisation so only one sperm gets in.
The **menstrual cycle** lasts about **28 days**. It prepares the female body for pregnancy.
**Days 1–5: menstruation** (a period) — the lining of the uterus breaks down and leaves through the vagina. **Days 5–14:** the lining **builds up** again.
**About day 14: ovulation** — an egg is released from an ovary and moves along the oviduct. The lining **stays thick**, ready for a fertilised egg.
If the egg is **not fertilised**, the lining breaks down and the cycle starts again. If it **is fertilised**, it settles into the lining and the periods **stop** during pregnancy.
Pregnancy is **most likely around ovulation**, when an egg is in the oviduct (sperm can survive a few days).

**Low fertility** — in males: a **low sperm count**, sperm that **cannot swim well**, or blocked sperm ducts. In females: **not releasing eggs**, or **blocked oviducts** so egg and sperm cannot meet. Age, smoking and heavy drinking can also lower fertility. Fertility treatments can help, for example drugs that make the ovaries release eggs, or **IVF**, where eggs are fertilised outside the body.

topics.title: Fertilisation, pregnancy and birth
topics.summary: How a fertilised egg grows into a baby, how the placenta looks after it, and what happens at birth.

images.caption: From sex cells to birth.

table.title: What crosses the placenta?
head: From mother to foetus
From foetus to mother
Harmful things that can also cross

facts: **Fertilisation** is when the nucleus of a sperm joins with the nucleus of an egg. It happens in the **oviduct**.
The fertilised egg divides into a ball of cells, the **embryo**. It moves to the uterus and **settles into the lining** (implantation).
**Gestation** is the time the baby develops in the uterus: about **9 months** (around 40 weeks) in humans. The developing baby is called a **foetus** once its organs have started to form.

The **placenta** is an organ attached to the uterus wall. It passes **oxygen and nutrients** from the mother's blood to the foetus, and takes **waste** such as carbon dioxide back. The two bloods **do not mix**.
The **umbilical cord** connects the foetus to the placenta. **Amniotic fluid** surrounds the foetus and **cushions** it from bumps.

**Harmful substances** can also cross the placenta: **alcohol**, **nicotine** and **carbon monoxide** from cigarettes, some drugs and some viruses. This is why pregnant women are advised not to smoke or drink alcohol.
**Birth:** the **cervix widens**, the **muscles of the uterus contract** and push the baby out through the **vagina**. The cord is cut, and the placenta comes out afterwards.

markScheme.modelAnswer: The foetus gets everything it needs from the mother's blood through the placenta, such as oxygen and nutrients. But harmful substances can cross the placenta too. Alcohol can damage the developing organs and brain. Smoking puts nicotine and carbon monoxide into the blood; carbon monoxide means less oxygen reaches the foetus, so it may grow more slowly and be born small or early.

questions.stem: Describe the stages from the production of sex cells to the birth of a baby.

acceptablePoints.point: sperm are made in the testes and eggs are in the ovaries

sperm are released into the vagina and swim through the cervix and uterus to the oviduct
fertilisation happens in the oviduct: the nucleus of a sperm joins with the nucleus of the egg
the fertilised egg divides into a ball of cells (an embryo), which settles into the lining of the uterus

at birth the cervix widens and the muscles of the uterus contract, pushing the baby out through the vagina

award.6: six of the points, in a sensible order
award.4: four points in a sensible order

markScheme.modelAnswer: Sperm are made in the testes, and eggs are stored in the ovaries. About once a month an egg is released (ovulation) and moves along the oviduct. Sperm released into the vagina swim through the cervix and uterus into the oviduct, where one sperm's nucleus joins with the egg's nucleus — fertilisation. The fertilised egg divides into a ball of cells, the embryo, which settles into the uterus lining. Over about nine months it grows into a foetus, fed with oxygen and nutrients through the placenta and umbilical cord and cushioned by amniotic fluid. At birth the cervix widens and the uterus muscles contract to push the baby out through the vagina.

questions.tip: Go in order: sex cells → fertilisation → embryo → foetus → birth.

topics.title: Natural selection
topics.summary: How competition and variation make a species change over many generations.

images.caption: Natural selection in peppered moths: on dark, sooty bark the dark moths are hidden, so more of them survive and breed.

facts: In Year 7 you met **variation** and **adaptation**. Year 8 joins them up: **natural selection** is how a species changes over time and why some species die out.
**Evolution** is the idea that the species alive today **descended from** species that lived long ago, changing slowly over **millions of years**.
Living things **compete** for resources they need: animals for **food, water, space (territory) and mates**; plants for **light, water, space and minerals**.

**Natural selection, step by step:** (1) individuals in a population **vary**; (2) they **compete**; (3) those **best adapted** are more likely to **survive**; (4) they **reproduce** and pass their **genes** to their young; (5) over **many generations** the helpful characteristic becomes **more common**.
Individuals do **not** change because they need to. A giraffe that stretches does not give birth to a longer-necked baby — only **inherited** features can be passed on.

**Charles Darwin** explained natural selection in his book *On the Origin of Species* (**1859**), using evidence such as the different beaks of **finches** on the **Galápagos Islands**. **Alfred Russel Wallace** came to the same idea at the same time.

**Peppered moths:** when factory soot blackened tree bark in the 1800s, dark moths were better hidden from birds, so they became common near cities. Since the air was cleaned up, pale moths are common again.
**Bacteria** reproduce very fast, so natural selection can be watched in a few years: bacteria that happen to be **resistant to an antibiotic** survive and multiply (for example **MRSA**).
keywords: the theory that species alive today descended from earlier species, changing over a very long time
the process by which a species changes over time as the best-adapted individuals survive and breed
a group of organisms of the same kind living in the same place
two or more living things struggling to get the same resource
something a living thing needs, such as food, water, light or space
having features that help survival in a particular environment
one step in a family line: parents, then their offspring, then theirs
when bacteria are no longer killed by an antibiotic

markScheme.modelAnswer: In the moth population there was variation: most moths were pale but a few were dark because of their genes. They passed the gene for dark wings to their young. Over many generations the dark form became the most common.

questions.tip: Go through the steps in order: variation → survive → reproduce → pass on genes → more common over generations.

topics.title: Evidence and extinction
topics.summary: What fossils tell us about evolution, and why species die out.
facts: **Fossils** are the remains or traces of living things preserved in rock — bones, shells, footprints, imprints of leaves.

Deeper layers of rock are usually **older**, so fossils in order show how living things have **changed gradually** — for example the horse, from a small dog-sized animal with toes to the large animal with one hoof today.
The **fossil record is incomplete**: soft-bodied animals rarely form fossils, and many fossils have been destroyed or not yet found. This leaves **gaps** in the evidence.
Other evidence for evolution: **watching it happen** today (antibiotic-resistant bacteria, peppered moths) and **comparing DNA** — closely related species have more similar DNA.
A species is **extinct** when no more individuals are alive anywhere. It is **endangered** when so few are left that it is at risk of becoming extinct.
Causes of extinction: a **change in the environment** (such as climate), a **new predator**, a **new disease**, a **new competitor**, **habitat destruction** and **hunting** by humans.
Species with **little variation** cope badly with change, because no individuals happen to suit the new conditions (Year 7 idea).

Examples: **dinosaurs** died out about 66 million years ago after a huge **asteroid** struck Earth; the **dodo** of Mauritius was hunted by sailors and its eggs eaten by animals they brought (rats, pigs); the **woolly mammoth** faced a warming climate and human hunters.

all the fossils found so far, in the order of the rocks they were in
when no more individuals of a species remain

topics.title: Biodiversity
topics.summary: Why the variety of life matters to ecosystems and to people, and how we can protect it.
facts: **Biodiversity** is the **variety of living things**. It can mean the **number of different species** in an ecosystem, or the **differences between individuals of one species**.
**Variation within a species** protects it: if the environment changes, some individuals are likely to survive (Year 7).
**Many species in an ecosystem** keep it stable: if one food source is lost, animals can eat others, so food webs do not collapse.

**Low biodiversity is risky.** Fields of one crop variety (a **monoculture**) can be wiped out by a single disease — in the 1840s **potato blight** destroyed Ireland's potato crop and caused a famine.

Biodiversity gives people **products**: food, timber, fibres such as cotton and wool, and **medicines** — aspirin came from **willow** bark and penicillin from a **mould**. Many medicines may still be waiting in plants we have not studied.
It also gives **services**: insects such as **bees pollinate** crops, plants make **oxygen** and help keep **water clean**, roots hold soil in place.

Ways to **preserve** biodiversity: **protected areas** (nature reserves, national parks), laws against hunting, **captive breeding** in zoos, and **gene banks** that store **seeds**, sperm, eggs and embryos frozen for the future.

**Seed banks** (such as the Millennium Seed Bank in Sussex) store millions of seeds in a small, cold, dry space. But seeds do not last for ever, and animals are much harder to keep — so protecting **habitats** is still needed.

topics.title: DNA, chromosomes and genes
topics.summary: How genetic information is packed into the nucleus, and who discovered the shape of DNA.

images.caption: Zooming in: a cell's nucleus holds chromosomes; each chromosome is a long, coiled strand of DNA; a gene is one section of that DNA.

facts: **Inherited characteristics** are features passed from parents to their offspring — in the form of **genes**.
**DNA** is a molecule in the **nucleus** that carries the genetic information. It is shaped like a twisted ladder: a **double helix**.
**Chromosomes** are thread-like structures made of **long, tightly coiled DNA**. Each chromosome holds **many genes**.
A **gene** is a **section of DNA** that controls one inherited characteristic, such as blood group.
Order of size, biggest to smallest: **cell → nucleus → chromosome → gene** (the gene is a short stretch of the DNA).
Human body cells have **46 chromosomes** in **23 pairs**: one chromosome of each pair came from the mother and one from the father.

In **1953** **James Watson** and **Francis Crick** worked out that DNA is a double helix. Their model used X-ray photographs of DNA taken by **Rosalind Franklin** (working with Maurice Wilkins) — without her data they could not have done it.

An organism's **genome** is all of its DNA. The **Human Genome Project** (finished in **2003**) read the whole human genome — about **20,000 genes**. It helps doctors find genes linked to diseases and design better treatments.

a molecule in the nucleus that carries genetic information

a section of DNA that determines an inherited characteristic

topics.title: How genes are passed on
topics.summary: How sex cells carry half the chromosomes, why brothers and sisters differ, and what decides boy or girl.

images.caption: Sex cells carry half the chromosomes. At fertilisation the full number of 46 is made again.
Boy or girl? Every egg carries an X; a sperm carries an X or a Y.

facts: **Gametes** (sex cells: sperm and eggs) carry **half** the chromosomes of a body cell: **23** in humans, one from each pair.
At **fertilisation** the nucleus of a sperm joins with the nucleus of an egg, making **46** chromosomes again (23 pairs). So you get **half your genes from each parent**.

When a body cell divides to make **new body cells** (for growth and repair), its chromosomes are copied first, so each new cell still has **46**. Making **sex cells** uses a special division that **halves** the number.
There is **more than one version** of most genes. For example the gene for blood group comes in versions for **A, B and O**.

Each sperm and each egg gets a **different, random mix** of the parent's chromosomes. So brothers and sisters **look similar** (genes from the same parents) but are **not identical** (different mixes). Only **identical twins** — one fertilised egg that splits in two — share the same genes.

Sex is decided by one pair of chromosomes: **XX = female**, **XY = male**. Every egg carries an **X**; half the sperm carry **X** and half **Y**. So the **sperm** decides, and there is a **50%** chance of a boy or a girl each time.

Some versions of a gene are **dominant**: they show even if you have only one copy. Others are **recessive**: they only show if you inherit **two** copies — so two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child.

questions.explain: 23 from the sperm + 23 from the egg = 46.

questions.stem: Why must sex cells have only half the number of chromosomes?
questions.answer: so that when they join at fertilisation the offspring has the normal number
choices: so that they can swim faster
because half the chromosomes are not needed in adults
so that the baby gets genes only from the mother
questions.explain: If gametes had 46 each, the baby would have 92 — and the number would double every generation.

questions.stem: A body cell divides to help a cut heal. How many chromosomes does each new cell have?
questions.answer: 46, the same as the original cell
choices: it depends on where the cut is
questions.explain: Chromosomes are copied before a body cell divides, so new body cells keep all 46.

questions.stem: Why are you similar to your parents but not identical to either of them?
questions.answer: you inherited half your genes from each parent
choices: you inherited all your genes from one parent
genes are not passed on, only learned
you made your own genes as you grew
questions.explain: A mix of genes from two people gives features of both but makes you different from each.

questions.stem: Why do brothers and sisters with the same parents usually look different from each other?
questions.answer: each sperm and egg carries a different random mix of the parents' genes
choices: they each have different parents' genes added later
the oldest child gets the best genes
genes change every year as the parents get older
questions.explain: Every gamete gets a different selection of chromosomes, so each child gets a different combination.

questions.stem: Why do identical twins have the same genes?
questions.answer: they come from one fertilised egg that split into two
choices: they come from two eggs fertilised at the same time
they grew up in the same house
they were born on the same day
questions.explain: One egg + one sperm, split into two embryos, so the genes are the same. Non-identical twins come from two eggs and two sperm.

questions.stem: Which sex chromosomes does a human female have?
questions.explain: Females have two X chromosomes; males have one X and one Y.

questions.stem: Which sex chromosomes does a human male have?
questions.explain: Males have an X from their mother and a Y from their father.

questions.stem: Which sex chromosome does every human egg carry?
questions.explain: The mother is XX, so she can only pass on an X.

questions.stem: Look at the diagram. What decides whether a baby is a boy or a girl?
questions.answer: whether the sperm carries an X or a Y chromosome
choices: whether the egg carries an X or a Y chromosome
questions.explain: Every egg has an X. A Y-carrying sperm gives XY (boy); an X-carrying sperm gives XX (girl).

questions.stem: What is the percentage chance that a baby will be a girl?
questions.explain: Half the sperm carry X and half carry Y, so it is 50 : 50 each time.

questions.stem: Blood groups A, B, AB and O show that…
questions.answer: there is more than one version of a gene
choices: each person has one gene in total
blood group is caused by diet
genes are the same in everyone
questions.explain: The blood-group gene comes in different versions; which ones you inherit decides your group.

questions.stem: A couple already have three girls. Their next baby is more likely to be a boy.
questions.explain: Each baby has its own 50% chance; earlier babies make no difference.

questions.stem: A recessive version of a gene only shows in a person if…
questions.answer: they inherit two copies of it, one from each parent
choices: they inherit one copy from either parent
questions.explain: One dominant copy hides a recessive one, so the recessive feature only shows with two recessive copies.

questions.stem: Two children have the same mother and father. Explain why they look similar but are not identical.

acceptablePoints.point: each child gets half their genes / chromosomes from each parent
both children get their genes from the same two parents, so they share many genes / features
each sperm and egg carries a different (random) mix of the parent's genes
so each child gets a different combination of genes
(environment, e.g. diet or lifestyle, also causes differences)

award.4: any four of the points, one mark each; the environment point counts as one mark only if the genetic points are also made

markScheme.modelAnswer: Both children inherited half their genes from their mother and half from their father, so they share many features and look alike. But each sperm and each egg carries a different random mix of the parent's genes, so each child received a different combination. Their environment, such as diet, can add more differences.

topics.title: Mutations and genetic modification
topics.summary: How a change in DNA can affect an organism and its offspring, and the arguments about changing genes on purpose.
facts: A **mutation** is a **change in the DNA** of a gene. It can happen by chance when DNA is copied, or be caused by **radiation** (such as UV light and X-rays) and some **chemicals** (such as some in cigarette smoke).
**Most** mutations have **no effect**. Some are **harmful** — for example they can make a cell divide out of control, causing **cancer**. A few are **helpful**.
A mutation in a **body cell** affects only that person. A mutation in a **sex cell** (gamete) can be **passed on to offspring** — and may then be in every cell of the child.
Some **inherited disorders**, such as **cystic fibrosis**, are caused by a faulty version of a gene passed on from parents.
Mutations create **new versions of genes**. They are the source of **new variation**, which natural selection then acts on — a helpful mutation can spread through a population over many generations.

**Genetic modification (GM)** means changing an organism's genes on purpose, often by **adding a gene from another organism**. Bacteria with the human gene for **insulin** make insulin for people with diabetes; some crops are given genes to **resist pests** or to add **vitamins** (golden rice makes vitamin A).

**For GM:** bigger harvests, more nutritious food, less pesticide, cheap medicines. **Against GM:** possible unknown long-term effects, genes might spread to **wild plants**, seed companies may control farmers, and some people think it is wrong to change living things this way.
keywords: a change in the DNA of a gene
energy such as UV light or X-rays that can damage DNA
an illness caused by a faulty gene passed on from parents
a disease where cells divide out of control
changing an organism's genes on purpose, often by adding a gene from another organism
a crop plant that has had its genes changed on purpose
a hormone that controls blood sugar; made by GM bacteria for people with diabetes

questions.stem: What is the name for a change in the DNA of a gene?
questions.explain: Mutations change the code in a gene, creating a new version of it.

questions.stem: Name one thing that can increase the chance of mutations.
questions.explain: Radiation (UV, X-rays) and some chemicals can damage DNA.

questions.stem: What effect do MOST mutations have?
choices: they always make the organism stronger
they turn the organism into a new species
questions.explain: Most changes are in parts of DNA that make no difference; a few are harmful and very few helpful.

questions.stem: Which disease can be caused when a mutation makes cells divide out of control?
questions.explain: Damaged genes that control cell division can lead to a tumour.

questions.stem: A mutation happens in a skin cell after sunburn. Can it be passed on to the person's children?
questions.answer: no, because it is not in a sex cell
choices: yes, all mutations are passed on
only if the person gets sunburnt again
questions.explain: Only changes in the DNA of sperm or eggs reach the next generation.

questions.stem: In which kind of cell must a mutation happen for it to be passed on to offspring?
questions.explain: Offspring develop from a sperm and an egg, so only mutations in gametes are inherited.

questions.stem: Mutations are the source of new versions of genes, which natural selection can then act on.
questions.explain: Without mutation there would be no new variation for natural selection to favour.

questions.stem: Name an inherited disorder caused by a faulty version of a gene.
questions.explain: These disorders are inherited from parents; infections like flu are caught from others.

questions.stem: What is it called when scientists change an organism's genes on purpose, for example by adding a gene from another species?
questions.explain: In GM, scientists choose a gene and put it into another organism's DNA.

questions.stem: Bacteria have been given a human gene so that they make which hormone for people with diabetes?
questions.explain: GM bacteria grown in large tanks make pure human insulin cheaply.

questions.stem: Which of these is an argument FOR growing GM crops?
questions.answer: they can give bigger harvests and need less pesticide
choices: genes might spread to wild plants
the long-term effects are not fully known
questions.explain: Pest-resistant crops lose less to insects, so farmers get more food with fewer sprays.

questions.stem: Which of these is an argument AGAINST growing GM crops?
questions.answer: the new genes might spread to wild plants
choices: they can be made more nutritious
they can grow in drier conditions
questions.explain: Pollen can carry genes to related wild plants, with effects that are hard to predict.

questions.stem: Golden rice has been modified to make a vitamin that many children in poorer countries lack. Which vitamin?
questions.explain: Lack of vitamin A can cause blindness; golden rice makes a substance the body turns into vitamin A.

questions.stem: Genetic modification and natural selection are the same thing.
questions.explain: Natural selection happens in nature over many generations; GM is a deliberate change made by scientists in one step.

questions.stem: Explain how a mutation in a sex cell could affect a person's future children.

acceptablePoints.point: a mutation is a change in the DNA / a gene
the sex cell (sperm or egg) is used to make the child, so the mutation is passed on / inherited
the changed gene is copied into every cell of the child
it may have no effect, be harmful (e.g. an inherited disorder), or occasionally be helpful

award.3: any three of the points, one mark each

markScheme.modelAnswer: A mutation is a change in a gene's DNA. If it happens in a sperm or egg and that cell is used at fertilisation, the child inherits the changed gene, and it is copied into every one of the child's cells. It might have no effect, it might cause an inherited disorder, or very rarely it could be helpful.

questions.stem: Scientists have made a GM crop that resists insect pests. Give arguments for and against growing it.

acceptablePoints.point: for: less of the crop is eaten by pests, so bigger harvests / more food
for: farmers need less pesticide, which is better for other wildlife / cheaper
against: the gene could spread to wild plants (e.g. by pollen)
against: long-term effects on health or the environment are not fully known
against: may harm insects that are not pests / reduce food for other animals / biodiversity
against: seed may be expensive or controlled by a few companies; some people think it is wrong

award.4: four points including at least one for and one against; if all are on one side, maximum 2

markScheme.modelAnswer: For: the crop loses less to insects, so farmers get bigger harvests and need to spray less pesticide, which saves money and harms less wildlife. Against: the new gene might spread to wild plants through pollen, the long-term effects are not fully known, and fewer insects may mean less food for birds. Some people also worry that a few companies control the seeds.

questions.tip: Give both sides — at least one point for and one against.

topics.title: Types of enquiry
topics.summary: The different ways scientists answer questions — and how to tell which one a question needs.

table.title: Types of enquiry
head: Type
What you do
Example question
rows: change one variable, keep the others the same, measure what happens
Does the temperature of water change how fast sugar dissolves?
look closely, sometimes over time or with a microscope, and record what you see
What parts of a cell can I see under a light microscope?
collect lots of data where you can't control everything, and look for a link
Do people with longer legs jump further?
sort things into groups by their features, often with a key
Which group does this animal belong to?
find out from books, websites or experts
What did Robert Hooke see with his microscope?

facts: A **fair test** changes **one** thing and keeps everything else the same, so you know what caused the result.
The variable you **change** is the **independent variable**; the one you **measure** is the **dependent variable**; the ones you keep the same are **control variables**.
An **observation** enquiry means looking carefully and recording what you see — for example cells under a microscope, or a plant growing over a week.
**Pattern seeking** looks for a link in lots of data when you can't control the other variables — for example surveys of people.
Clue words: “Does … affect …?” → fair test. “What can I see …?” → observation. “Do people/things that … also …?” → pattern seeking.
keywords: change one variable, keep the rest the same
look for a link in lots of data

questions.stem: What type of enquiry is this question: “What parts of an onion cell can I see under a microscope?”
questions.explain: You look and record what you see — observation.

questions.stem: What type of enquiry is this question: “Does the temperature of water affect how fast salt dissolves?”
questions.explain: Change one thing (temperature), keep the rest the same, measure — a fair test.

questions.stem: What type of enquiry is this question: “Do people with bigger hands have bigger feet?”
questions.explain: You can't change people's hands — you collect lots of data and look for a link.

questions.stem: What type of enquiry is this: sorting leaves into groups with a key?
questions.explain: Sorting into groups by features is identifying and classifying.

questions.stem: In a fair test, what do you call the variable you change?
questions.explain: Independent = the one you choose to change.

questions.stem: In a fair test, what do you call the variable you measure?
questions.explain: Dependent = it depends on what you changed.

questions.stem: What are the variables you keep the same in a fair test called?
questions.explain: Keeping them the same makes the test fair.

questions.stem: In a fair test you change two things at once to save time.
questions.explain: False — change only one thing, or you can't tell which one caused the result.
